London Fashion Week 2026: The five trends we'll see in spring

BBC News Mon, 21 Sep 2026 16:23:25 GMT

This London Fashion Week has been about return and renewal - as two of Britain's biggest designers showcased their spring/summer 2027 designs.

The first was Alexander McQueen, which as a brand moved to London after 25 years of showing in Paris - something Laura Weir, CEO of the British Fashion Council, told the BBC was "quite a big deal for us".

Creative director Seán McGirr brought the brand back to its roots, with a runway of devil horns, lace corsets and chainmail skull dresses.

Mulberry was the second designer to make its big return, this time after a nine-year absence, with Christopher Kane's debut collection centring around the brand's Baywater bag, while going big on leather in the form of coats, skirts and loafers.

Weir says the "big mission" for her and her team this season was to "re-platform London Fashion Week as not only a home for British design, but an engine for creativity and commercial growth".

Here are some of the major trends to come out of London Fashion Week 2026:

"The number one trend for this season is messy girl," says Elektra Kotsoni, deputy director for Vogue Business and Vogue Runway, whose team predicts the trends ahead of each season.

She tells the BBC: "We're going to be having a messy girl summer" and says "it's a reaction to the clean girl and quite luxury aesthetics that took over our Instagram feeds," last year.

Kotsoni says as "the world is quite messy" this form of dressing is a sign of "resilience" and rebellion.

She says if you are looking to replicate this trend, mix pastel colours, dreamy florals, and tactile materials to form "unexpected clashes" that "look really messy".

This form of what Kotsoni calls "crazy styling" was on display at London Fashion Week - with the noisy clashes at Chopova Lowena, Sinead Gorey and Conner Ives.

According to Kotsoni - gardening is officially cool in the fashion world.

A new twist on the cottage-core looks that emerged post-pandemic, instead of gingham, wicker bags and sourdough starters, it's all about looking like you're fresh from planting seeds or operating a lawnmower.

"There are lots of gardening appropriate silhouettes on the runways," she says, including aprons, waterproof materials and trench coats.

It started with Spanish fashion house Loewe launching a watering can-shaped handbag a couple of months ago and has now translated on the runway with Erdem, Yuhan Wang and Bora Aksu.

Kotsoni says "fashion is always a reflection of what's happening in the world" and likes how designers have been able to "take an interest like gardening and present it as something" tangible in a fashion show.

Whilst some designers have been taking cues from the great outdoors - others have been inspired by film.

Another key trend identified by Kotsoni's team is the idea of the modern goddess - a take on the styles of Ancient Greece and a nod to Christopher Nolan's hit film The Odyssey this summer.

Kotsoni says the items to look out for are "draped garments, breezy materials and lots of bohemian and flowy silhouettes".

Pauline Dujancourt's London Fashion Week show epitomised this style - focusing on maximum volume and billowing fabrics.

Kotsoni says these looks are in opposition to how guests themselves have been dressing at this fashion week, suggesting a turning of the tide.

"Everybody has been dressed really minimalist in a specific quiet luxury way and I think people are tired of that," she notes.

Whether your preference is melon, tangerine, ginger or coral - orange appears to be the big colour trend for next year.

Kotsoni says she is hedging her bets on whether a shade of orange will be Pantone's colour of the year for 2027 as it has already been making its way into celebrity styling (it's not too late to replicate Kylie Jenner and Timothée Chalamet's matching neon outfits at the Marty Supreme premiere for Halloween) and on the runway.

Mulberry, Justin Cassin, Enny Atelier and Vin + Omi all featured orange in their London shows and presentations over the last couple of days.

Ever the fashion muse, Chalamet is once again at the centre of another trend for 2027 - ballet.

After he said "no one cares" about the discipline in May this year, Kotsoni says she "thinks it's interesting" that it's now being forged as a clear trend for next year.

Edeline Lee put on a striking show in London - complete with models taking to the runway en pointe in a transformed school sports hall.

"Ballet is very much in fashion," she says, noting that this month's Vogue Italia has La Scala's principle dancer Roberto Bolle on the cover, whilst Royal Ballet dancer Francesca Hayward has recently been modelling for Armani and Chanel.

"Ballet flats are massive and still will be [next year] and small silhouettes for shoes are going to be prevalent next season," Kotsoni adds - encouraging fans of the style to seek out items in charity and vintage shops if they want to replicate the look.

Was Neville right to call out Man Utd for a 'lack of effort'?

BBC News Mon, 21 Sep 2026 15:39:36 GMT

Gary Neville started for Sky Sports as a pundit and co-commentator in 2011

"I've watched Manchester United since the age of five and that's the worst 15 minutes I've ever seen. Absolutely pathetic."

Gary Neville did not hold back in his criticism of Manchester United's performance during Sky Sports' coverage of Sunday's 1-1 draw at Fulham.

The players had just laboured through the opening stages of the second half, culminating in a Lisandro Martinez own goal gifting the home side the lead.

"I've never seen such a lack of effort," Neville added. "What must Michael Carrick be thinking?"

Neville played 602 games for United over a 19-year career, winning everything the club game had to offer. So his criticism comes from a qualified position.

This season's out-of-possession stats would appear to back it up too, with the Red Devils ranking 16th for distance covered, and 17th for total number of sprints.

But does that tell the whole story?

How did United play under Carrick when they were winning games towards the end of last season?

And, as Neville makes the headlines, what does this say about his influence in the media around Manchester United?

This video can not be played

Cunha's late strike denies Fulham first league win of the season

United's dismal running and sprinting stats made for stark reading in the wake of Neville's criticism.

After all, the former right-back had directly questioned a lack of effort, and referred to the players as "mannequins".

He said United - and Fulham - were walking too much during the game.

In the Premier League this season only four teams have covered less distance than the Red Devils, and just three teams have produced fewer sprints.

It comes alongside United's joint-worst start to a Premier League season, with four points from five games.

So is this down to the running and the effort?

Let's take a look at the second half of last season, after Carrick had been appointed as manager.

Between 17 January and the end of the season, United picked up more points than any other team - 39 points from 17 games.

Yet only four teams ran less than United, and only two clubs had fewer sprints.

There is no material difference in the running stats, but United were returning 2.29 points per game compared to the 0.8 this season.

Something is clearly different, but it does not appear to be linked to this particular stat because barely anything has changed - apart from the results. Maybe this United squad simply does not have runners.

Then there is the comparison to rival teams.

Manchester City have won all five Premier League matches but have covered less distance than United. Enzo Maresca's squad have also recorded the lowest number of sprints in the division.

Brighton, one of the most exciting teams in the league this season and the top goalscorers, are one place above United for sprints.

Maybe United's problem is tactical rather than a simple case of not running enough?

Neville setting the media agenda when it comes to United is not a new thing.

The former England international has called out the team's shortcomings on many occasions.

Look back to December 2021, and a poor first-half performance against a struggling Newcastle side when Ralf Rangnick's side trailed 1-0 at the break.

"They're a bunch of whinge-bags," Neville said at half-time on Sky Sports. "I'll not go into names but they're whinging at each other, arms up in the air complaining about everything.

"There's no pressing, no urgency, the basics of the game."

Edinson Cavani rescued a point at St James' Park, but Neville's comments had already made the headlines.

You only need to look at how the post-match coverage went after the Fulham draw.

Neville's remarks were put to Carrick at full-time. The United manager said fitness levels of his players were not an issue.

But the die was cast.

"Neville: That was the worst ever", read the back page of Monday's Daily Telegraph.

"15 minutes of shame", was the lead for the sports section of the Daily Star.

"United boss keeps calm after Neville Ful blast," said the Daily Express.

It was picked up across online media, and discussed at length on radio talk shows - including across the BBC, as evidenced by this piece.

This video can not be played

Carrick impressed Man Utd 'kept belief' to earn draw at Fulham

When Neville criticises his former club, it carries weight.

In January, with Ruben Amorim under pressure for poor results, the Portuguese head coach said that "if people cannot handle the Gary Nevilles and the criticisms of everything, we need to change the club".

Amorim was dismissed the following day.

There always seems to be a strong influence in the media related to the dominant team of a previous era.

For example, throughout the 1990s and 2000s, former Liverpool stars such as Alan Hansen, Mark Lawrenson and Phil Thompson dominated a lot of the conversation.

It stands to reason that now members of the all-conquering United squad will have a leading role in the media.

But for Neville, it is bigger than anyone apart from Gary Lineker and his Goalhanger production company.

How Lineker and Neville became rival media moguls

Neville calls Man Utd 'pathetic' - but Carrick maintains belief

'I've asked for forgiveness' - Eckert and Southampton braced for Spygate verdict

"When does Sky wonder if they are paying a lot of money in wages to train their next competitor?"

It is a question posed by Richard Gillis, who hosts the Unofficial Partner sports business podcast.

While Neville started out in the media as a pundit with Sky Sports, the 51-year-old is now one of the biggest players in a rapidly changing industry.

After co-founding the sports entertainment production company Buzz16 in 2016, Neville launched YouTube platform The Overlap in 2021.

The Overlap produces Stick to Football - one of the UK's most popular football content channels with 2.2 billion views across all platforms in 2025.

Earlier this year it entered into a strategic partnership with radio giants Global, with the aim to create a multi-format sports media network.

Neville this summer exited Buzz16, focusing his attention on The Overlap, which has branched out into cricket and rugby, and secured live Bundesliga rights.

The YouTube channels of United influencer Mark Goldbridge were recently acquired, a further sign of the influence Neville now wields in football's media industry.

Goldbridge made his name with expletive-laden rants during streamed 'watchalongs' of United matches, and his channels have about four million subscribers.

Gillis points out that Neville was attracted to the Goldbridge brand, and his United Stand podcast, because it creates noise when there is no football.

"Noise is valuable," Gillis told BBC Sport. "Man Utd generate more of it than any other club in the Premier League.

"Anger creates engagement. And from the Sky commentary box, Neville is well placed to create anger."

In a bid to ramp up its content, The Overlap is believed to have targeted national newspaper journalists to come on board and cover United.

"It poses questions," Gillis says of this development.

"Currently, Neville is the story. He says something, the media reports it, the fans respond to it. A valuable loop.

"At what point does The Overlap and the United Stand [a Goldbridge channel] become the rivals of the media?

"What is the United Stand now? A noise merchant, or a news organisation?"

To many, it probably does not matter whether Neville's comments about United's running are valid or not.

They create headlines, column inches and legitimate talking points under the Sky Sports name.

Yet Neville is himself a media mogul who also works within another organisation.

And at present, when measured by media coverage and impact, all parties are winners.

Xhaka under investigation over Covid-19 certificate

BBC News Mon, 21 Sep 2026 15:24:51 GMT

Granit Xhaka captained Switzerland at the World Cup earlier this year

Switzerland captain Granit Xhaka is under investigation by Swiss prosecutors over allegations he obtained a forged Covid-19 vaccination certificate.

The 33-year-old is alleged to have obtained the certificate in 2022, when it was a requirement in Switzerland for some travel abroad.

The public prosecutor's office of the city of Lucerne confirmed the investigation was under way to determine whether any criminal behaviour took place in obtaining a "false or forged" certificate.

The Sunderland midfielder, who was playing for Arsenal at the time, posted a statement on social media on Monday saying he had a "mistrust" towards the vaccine and had been "influenced by worries and uncertainty".

He said: "In this troubled state of mind I acquired a vaccine certificate, instead of clarifying my unanswered questions in the proper way.

"Today I see clearly, that this way was not correct. It was a mistake. I'm sorry.

"I take responsibility for this decision, will engage with the process of establishing the facts and fully co-operate with the relevant authorities."

The Swiss office of public health confirmed that while there was never a general legal requirement to obtain or hold such a certificate, it was needed for access to various activities, venues and travel, meaning that participation was restricted for anyone who did not possess one.

These measures in Switzerland were in place until spring 2022. After that point, Covid-19 certificates continued to be issued, primarily to enable members of the public to meet entry requirements when travelling abroad.

It is unclear what punishments Xhaka could face, but in 2023 the then Switzerland men's ice hockey coach Patrick Fischer was found guilty of using a fake Covid-19 certificate to work at the 2022 Winter Olympics ‌in Beijing.

Fischer was fined 38,000 Swiss francs by a criminal court. In April this year, he was sacked from the Switzerland job and earlier this month, he was banned for four years by the International Ice Hockey Federation.

The Swiss Football Association said Xhaka, the country's record appearance holder with 152 caps, had withdrawn from the Swiss camp for their upcoming Nations League matches against Scotland, North Macedonia and Slovenia following his statement.

It added the decision to withdraw had been made jointly by the player and management and that they would discuss Xhaka's future with the team after the international window.

Switzerland have away fixtures against North Macedonia and Scotland on 26 and 29 September, before facing Slovenia and North Macedonia at home in early October.

Sunderland boss Regis le Bris refused to comment on the allegations following the Black Cats' defeat at Manchester City on Sunday.

"It is not my area to speak about those problems or situations," he said. "My area is football. About football, he is really good."

Xhaka captained Switzerland at the World Cup earlier this year, where they were knocked out in the quarter-finals by eventual runners-up Argentina.

Yemenis flee across Red Sea as Houthis and Saudi-backed forces escalate war

BBC News Mon, 21 Sep 2026 14:14:16 GMT

Ibrahim Issa, 50, is from the Yemeni coastal town of Dhubab, right on the front lines of the war between Yemen's Houthis and the Saudi-backed pro-government forces fighting them.

Today he sits, surrounded by his family, on a tarpaulin spread over a sandy floor inside a vast open-sided warehouse at Markazi camp in Obock, northern Djibouti, packed with Yemeni families who have fled by boat across the narrow Bab al-Mandab Strait.

After their sea crossing, Yemeni refugees have made their way by truck and on foot to this camp, jointly administered by the government and the UN.

"How could I just sit there when my kids are screaming and shaking in terror?" says Ibrahim Issa. "When the sound of the planes start, and the kids hear the planes, they begin shouting and screaming. As parents it is our responsibility, what can you do when you see this? That is why we fled, to save them."

As a fisherman, Ibrahim Issa already owned a boat large enough to bring out his family from Yemen.

He even brought several of the family's goats which I can now see nibbling at scraps nearby, foraging amidst the discarded canisters of cooking gas and empty plastic bottles. Some families have been able to bring small bundles of possessions with them from Yemen – one family has even brought a "jeraak", a tall metal shisha pipe – but others have arrived, exhausted, in just the clothes they left in.

In just the last few days more than 3,000 refugees have arrived here from Yemen, many entire families. The UN estimates that in all, more than 120,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the sudden surge in fighting along Yemen's Red Sea coast.

This month, the country's Houthis, who had already seized most of the populated parts of Yemen years ago, made a lightning dash down the coast towards Bab al-Mandab, the narrow, maritime chokepoint where the southern Red Sea flows into the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean.

Saudi Arabia, which backs the internationally recognised government of Yemen, has responded with hundreds of air strikes along the flat, coastal plain where the Houthis are now digging in. The Houthis have also launched hundreds of drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia.

"We don't care which side it is that's attacking," is the message I got loud and clear in Arabic from everyone here I spoke to. "It's the bombs falling all around us that have caused us to flee."

Djibouti, a tiny former French colony that sits just across the water from Yemen, has made it clear it has no intention of involving itself in the war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.

And yet Djibouti is one of the most militarised nations in Africa. Since 2003, the US has run a huge multinational base here, Camp Lemonnier, once home to the French Foreign Legion. China too has a major base here, its largest military presence on the Indian Ocean and recently upgraded.

Back in Markazi camp, one of those I spoke to is Qassim Abraham Abssy. Once also a fisherman, his identity card shows him to be 100 years old.

"What led us to come here?" he asks rhetorically.

"It was the planes. The sounds of the planes, boom! That's what made us flee, for the sake of our children. It burns ours hearts. We don't know which side they are from. They are bombing everywhere, because the Houthis are everywhere, in the mountains, in the roads. A plane comes, bombs everywhere."

Outside in the blazing 37C heat, close to the neat lines of tents supplied by the UN refugee agency, UNHCR, I met Mohammed Abdullarim from Aden, a 63-year-old former tour guide old enough to have been born when Aden was still a British protectorate.

Unlike the new arrivals, Mohammed has been here since 2015. He fled to Djibouti soon after the fighting first flared up between the Houthis and the government of the now-ousted President Abdrabbuh Mansour Hadi.

He has been at the camp ever since but suddenly, as we were talking, the sadness of what is happening to his country overwhelmed him and he turned his head away, choking back tears.

"Most of the people here are in the worst condition, inside the tents here. I am very touched, I'm crying for these people, for my people, for their suffering. I want our voices to be heard by the NGOs and the Djibouti government. And I'm thankful to them for accepting us."

How long will they have to stay here? That depends, of course, on the fighting. Yemen has been wracked by a horrific civil war that has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced millions since 2014.

A shaky, UN-brokered 2022 truce between the Saudis and the Houthis has broken down spectacularly in recent months, with the two sides trading missiles, drones and air strikes.

Yemen's war may be a remote one to most people but the effect of choking off Saudi Arabia's oil exports through the Bab al-Mandab Strait are well publicised. But as ever, it is often the human cost that goes unnoticed.

Sitting beside his wife on their tarpaulin, amid the cacophony all around them, Qassim Abssy the fisherman is wary of leaving the safety of Djibouti: "If the war continues then we're not going back because we have peace here."

His wife, Aisha Abdulkadir Mohammed, agrees. "We are willing to go back in peace if peace returns to our country, and we are praying to God that peace does return. All we need is peace, even for our children's future, they get safety first, then food, water and an education.

"As you see we just fled with our clothes, and left everything behind, because [in Yemen] there is no peace."

Merz's political crisis threatens Germany's obsession with stability

BBC News Mon, 21 Sep 2026 13:30:45 GMT

Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz is a political record-breaker.

The problem for him is these records are overwhelmingly negative and he is at risk of losing his job over them.

The problem for the EU and for Europe more broadly is this has a destabilising effect far further afield.

At a paltry 13%, Merz's popularity rating is the lowest for any German chancellor since polling began.

German voters' ardour for him started lower and fell faster than any of his predecessors. The former corporate lawyer is perceived by many to be arrogant and out of touch with their problems.

He has only been in government for 16 months but under his chairmanship, Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Unionist (CDU) party has suffered three very poor showings in regional elections over the last couple of weeks.

The state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern broke another record on Sunday according to preliminary results: Merz's conservative CDU party did not even reach the 5% threshold to enter the regional parliament.

Conversely, the anti-immigration, nationalist right Alternative for Germany (AfD) - a political party Merz had promised to slash support for when he was running for CDU leadership - has performed spectacularly well.

It became the biggest political faction in two out of those three recent state elections and broke another record: they have a chance at governing in one of those states, Saxony Anhalt, despite the German authorities labelling them in part anti-democratic and far-right extremist.

The AfD also tops opinion polls nationally, a particularly sensitive issue for Germany after its Nazi past.

The party rejects the far-right label. Its German name, Alternative fuer Deutschland, means Alternative for Germany. That is exactly what they say voters now want.

Following this month's regional election surge in success for the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, plus its gains in Berlin - where the victors were the hard left Die Linke party - AfD co-leader Alice Weidel said on Monday that her party had effectively replaced the center-right CDU as Germany's true Volkspartei, or catch-all people's party.

The AfD accuses Merz of failing to fulfil his key election promises to improve the spluttering German economy - once seen as the financial engine of Europe - and to find workable solutions to voter fears about immigration and security on their streets.

High time for political change, says the AfD.

Merz's position as German chancellor certainly looks wobbly. There have been rumours for weeks of a brewing palace coup, where he would be replaced by a more popular CDU politician.

Possible candidate names are swirling but no individual will stick out his or her neck in public until they know they have the backing of the party.

I have reported on Germany for decades. This is a stability-obsessed country. This kind of political upheaval is deeply unusual.

Even if Merz stays in post, his political clout and credibility, his room for manoeuvre inside a fractious coalition government, will be restricted.

Looking uncharacteristically forlorn on Sunday evening, Merz jumped to make a televised address even before the regional election results were confirmed.

He would press ahead with tax, welfare and economic reforms to bring about prosperity, he said. "Backbone, steadfastness and patience" were required.

But German patience is running thin.

Voters in Germany, as across much of Europe, have repeatedly elected traditional parties of the centre-left, such as Germany's SPD party, or centre-right, like the CDU, since World War Two - but increasingly they feel let-down and frustrated as they fear for their economic future.

Voter resentment really started to mount after the financial crisis of 2007/8, when these traditional parties were seen bailing out big banks, while families felt their savings and living standards dropped.

Then came the 2015 migration crisis, when more than one million refugees and other migrants arrived by people-smuggler boats across the Mediterranean and made their way across Europe, often by foot, trying to settle in wealthier countries like Germany and Sweden. Germany took in one million people.

Integration into German society has been mixed and Germans have been shocked and scared by a number of headline-making attacks by migrants over the years, some with a history of mental illness, others linked by the German authorities to Islamist extremist groups or ideology.

In December, for example, police said they arrested five individuals suspected of plotting a Christmas market attack in Munich "based on an Islamist motive".

Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has had another scarring effect.

Germans pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe. The loss of access to cheap Russian energy that German car factories and other industries relied on, plus Donald Trump's trade tariffs and aggressive economic competition from China, have had a heavy toll on this country's export-driven economy.

Germany is Europe's, and therefore the eurozone currency's, largest economy. It is the world's largest single donor to Ukraine right now and it is the biggest net payer into the EU budget.

When Germany's finances are in trouble and the country turns inward because of a political crisis, the knock-on effect beyond its borders can be considerable.

Under financial pressure, Merz has been pushing hard, along with a group of other wealthier EU countries to slash their contributions to the bloc's budget, for example.

This comes at a time when the EU wants to spend more, not less, on common defence projects, migration and AI and tech.

Faced with perceived threats from Russia and China, wars in the Middle East affecting energy supplies and prices, plus the unpredictability - and many in Europe say, unreliability - of the US under Trump, now is a time Europeans must stick tightly together, says Brussels.

The EU is watching Merz's travails, plus the strengthening of the AfD on the right and the hard left Die Linke too, with concern.

These regional German votes come at the start of bumper election season across the EU, where all the big powers - (including France, Italy, Spain and Poland - go to the polls.

Nationalist, Eurosceptic, anti-immigration parties are predicted to do well. And Beijing and Moscow are watching closely.

British Museum bans visitors from photographing Bayeux Tapestry

BBC News Mon, 21 Sep 2026 12:21:40 GMT

The British Museum has banned visitors from taking photographs of the Bayeux Tapestry over concerns that they were taking too long to view the historic work.

Curators had initially allowed photos to be taken but reversed that decision after long queues delayed ticket-holders from accessing the exhibition.

The medieval embroidery, which is on display in Britain for the first time, depicts the events leading up to the Norman conquest of England and the Battle of Hastings in 1066.

Visitors are being allowed into the sold-out exhibit in groups every 40 minutes and told to keep moving along the 68m (230ft) work in one direction.

But people stopping to take photographs along the way was restricting that flow and delaying later visitors.

A British Museum spokeswoman said: "There has been enormous interest in viewing the tapestry, and our priority is to ensure that all visitors have the best experience possible.

"In order to do this, we have made the decision to restrict photography while people are moving along the length of the tapestry."

The 11th Century artwork - which is not a tapestry and was actually embroidered in England - is currently on loan from its home in Normandy, France, and will be displayed in London until July 2027.

British Museum bosses decided that the embroidery would be displayed in a single, straight line, unlike the horseshoe-shaped gallery in which it is displayed in Bayeux.

The loan was confirmed following a Franco-British summit in 2025, following years of planning between the two countries.

Under the agreement, the British Museum is funding the costs of move while insurance is provided by the UK government.

The artefact was carefully packed in a climate-controlled crate and was given a police escort along the unprecedented 350-mile (560km) journey from its home to central London.

Some would-be visitors have criticised the high price of tickets - as much as three times what it costs to see the Bayeux Tapestry in France - to cover the museum's expenses.

Tickets for the exhibition are sold out until 31 December but more are expected to go on sale in October.

Alternately, a full-scale replica of the Bayeux Tapestry is available to see for free in Tewkesbury Abbey in Gloucestershire and at Reading Museum.

BBC removes 11 Mitchell and Webb comedy sketches from iPlayer

BBC News Mon, 21 Sep 2026 11:05:13 GMT

The BBC has removed nearly a dozen comedy sketches from That Mitchell and Webb Look after deciding they no longer "work today".

The Bafta-winning comedy, written by and starring David Mitchell and Robert Webb, originally ran for four series between 2006 and 2010.

The show recently returned to the BBC's iPlayer to mark its 20th anniversary. But 11 old sketches, including one that reportedly showed the comedy duo satirising racism while in blackface, have now been cut.

A BBC spokesman said in a statement: "This is a 20-year-old sketch show; in consultation with the programme makers, we have included the ones that still work today and not the ones that don't."

The Times reported the removed material included scenes featuring the English comic actors as war re-enactors in blackface, a sketch about a contestant on a makeover show wearing a burka and a "tribe" living in a garden centre.

BBC News has asked Mitchell and Webb - who rose to prominence on the popular Channel 4 sitcom Peep Show - for a comment.

That Mitchell and Webb Look grew out of a similar radio show titled That Mitchell and Webb Sound, which began on Radio 4 in 2003, and went on to win the Bafta for best comedy programme in 2007.

Defending the double act, fellow comedian Dom Joly, of Trigger Happy TV, questioned the BBC's "censorship" of itself.

Joly told The Times: "I totally get it if the BBC is putting out something really racist, which is laughing at and encouraging other people to feel that it's OK to do that.

"But it's so clear that Mitchell and Webb are not doing that. Their intent was not to be racist."

Jimmy Mulville, the co-founder of Hat Trick Productions, which makes the satirical news quiz Have I Got News For You, told the same newspaper he could understand the corporation's predicament.

"The BBC are in an impossible position," he said.

He added that producers had "to be careful", though, "that this is not the thin end of a wedge where we cut things out".

Perhaps Mitchell and Webb's best known sketch, which sees them both dressed as Nazis while begging the question: "are we the baddies?", remains online.

They are not the first comedians to have had their work edited or removed in recent years, as societal attitudes have shifted. Some artists themselves also began reassessing their work in the aftermath of the Black Lives Matter movement.

Matt Lucas and David Walliams' hit show Little Britain was removed from iPlayer, Netflix and BritBox in 2020, after objections resurfaced about some of their characters portraying people from different ethnic backgrounds.

At the time, both the BBC and Britbox noted how "times have changed" since the Little Britain first aired in the early noughties.

The show is now back on iPlayer but, like with Mitchell and Webb, some sketches have been removed.

Why Cardiff is set to win race to host Fury-Joshua

BBC News Mon, 21 Sep 2026 10:51:22 GMT

Anthony Joshua's fight against Tyson Fury is set to be held in Cardiff

The long-awaited heavyweight fight between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua is expected to take place at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on Friday, 11 December.

While BBC Sport understands final details are still being hammered out between Netflix, Saudi Arabian organisers Sela and both fighters' camps, Cardiff has firmly emerged as the frontrunner, with an official announcement expected this week.

It marks another dramatic twist in a saga that, only weeks ago, appeared destined for New York. A date at Madison Square Garden was so close to completion that plans were already being drawn up for a Manhattan news conference.

Instead, after Joshua and promoter Eddie Hearn refused to budge on their contractual right to stage the fight on British soil, the Welsh capital has taken centre stage.

BBC Sport takes a look at how Cardiff became the leading candidate to host what would arguably be the biggest event in British boxing in the 21st Century.

Wembley Stadium was long assumed to be the natural home for a meeting between the two defining British heavyweights of their generation. However, the path to making the fight was complicated by Joshua and Fury having signed separate agreements with Sela rather than a joint contract.

Joshua's deal explicitly stipulated that the bout must take place in the United Kingdom, whereas Fury's contained no such restriction.

That distinction proved critical when organisers and broadcast partner Netflix began lobbying to move the show to the United States.

Hearn acknowledged that virtually every other party involved preferred New York, with Matchroom even exploring what compensation would be required to waive the UK clause.

For a moment, that stand-off threatened to scupper the entire event. Fury publicly accused Joshua of stalling and briefly floated the prospect of a trilogy fight with Oleksandr Usyk.

But once Fury relented, organisers needed to find a British venue capable of satisfying the broadcast demands without leaving fans exposed to the British winter.

Cardiff, almost by process of elimination, became the answer.

Cardiff's Principality Stadium has a retractable roof

The fight had initially been discussed for November but, with negotiations over the venue dragging on, it now looks set for December.

Staging an open-air stadium fight in the UK at that time carries immense risk.

While Wembley offers unmatched prestige, exposing tens of thousands of fans and a massive international broadcast operation to potentially freezing temperatures, wind and rain was deemed unacceptable.

Moving the event indoors to an arena like London's O2 would eliminate weather risks, but at the cost of sacrificing tens of thousands of ticket sales.

The Principality Stadium's retractable roof allows organisers to capture the immense scale, atmosphere and gate revenue of a stadium show while offering full protection from the elements.

The venue's official seated capacity is just under 74,000, but boxing configurations allow for even larger crowds.

Joshua has already proven he can sell out the venue, having defended his WBA and IBF titles there against Carlos Takam in front of nearly 80,000 fans in 2017 before adding the WBO belt against Joseph Parker five months later.

We want Fury v Joshua at Wembley - London mayor

Fury says he is looking for new opponent, calls out Usyk

'Bring it on' - Cardiff businesses react to Fury vs Joshua rumours

Perhaps the most difficult hurdle has been aligning the event with Netflix's preference to broadcast during prime-time hours in the United States.

A projected UK ring walk of about 01:00 GMT - 20:00 on the US east coast - created a logistical headache for London. Wembley operates under a strict 23:00 event curfew.

While Mayor of London Sadiq Khan offered his support and Wembley officials were open to discussions, securing the necessary approvals from Brent Council and local safety advisory groups for a 01:00 start presented an administrative hurdle.

Cardiff offers a far smoother path. The Welsh Rugby Union, which owns and operates the Principality Stadium, previously indicated it would be delighted to host the fight and confirmed a late-night finish would not be a dealbreaker.

While early-hours finishes still require extensive coordination around transport, policing and crowd management in the city centre, the venue already holds a clear precedent for late-night boxing. In 2007, Joe Calzaghe's super-middleweight unification victory over Mikkel Kessler did not start until 02:00 local time to satisfy American television network Showtime.

For all the delays and frustrations that have plagued this rivalry over the past decade, Fury against Joshua remains the pinnacle of domestic boxing. Downgrading to an indoor arena would diminish the magnitude of the occasion.

Crucially, taking the fight to America would have deprived domestic fans of a generational spectacle. British supporters have driven the commercial value of this rivalry for years, filling stadiums for both fighters' respective careers and following every collapsed negotiation.

Staging the bout on home soil serves as a long-overdue reward for that loyalty, even if both men are now former world heavyweight champions.

A stadium fight of this magnitude dominates the national conversation in a way a 04:00 New York or Las Vegas broadcast simply cannot, and local amateur boxing clubs could see a surge in interest when the country's biggest stars compete on home soil.

Wales also has history of staging a huge fight between two British heavyweights: In 1993, Lennox Lewis defended his WBC title against Frank Bruno at Cardiff Arms Park - the venue that the Principality Stadium replaced.

When the demands surrounding the event are broken down, Cardiff's emergence becomes easier to understand.

Will you get £13,000 a year when you stop working? Here's how to check

BBC News Mon, 21 Sep 2026 08:49:45 GMT

It may well be decades away, but do you know how much money you will get when you stop working?

The current state pension is soon likely to top £13,000 a year.

Yet one in eight people surveyed by the UK tax authority have never checked how much money they are forecast to receive.

Here's how to find out, and what you can do now to boost it.

If you're working, it is highly likely you're contributing to the state pension - paid by the government when you hit pension age in your late 60s.

At the moment:

Many people on the old basic state pension may receive a top-up called the additional state pension.

Most pensioners have other income, primarily from pension savings built up over their career.

The state pension goes up each year in line with the highest of either inflation, wage increases, or 2.5%. So next April, the flat-rate state pension is expected to go above £13,000.

Workers pay National Insurance (NI) contributions. In general, you need 35 years of qualifying contributions to get a full state pension.

You may have gaps in your NI record if, for example, you have lived abroad. If you've taken time away from work to care for children or family members, then you get NI credits if you receive child benefit or carer's allowance.

It's possible to boost your contribution history with voluntary payments. Since April 2025, you have only been able to make payments for the previous six years.

That's one reason why it is important to check your state pension forecast well before you retire, experts say.

You can see what you are forecast to receive:

To get a state pension, you will need to prove your identity using official photo ID.

Importantly, never click on a link sent in an unsolicited email or text message, even if it looks official, as it could be a scam.

For more general information about tax and pensions, HMRC has launched a Tax Confident website.

And the government-funded, independent Money Helper website has a free retirement guidance tool to walk you through the options.

The most common reason for not checking a state pension forecast was feeling that retirement was still too far away to think about, a recent survey of 5,000 consumers by HMRC found.

Losing track of pension pots from previous jobs, and concerns about how career breaks might affect their entitlement, were also frequent responses.

People aged 45-54 were the most likely to have never checked.

"Whether retirement is decades away or just around the corner, I'd encourage everyone to check their forecast and see if there's anything they can do now to boost their entitlement later," says Myrtle Lloyd, HMRC's chief customer officer.

Young people aren't snowflakes - mental distress is rising, says head of official review

BBC News Mon, 21 Sep 2026 04:00:05 GMT

Accusations that the young are a snowflake generation are wrong, the head of an independent review into mental health, ADHD and autism has told the BBC.

Prof Peter Fonagy said in an exclusive interview that there had been a real rise in mental distress among children and young people, with anxiety, depression, self-harm and eating disorders the most common.

He said it was "harder to be young" now given the economic and employment uncertainty young people face, coupled with the challenges presented by social media.

His review was ordered nine months ago by Wes Streeting after the then-health secretary claimed in an interview that young people were over-diagnosed and "written off".

It is likely to feed into government policies on everything from NHS services and benefits to support for young people who are not in education, employment or training.

Fonagy said he chose to speak to the BBC ahead of the publication, which is expected later this week, because he was concerned the debate around ADHD and autism would "obscure" the wider issue of mental health.

More than 100 experts and families with experience of mental health problems have worked on the review with Fonagy, a clinical psychologist and adviser to NHS England.

He said it will conclude that the rise in mental health problems since the 1990s was real, with about one in four 16 to 24-year-olds now struggling.

The data on this is contested as some sources rely on self-reporting, while sceptics argue greater awareness and reduced stigma around mental health mean more people are coming forward.

Some have also questioned whether society was now over-medicalising distress in people's lives – giving people diagnoses when what they are facing is temporary stress that they should learn to cope with.

Last year, the BBC found that many GPs had concerns about over-diagnosis and felt normal life stresses were being over-medicalised.

NHS figures show the number of children and young people in contact with mental health services in England has risen by 50% in the past five years.

Fonagy said his personal battle with mental health when he was young was a driving factor in his desire to help young people.

He experienced suicidal thoughts as a teenager after moving to London from Hungary without his parents. But he says he was fortunate to get therapy from a local service that "saved his life".

"It's harder to be young now," the 74-year-old said, adding that his review "dismisses the idea of a snowflake generation".

"I'm in awe of the way they have adjusted to an environment that is far more difficult than I ever had to face."

He said economic and employment uncertainty, as well as the pressures of social media, had created a "very toxic" environment for young people.

"They are a generation that has real serious challenges that I would not wish to have had when I was their age.

"Adults have let them down. We're the first generation that probably collectively feels we had a better life than our children will have.

"So, to the person who says it's a snowflake generation, just try living 24 hours as a 16-year-old."

Fonagy is adamant that what young people are experiencing represents a real rise in mental health problems.

But he also accepted that greater awareness was leading to more people seeking medical help.

The trend is affecting both boys and girls, but becomes particularly pronounced in girls from about the age of 12.

Sexual aggression from boys was a big concern, he said, but added that the expectations society placed on girls and young women was a factor.

"It's very difficult to be a young woman now in secondary school."

Fonagy said young people were struggling with a range of different conditions from eating disorders and anxiety "that's so powerful people avoid going to school", through to depression that was "so strong people cannot sleep at night and lose their appetite and feel their life is not worth living".

His report will say these problems were exacerbated by the pandemic because of the disruption it caused to their lives.

Young people the BBC spoke to who have struggled with their mental health say it is important that the government acts on the findings of Fonagy's report when it comes out.

"It's all very well having this flashy report, but it's useless if they don't put that into practice," Omari, 22, said.

He had a tough time at school, but said his teachers did not listen.

"I made an attempt on my life because I was really struggling with bullying. I was 15.

"Suddenly, when I did end up in hospital, they all wanted to care. But it's like you're a bit too little, too late here."

Others expressed concern about their futures. Mattea, 17, is in temporary social housing and has struggled with anxiety and depression.

"I don't know what's going to happen to my life," she said, adding that she felt like adults had let her down.

"No one's going to come and sort my life out for me. I have to do it on my own."

Fonagy said the support being provided to young people needed to be improved.

The NHS, he said, was simply "not fit for purpose".

He said too many people were being left on waiting lists, pointing to figures that show one in three people referred to mental health services were still waiting for help after a year.

There were some positives steps being taken, he said, including the rollout of mental health teams to work closely with schools.

However, he said tackling the problem will require action across society – in education, employment, housing and families themselves.

For example, Fonagy blamed cuts in youth services over the past decade or so for leading to fewer places for young people to mix and develop a sense of belonging.

"We need to have opportunities for them to participate, because participating in things... maintains good mental health."

He also said it was striking that loneliness among young people had increased since 2000, linking it to the rise in use of phones and social media, which have reduced face-to-face contact and disrupted sleep patterns, both of which are damaging to mental health.

But as well as addressing phone use, he said there were other things families and friends could do.

"Saying to someone, 'I notice you're not quite the same as yesterday. Is there anything the matter?' Knowing there is someone who knows makes an enormous difference."

His hope? That working together, society can make a difference. "I want young people to hear that when they feel anxious, depressed or distressed, that it's a real problem, but a problem we can do something about.

"When I needed help, I got it. I want everyone to have that chance."

Russia's elections had few surprises - but how the Kremlin uses the results will be crucial

BBC News Mon, 21 Sep 2026 00:05:11 GMT

Many things about Russia are hard to predict.

The result of this election wasn't one of them.

In a political system tightly controlled by the Kremlin, the party of power – United Russia –had been widely expected to remain the largest in parliament by a large margin.

There were no upsets. No surprises. No other party came close.

Preliminary results suggest that United Russia, which is supported by President Putin, is on course to retain its constitutional majority in the State Duma - with even bigger numbers than last time round.

And that's after more than four-and-half years of war on Ukraine, which have resulted in massive battlefield losses for the Russian army, economic difficulties and, most recently, widespread petrol shortages due to Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil facilities.

Those parties trailing far behind, but which have cleared the 5% threshold and made it into the new Duma, featured in the previous parliament, too: a Duma that was fully behind the Kremlin and the so-called special military operation.

One party that didn't make it into parliament was Yabloko.

Yabloko had been the only anti-war political party permitted to take part in the election - permission that was short-lived.

Just twelve days after being registered for the vote it was removed from the ballot (the party list) by the Supreme Court, an indication of Kremlin concern that Yabloko's pro-peace message was gaining too much traction with the public.

The party isn't surprised that the new Duma looks like being as pro-Kremlin as the previous one.

"What other result can there be if there were ten parties on the ballot and they all support the policies of Putin?" Yabloko party chairman Nikolai Rybakov tells me.

"I don't think the Duma will change. They'll vote 100% for the policies of Putin just like they did."

Although Yabloko had been struck off the party list, around a hundred of its candidates remained in individual constituency races. According to preliminary results, none have won seats. The party claims it has come under sustained pressure.

"Some of our candidates, who should have been running, are in jail, many were barred from running and some of our election observers weren't registered and were unable to keep an eye on the voting," Nikolai says.

Ahead of the final day of this three-day election, Ukraine launched a large-scale drone attack on the Moscow area. Three people were killed in Moscow Region, while in the capital the city's oil refinery was hit.

At a polling station near the oil refinery, I spoke to voters about the attack.

There was no sense of surprise. More a quiet resignation. With Russia's war on Ukraine now in its fifth year, Muscovites have grown used to their city periodically becoming a front line.

"People in the Donbas, as well as in Bryansk, and Belgorod near the Ukrainian border, hear this kind of thing every day," a voter called Viktor told me.

"And they just get on with their lives."

The outcome of this election was predictable. What happens next is less clear.

The Kremlin is likely to use the result to claim that most Russians have rallied behind the president, and to justify future policies and subsequent decisions on the course of the war.

The key question: what will those decisions be?

President Putin recently ruled out another wave of mobilisation.

"There is no scenario today that would require it," he declared.

Not today, then. But what about tomorrow?

Despite official denials, in Russian society there remains deep anxiety about the possibility of a new round of mobilisation.

At the very least, the Kremlin is likely to treat the election result as a 'mandate from the people' to continue the war.

See the dazzling images that won Astronomy Photographer of the Year

New Scientist September 17, 2026

The astonishing diversity of the cosmos is on display in the 2026 Astronomy Photographer of the Year competition, organised by the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London. From our own solar system to distant nebulae, these images showcase the many wonders we can observe from the ground on Earth.

The overall winner (above), The Quiet Predator, was taken by Ali Alobaidly in Kuwait. It shows a dense nebula 650 light years away, in the constellation Cepheus. This cloud of dust, called the Shark nebula, contains a few bright stars that make their surroundings glow blue. The nebula is so dark and distant that it took Alobaidly more than 28 hours of observing to create this image.

The runner-up in the competition (above) is Beyond the Wormhole, taken by Kfir Simon in Israel. While the image may evoke a hole in space-time, it actually depicts the centre of the Helix nebula, which is about 650 light years away in the constellation Aquarius. Beyond the central star that formed the nebula when it shed its outer layers thousands of years ago, extraordinarily distant galaxies shine through the dust and gas.

Advertisement

In the Our Moon category, Venusian Pearl on the Moon (above) took the prize. Petr Horalek took this photograph in the Czech Republic as the moon passed in front of Venus in the middle of the day. He captured this relatively rare event, called an occultation, just as Venus slipped behind the crescent moon.

The runner-up in the Our Sun section is, unsurprisingly, an image of the sun. However, Anatomy of the Chromosphere (above), captured by Peter Ward in Australia, isn’t a simple photograph. It represents two different wavelengths of light, one of which captures emission from hydrogen along the sun’s edges, represented in red, while the other shows emission from calcium, shown in lilac. Together, they reveal the structure of the sun’s chromosphere, which is the layer just above its visible surface, but below its corona.

Comet C/2025 A6 (Lemmon) jets across the sky in this highly commended image by Julien DeWinter and Landon Boehm, taken from Texas. When it was captured, in October 2025, the comet was almost at its closest point to the sun, about 101 million kilometres from Earth. That proximity to the sun caused remarkable activity on the comet, creating two long plumes, one made of dust and the other of electrically charged plasma.

With a more earthly setting, the winner of the Skyscapes category is Botswana Star Trail, taken by Stefano Pellegrini. It captures the movement of stars above a grove of baobab trees over the course of 340 camera exposures, each lasting 30 seconds.

The winning images from the competition will be exhibited at the National Maritime Museum in London from 18 September.

Robots clash in first naval engagement between uncrewed sea drones

New Scientist September 17, 2026

In the first-known naval engagement between uncrewed vessels, a Ukrainian robot boat sank a Russian opponent in the Black Sea.

The action between the remote-controlled uncrewed surface vessels (USVs), or sea drones, took place earlier this month. A video released by the Ukrainian Navy shows its USV, identified as a Sargan-3000, firing a 12.7-millimetre heavy machine gun at the Russian vessel, which appears to be of the Orcan type, until it sinks.

Both sea drones are propelled by water jets. The Sargan is around 7 metres long with a top speed of over 80 kilometres per hour, while the Orcan is about 5 metres long and can reach 64 km/h.

Advertisement

Fully autonomous drones have killed human soldiers for the first time

This is the first-known clash of its type in the history of naval warfare, according to independent naval expert H. I. Sutton. But it didn’t come as a surprise.

“It was inevitable that there would be USV-on-USV combat,” says Sutton. “We have seen the same in the air, and on the ground.”

Ukraine developed USVs after scuttling its only major warship early in 2022 to prevent its capture. In October 2022, Ukraine carried out a successful attack with seven sea drones, damaging a Russian frigate and a minesweeper at the Sevastopol naval base in Crimea.

Since then, Ukraine has moved from improvised USVs based on speedboats and jet-powered watercraft to advanced designs, including the Magura and Sea Baby series. In conjunction with shore-based anti-ship missiles and aerial drones, Ukraine’s uncrewed vessels have sunk or damaged a third of the Russian Black Sea fleet. The remainder is now largely confined to port behind booms and other defences.

Subscriber-only newsletter

Initially, Ukraine’s USVs carried explosive charges for one-way attacks. More advanced versions are now armed with surface-to-air missiles, with one Ukrainian USV being the first ever to shoot down a helicopter, in 2024. Others are fitted with machine guns and unguided rockets. Some Ukrainian USVs are miniature aircraft carriers, launching aerial drones.

From 2024, the Russians copied Ukraine, building small, fast USVs with explosive warheads to attack ports, bridges and shipping. The Russian Orcan in this month’s action was likely to have been heading towards the Ukrainian port city of Odesa as part of a campaign targeting cargo ships.

“It was a small vessel with an explosive charge and no gun turret, intended for an offensive operation ramming a larger vessel,” says Sutton. “The Ukrainian one was armed with a machine gun, showing that it had a more defensive role. So, it was to be expected, although not guaranteed, that the Ukrainian one would win this duel.”

Ukraine is racing to design faster, more capable interceptor drones to tackle Russia's new generation of jet-powered Shahed attack drones

Sutton says the action is likely to drive further evolution of USVs on both sides. Just as helicopters being used against sea drones led to the design of new models equipped with surface-to-air missiles, attack USVs may start carrying machine guns or other defensive weaponry, or travel with escorts.

This first robot naval action is unlikely to be the last. “Probably in future we will see Ukrainian USVs interdicted by Russian ones close to Russian naval bases,” says Sutton.

Naval experts believe the Black Sea campaign is a special case, saying that its lessons may not apply in other theatres of operation where actions take place over much greater ranges and timescales. But the continued rise of robot boats is another sign of warfare’s changing face.

Beautiful new cat species is first to be named in a century

New Scientist September 17, 2026

A new cat species has been scientifically described – the diminutive, spotted tilcayo from Bolivia.

Several species of small cat in the Leopardus genus live in South America, including the ocelot, margay, kodkod, Geoffroy’s cat and the tiger cat or oncilla. The similar appearance of these nocturnal and hard-to-spot cats has made separating them into distinct species difficult.

This is particularly true of tiger cats, which are about the size of a house cat, and are found in Costa Rica in Central America, and across a vast swathe of South America including Bolivia, Brazil, Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru. Historically, there have been many local and scientific names for them, but they all got subsumed into a single species, Leopardus tigrinus.

Advertisement

Tiny orange frog around the size of a pencil tip is brand-new species

Genetic studies have since divided the species into four, resurrecting three of the species names that scientists once used before they were all lumped together under the name L. tigrinus. This process saw the official recognition of the southern tiger cat (Leopardus guttulus) in 2013, Leopardus emiliae in 2017 and the clouded tiger cat (Leopardus pardinoides) in 2024.

Now, Eduardo Eizirik at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul (PUCRS) in Porto Alegre, Brazil, and his colleagues have analysed the complete genomes of 38 individuals from the Leopardus genus, including 26 tiger cats from across their known range.

The genomics revealed a fifth distinct species living in the Bolivian Yungas forests on the east slopes of the Andes mountains. The researchers describe it under a completely new name: Leopardus tilcayo, naming it after the local term used for this cat.

Subscriber-only newsletter

“We’ve discovered a new species of cat that had not been scientifically named before,” says Eizirik, adding that this is the first time this has happened for a century.

“There are more cat species. Who can’t love that?” says Leslie Lyons at the University of Missouri. “They’re hard to find and see, so it’s not surprising that some of the early taxonomy needs to be modified now we have more data.”

L. tilcayo has a combined head and body length of between about 42 and 50 centimetres and weighs between 1.5 and 2 kilograms. The genomes revealed that it diverged from the lineage containing L. tigrinus and L. pardinoides nearly 1.4 million years ago.

Domestic cats originated in North Africa and spread to Europe in the past 2000 years, according to DNA evidence, while in China a different species of cat lived alongside people much earlier

Telling the new species apart visually is not easy. “The five tiger cat species are all cryptic species. They’re morphologically very similar,” says team member Jonas Lescroart at University of Antwerp in Belgium.

The researchers also found that in the Peruvian Yungas forests, on the west side of the Andes, there is a distinct group of cats in the L. tigrinus lineage that they describe as a novel subspecies, L. tigrinus antisuyo.

There are so many barriers in South America that can geographically isolate animal populations from each other, including mountains and rivers, that more cat species may be waiting to be found, says Lyons. “It’d be rather cool if we could find another species out there.”

L. tigrinus is listed as vulnerable by the IUCN Red List, but the new species and subspecies will have to be evaluated and protected as distinct units, says Eizirik, especially as the forests they live in are shrinking as agriculture expands.

Short bursts of exercise can boost your cognition

New Scientist September 17, 2026

Tiny bursts of exercise once an hour could boost your cognition at school or at work, adding to the evidence of how important it is to take occasional breaks.

“Exercise improves pretty much every domain you can think of, including cognition over the long term. The interesting thing here is that this is immediate,” says Mike Trott at the University of Queensland in Australia, who wasn’t involved in the research.

It is well known that exercise is good for our overall health, cognitive powers and mental health, but it can be hard for adults to hit the World Health Organization’s recommended minimum weekly levels of physical activity of 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity. About 31 per cent of adults fail to hit these targets, so interest is rising in “exercise snacks”: sessions of physical activity that last no more than 10 minutes, performed at least twice a day.

Advertisement

Exercise may relieve depression as effectively as antidepressants

In the past few years, studies have found that short bursts of exercise can help keep your heart healthy or add years to your life. To see if they can similarly boost our brains, Yongming Li at Shanghai University of Sport in China and his colleagues reviewed 25 randomised controlled trials investigating the cognitive effects of exercise snacks.

The review included a total of 1115 people of all ages, with the mean age of participants in the studies ranging from 8 to 78 years. They involved people sitting for hours, interrupted by a couple of minutes of exercise either every 30 minutes or every hour.

The exercises included yoga, chair-based stretching, climbing two flights of stairs, walking on a treadmill, resistance exercises, stationary cycling, or high-intensity exercises like running on the spot for a minute or leg raises and jumping jacks.

Free newsletter

The researchers found that these short bursts of exercise gave a modest immediate boost to working memory, cognitive flexibility, attention span and the ability to ignore impulsive reactions, assessed across the studies by a statistical measure known as Hedges’ g. With this measure, 0.2 indicates a small effect, 0.5 a medium one and 0.8 or above a large effect. Overall, the measure for the study was 0.24.

The cognitive benefits were stronger if the exercise habit continued for several weeks (g = 0.51), and if it happened in school or in the workplace (g = 0.61).

It is hard to interpret the overall effect size because the youngest and oldest people in the study were at very different stages of cognitive development, says Mark Hamer at University College London. However, he thinks the findings are plausible.

We now have a greater understanding of how exercise slows cancer

“It’s interesting with the kids in particular and this concept of trying to break up lessons, which could involve a teacher getting the kids to stand up or jump on the spot,” he says.

The review also found that gaps of an hour between exercises provided slightly more of a boost than gaps of 30 minutes, which makes sense biologically, says Trott.

The leading hypothesis for how exercise affects the brain is that it makes the body release dopamine and noradrenaline, increasing blood flow, he says. This gets everything working a little bit better, and studies show that, over longer periods of time, this can boost the size of the hippocampus, which is involved in memory, and the performance of the prefrontal cortex, which is involved in focus and decision-making.

We all know that walking is good for us, but growing evidence reveals that the right hike can exponentially enhance the health benefits

“The immediate effects of dopamine and noradrenaline last for over an hour, so if the exercise snacks are more frequent than that, any extra effect is going to be really small because you’re still riding the wave of the first one,” says Trott.

Current health messaging about taking breaks during the day is generally based on evidence of cardiovascular and metabolic effects, and the exercise snack work adds to evidence of how beneficial it is to break things up frequently, says Hamer. “Even if that’s just by standing up or going up and down the stairs.”

For most objects, for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. But if you are swimming upstream in a river of quantum light, the normal rules don’t apply. Physicists have demonstrated that breaking Isaac Newton’s third law of motion in such a setting can be useful, leading to new ways of controlling quantum light in experiments and devices.

Sperm caught breaking Newton’s third law of motion

The action-reaction principle of Newton’s third law would have the swimmer and the river experience the same type of force – either repulsive or attractive – similar to how gravity leads to mutual attraction between our bodies and Earth. Earth attracts us downwards, and experiences an upwards attraction towards us. In contrast, in the experiment, the swimmer experienced an attractive interaction with the river, but the river experienced a repulsive force on the swimmer. This was a “non-reciprocal” interaction that breaks the action-reaction principle. Its net effect was an upstream force on the swimmer, says Hu.

“For me, the biggest takeaway is that active behaviour does not necessarily require an intrinsically active particle or swimmer,” he says.

Mathias Albert at Côte d’Azur University in France says that upstream motion has previously been achieved in other quantum fluids of light, but it always relied on creating tiny vortices behind the swimmer in the fluid, with the recoil from their creation pushing the swimmer, so the new experiment demonstrates a fundamentally different mechanism for motion.

Subscriber-only newsletter

We already know that non-reciprocal interactions can be crucial for shaping the motion of “active matter” systems where objects consume energy to move, such as bacterial mixtures, flocks of birds or swarms of tiny robots. But the experiments by Hu and his colleagues focused on an object that doesn’t consume energy, yet still benefited from non-reciprocal interactions. Their work could therefore usher in the creation of a new type of active matter in a quantum system.

“This question is very much in the air at the moment, with several groups exploring how the concepts of active matter can be combined with quantum fluids and photonic systems,” says Albert.

Sonoluminescence, in which small bubbles in a liquid produce flashes of light when they collapse, is now known to be a quantum process

He says that, eventually, the ability to control chunks of light so they move in some preferred direction could be useful within devices that use quantum light. Such devices are prevalent in, for example, communications or quantum information processing.

Hu says that the team now wants to construct more complex experiments where they could control the swimmer’s motion more precisely or add several swimmers to the fluid at once.
