The collapse of the AMOC would be catastrophic. How will we know when it’s coming?

New Scientist September 21, 2026

On a sunny evening in July, a research ship called the Sir David Attenborough was working near the Sorgenfri glacier in south-eastern Greenland when a kilometre-long wall of craggy, bulging ice collapsed into the fjord. The scientists on deck watched in stunned silence as an estimated 18 million tonnes of ice slowly flipped over, sending up vast plumes of spray.

Iceberg calving on this scale was once relatively rare – but it has become commonplace in recent years as Earth warms. And that acceleration could have catastrophic impacts that extend far beyond Greenland. It is weakening a system of ocean currents in the North Atlantic that is vital to societies in Europe and around the world. If the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) were to shut down, the continent would plunge into “ice age” winters with year-round long droughts, and agriculture would become close to impossible.

Yet whether the AMOC really will fail, when that might happen and how quickly – these points all remain highly uncertain. And because of that, the threat remains a distant one in policy-makers’ minds. That is why an £81 million plan is now afoot to build an early warning system that could alert humanity if AMOC is nearing a dangerous tipping point.

Advertisement

Oceans are darkening all over the planet – what’s going on?

Data now being collected by the Attenborough research ship is core to that plan. “We might be committed to centuries of change without knowing it,” said ocean scientist Paul Holland at the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) as he prepared to set sail from the port of Harwich, UK, some weeks earlier. “We might be passing these tipping points without realising.”

So how worried should we be about the AMOC collapsing, what will it take to build an early warning system, and will the alarm bells persuade governments to pull back from the point of no return – or at least to prepare for the consequences?

The AMOC is a vast current system that circulates in the ocean between North America and Europe, driven by temperature and salinity. Around the Gulf of Mexico, the harsh sun heats the ocean and drives evaporation. The resulting warm, salty water flows towards the seas between Greenland and the UK in a part of the AMOC called the Gulf Stream. As the circulation pushes north, the atmosphere cools the salty water, so that it becomes denser and cascades towards the ocean floor like a subsurface waterfall. From there, water flows southward along the seafloor back towards the Americas. To replace the water sinking in the North Atlantic, more warm water must then flow from the Gulf of Mexico, powering the circulation.

The AMOC is a crucial section of an undulating but well-established conveyor belt of ocean currents that flow around the globe. Traversing the entire belt takes a typical “parcel” (about 1 cubic metre) of water about 1000 years.

Like the rest of this conveyor belt, the AMOC, which circulates between North America and Europe, is driven by temperature and salinity. Around the Gulf of Mexico, the harsh sun heats the ocean and drives evaporation. The resulting warm, salty water flows towards the seas between Greenland and the UK in a part of the AMOC called the Gulf Stream. As the circulation pushes north, the atmosphere cools the salty water, so that it becomes denser and cascades towards the ocean floor like a subsurface waterfall. From there, water flows southward along the seafloor back towards the Americas. To replace the water sinking in the North Atlantic, more warm water must then flow from the Gulf of Mexico, powering the circulation.

Without the AMOC, models predict that sea ice would cover the North Sea down to Norfolk in the UK and Friesland in the Netherlands. London would experience an average winter temperature of 2°C (36°F), with cold snaps of -20°C (-4°F). Similar cold would descend on Amsterdam, Brussels, Dublin and Paris. Oslo would see deep freezes of -48°C (-54°F) or below at least every 10 years.

“The winter is like being in the ice age, and in Scotland, it’s in the ice age for half the year,” says Earth system scientist Tim Lenton at the University of Exeter, UK.

Yet this vital circulation is also the section of the global conveyor belt most likely to slow down, or shut down completely, in the coming decades or centuries due to climate change. This possibility was first suggested in a 1987 paper by geochemist Wallace Broecker at Columbia University in New York. Fluctuations in Earth’s climate aren’t always gradual, he wrote, and human-made “global warming”– a term he popularised – could disrupt the feedbacks fuelling the AMOC.

At the time, evidence was mounting that AMOC had shut down in the past because of natural changes in the planet’s temperature. About 12,900 years ago, as the last glacial period was ending, the northern hemisphere suddenly slipped back into near-glacial conditions for 1300 years – a period called the Younger Dryas, after an Arctic flower that spread through Europe then. Shortly after Broecker’s paper was published, geochemists studying the composition of shells trapped in marine sediments found that the AMOC was sending less surface water to the seafloor during the Younger Dryas.

Can everyone live a ‘good life’ without destroying the planet?

Broecker and others argued that the melting of an ice sheet over North America had injected fresh water into the North Atlantic, diluting the salty water arriving via the Gulf Stream and slowing its cascade towards the seafloor. “We play Russian roulette with the climate,” he wrote at the time.

Today, a similar process may be happening again, only with fresh water from Greenland. “There are 200 fjords around Greenland… pumping out icebergs and gushing out meltwater five times faster than they were 30 years ago,” says marine geophysicist Kelly Hogan, who is part of the BAS mission.

Since 2004, sensors measuring water flow have been anchored across the Atlantic as part of the Rapid Climate Change programme. Although it has found early indications that AMOC is weakening, it will take several further decades of data collection to confirm this. Alongside this monitoring, an analysis of how historical Atlantic surface temperatures have shifted concluded that AMOC has slowed 15 per cent since 1950. And the appearance of a “cold blob” in the North Atlantic – the only part of Earth’s surface that has been cooling over the past 150 years – suggests the AMOC is delivering less warm water to the area than before.

These aren’t good omens. Yet climate models still vary hugely in terms of how soon they predict the AMOC could reach a tipping point, and how soon after that it would shut down. In June, for instance, a study found a 10 to 20 per cent chance the AMOC has already crossed the point of no return, in which case it could collapse as soon as 2060. But other research this year found the AMOC would weaken only gradually or, if humanity emits carbon at a lesser rate, not at all.

The Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA), a UK government-backed science agency, is building an early warning system to improve these forecasts and update them in almost real time – rather than waiting years, or decades, for studies to come to fruition. To do this, researchers first need to figure out the amount of meltwater from Greenland that is entering the AMOC, what form it is in and how that is altering its flow.

On the Attenborough research ship before the expedition, Holland pulled up a map of results from the UK government’s flagship climate model on a screen. Red pixels south of Greenland indicated where dense, salty water is sinking in the AMOC today. Then Holland switched to a forecast for intense global warming in 2090. The red sinking pixels had almost completely disappeared. “This is a really terrifying prospect. So the question is, is this realistic?” he said.

Roughly half of the fresh water from Greenland comes from the surface of the ice sheet, which is being melted by warming air temperatures. The other half comes from the fjords, where warming ocean waters melt the glaciers from below, and where icebergs calve off, like the enormous ice face that toppled in front of the ship.

The second half is difficult to model. For instance, many fjord glaciers rest on relatively shallow sills of bedrock. If they recede into deeper regions of the fjord, the calving can speed up. “It’s an unstable, self-sustaining process,” says oceanographer Pierre Dutrieux at BAS. “It’s going to retreat like crazy until it finds another sill.”

As a result, the UK’s top climate model may be either under- or overestimating the fresh water coming from Greenland. And because icebergs can float thousands of kilometres before they melt, it may be incorrectly predicting where and when that fresh water hits the AMOC. “We need to measure the entire chain of processes,” said Holland.

To do that, researchers on the ARIA-funded Greenland Ice to Atlantic (or GIANT) mission have a suite of gadgets at their disposal. “GIANT is the James Bond of science projects,” joked Athena Dinar, head of communications at BAS. Boaty McBoatface, an autonomous underwater vehicle shaped like a fat yellow torpedo, will scan the position of icebergs and bergy bits in the fjords; DriX, a red surface robot with a sonar pod underneath it, will map the geometry of ice sheet faces; and small bundles of sensors will, once delivered by a robot, automatically drill themselves into glacier fronts, all to measure how much of the retreat is due to calving versus ice melt. This information will then be fed into ice-sheet models, which will be included in climate models to improve AMOC tipping-point forecasts.

The next phase of the ARIA project will focus on finding a way to give routine updates about these risks. One idea is to build an AI model that can reproduce these forecasts without weeks or months of supercomputing time. The AI would automatically analyse satellite imagery of ice fronts to spot accelerations in glacier loss that could increase the freshwater input to the AMOC. As a side point, regular warnings like these would be valuable to local Inuit who fish and hunt seals and whales in Greenland’s coastal fjords. They would know that an outpouring of meltwater or icebergs was coming that might affect these crucial hunting grounds.

An early warning system would also need to analyse changes in AMOC ocean circulation. Climate scientist Jon Robson at the University of Reading, UK, is on one of several ARIA-funded teams that are focusing on a crucial part of the AMOC called the subpolar gyre, a vast swirl of ocean currents south of Greenland where warm, salty water is cooled by the atmosphere and sinks.

The ice sheet’s melt is expected to slow down the rotation and sinking of that water. Then, a sudden shock could push the weakened AMOC past its tipping point. Because we have never directly observed AMOC collapse – or any climate tipping point – we need to figure out what to look for, says Robson. He and his colleagues are trying to find potential shocks, such as a sudden influx of fresh water from disintegrating Arctic sea ice. “It may be that there is a very definite threshold in the system,” he says. “But it could be that it’s much more blurry.”

Although it is challenging to pin down exactly when the AMOC could shut down, its impacts are more certain. Besides lowering winter temperatures across Europe, AMOC collapse would amplify the North Atlantic storm track, bringing more frequent winter storms and causing wild swings between these cold snaps and warm spells. European summers would be almost as hot as today, thanks largely to continued global warming. But the weather would be drier year-round, especially in southern Europe. Droughts like the one that has helped fuel record wildfires in France and Spain this summer would become more frequent and intense. The cold and especially the dryness would wipe out agriculture in some places. Only 7 per cent of the UK would be arable, down from 32 per cent today.

AMOC collapse would also diminish monsoon rainfall by almost 30 per cent in West Africa and 20 per cent in India. This could undermine food supplies not only in these areas, where most agriculture relies on the annual rains, but also around the world, since India is the biggest producer of rice and the Ivory Coast of cocoa.

“You’re getting a whole-system shock,” says René van Westen at Utrecht University in the Netherlands. “Our global society is built around a strong AMOC.”

Free newsletter

The ARIA team is aiming to have a prototype early warning system ready by 2030. They hope that by giving governments and key industries an evolving forecast of how imminent a tipping point is, it could spur them to invest in adapting to the potential consequences, as well as in trying to avoid collapse altogether.

Discussions about how this would work in practice are only just beginning. Each year, the Met Office, the UK’s weather service, issues a forecast of global temperature and weather trends over the next decade, such as the per cent chance that global warming will exceed 1.5°C. That could be expanded to include the latest probability of AMOC collapse, says Robson. In addition, an early warning system could issue monthly reports of the risks. These could range from a level one, representing no elevated threat, to level three, indicating imminent subpolar gyre collapse, to level five, showing the AMOC tipping point has been crossed, says Lenton.

In July, ARIA met with representatives from the UK and other European governments, as well as from industries like water, insurance and finance, to ask what information they would find useful. One idea is that the system could give a running menu of the options available for adapting to AMOC collapse, such as building reservoirs or desalination plants, and insulating houses. “[We could put] it in terms of, well, in 10 years’ time, those opportunities might be more limited or more expensive,” says Gemma Bale, programme director at ARIA.

An ambitious form of climate modelling aims to pin the blame for disasters – from floods to heatwaves – on specific companies. Is this the tool we need to effectively prosecute the world’s biggest carbon emitters?

Researchers’ biggest fear isn’t that the ARIA programme will fail to build an early warning system, but that governments and industry will fail to heed the warning. They have been alerting politicians to the dire consequences of climate change, including AMOC collapse, for almost 40 years. Other attempts to warn of risk thresholds, such as the goal to limit global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels, have failed.

Even today, in the UK’s relatively mild and stable climate, 13 per cent of households have trouble keeping their homes warm, while the government doesn’t keep grain reserves and no new water reservoirs have been built since 1992.

Van Westen sees little point in building an early warning system. “The risk of reaching the tipping point… is too high to ignore,” he says. “That should be already enough motivation.”

But Hogan argues that the ARIA programme is our best hope of avoiding these catastrophic outcomes before it’s too late. She has a 16-year-old daughter who could live to see the societal upheaval caused by a slowing AMOC.

“I look at her future and think, what’s it going to be like for them?”

SpaceX’s Starship will orbit Earth for first time during next flight

New Scientist September 18, 2026

SpaceX’s reusable rocket, Starship – the tallest and most powerful ever launched – will orbit Earth for the first time within days. And because it will also release working Starlink V3 satellites, it will be the first commercially useful Starship mission.

The company has announced that a launch window will open at 7.15am CDT (1.15pm BST) on 22nd September, during which Starship will launch from the company’s Starbase site in Texas.

The flight – Starship’s 14th – will reach an altitude of 275 kilometres and complete six orbits of Earth over 10 hours, with re-entry and splashdown targeted in the Pacific Ocean, to the west of Chile.

Advertisement

SpaceX’s 1 million satellites could avoid environmental checks

This will make it by far the longest and most ambitious test flight of Starship to date. All 13 previous Starship test flights have been, at best, sub-orbital.

Starship is made up of two parts: an upper stage, confusingly also called Starship, and a lower stage, called Super Heavy. Currently, SpaceX is testing the latest third generation of each section using a fail-fast, learn-fast strategy more common to Silicon Valley than the conservative world of space exploration.

SpaceX is several years into its development programme for Starship, intended to be a rapidly reusable and extremely powerful launch vehicle that will take over the rollout of the company’s Starlink satellites and be a central part of NASA’s Artemis moon missions.

Free newsletter

The 14th flight will also see 26 Starlink V3 satellites launched for the first time. Thousands of these new devices will join the existing constellation of satellites that provides internet connections around the world. Until now, Starship test flights have launched only dummy test satellites.

Davide Amato at Imperial College London says that an orbital test is indicative of confidence within the company that the rocket will at least survive the journey to orbit and the release of satellites. But he says that re-entry, where the company has faced problems during recent tests, may be another matter.

“In short, they’re making good progress towards introducing Starship as a successful commercial launcher,” says Amato. “Whether Starship will be ‘revolutionary’, as promised by their CEO, will depend on whether they will be able to achieve a high launch cadence and on whether their design is cost-effective.”

SpaceX is about to launch tallest and most powerful rocket in history

Leah-Nani Alconcel at the University of Birmingham, UK, says that the 14th test flight will be a key step for SpaceX. Not only will the release of V3 satellites help the company update its Starlink constellation – the new satellites fly in a lower orbit than existing Starlink satellites and have higher data capacity – but their larger size than previous models will go some way to showing whether Starship is up to the task of launching its proposed Starmind data centre spacecraft, which are substantially larger.

“I don’t think it’s a huge jump in operational complexity for the launch vehicle, but demonstrating the Starlink V3 delivery to orbit is a significant step,” says Alconcel. “It may not be as flashy as the ‘chopstick catch‘ for the vehicle stages, but it would be a big boost to their commercial capabilities to have both the already-established high-cadence Falcon 9 and a proven Starship in their repertoire.”

A rocket launched last year is thought to have smashed into the lunar surface this morning, creating the moon’s newest crater

Three of the satellites due to be released on this flight have been modified to include cameras that can scan Starship’s heat shield whilst in orbit and transmit images to engineers on Earth.

During the 13th test flight, the booster stage made its ascent as planned, but during descent only eight of the 13 engines intended to slow its fall reignited, causing it to make a hard splashdown into the ocean rather than the planned gentle simulated landing on water. Neither the booster nor upper stage will attempt to make a controlled landing on the 14th flight.

Only two Starship flights have taken place so far in 2026, with flight 14 due to be the third. The upcoming flight will also be the second since SpaceX’s flotation on the stock market, which made controversial founder Elon Musk the world’s first trillionaire. The number of flights has fallen far beyond bold estimates made in previous years; SpaceX officials hoped to launch as many as 25 Starship test flights last year. In reality, only five test flights occurred that year.

SpaceX didn’t respond to a request for an interview, but the company says on its website that “there have been several modifications to hardware and software to address issues seen on the previous flight”.

Physicists are scrambling to make sense of possible dark matter signal

New Scientist September 18, 2026

We may have finally spotted a dark matter particle – but figuring out exactly what kind of particle it was is a daunting task. Even as researchers race to confirm they really did detect an unknown particle, physicists around the world have already started working out what sort of dark matter particle it might have been.

The potential particle in question was found at the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) detector in South Dakota and announced on 1 September. The detector uses a huge tank of liquid xenon to look for signatures of dark matter particles smashing into the nuclei of xenon atoms, which are expected to produce a burst of light in response to any collision that would then be picked up by the arrays of cameras surrounding the tank.

The LZ group recorded only a single burst of light, and there is about a 1-in-200 chance that the signal was a fluke event rather than evidence that dark matter was there – but nevertheless it is tantalising.

Advertisement

Unexpected hints of dark matter should breathe life into particle physics

What makes the signal even more intriguing is that it was at a higher energy than would be expected if the particle were a standard weakly interacting massive particle, or WIMP, the simplest proposed type of dark matter. “It’s an anomalous event,” says Henning Flaecher at the University of Bristol in the UK, part of the LZ group. “It’s not what you would expect from the most general dark matter models.” The fact that this high-energy event was spotted, with no accompanying lower-energy collisions, makes it exceedingly unlikely that this particle, if it exists, is a “vanilla” WIMP, he says.

In the weeks since the announcement, theorists have released scores of papers digging into the data, searching for answers. “The large number of papers is less a statement that theorists believe the event is a [true] dark matter discovery and more a reflection of the fact that, if it persists, its energy already tells us quite a lot about types of physical processes that could produce it,” says Juri Smirnov at the University of Liverpool in the UK.

Many of those papers debate the possibility that the particle could be what is called a higgsino, a type of non-“vanilla” WIMP. It arises from a theoretical framework called supersymmetry, in which every known particle is proposed to have a “superpartner”, with some similar properties but different spin. In supersymmetry, the higgsino would be the superpartner of the Higgs boson.

Subscriber-only newsletter

A higgsino is the simplest WIMP explanation still available to explain the LZ signal, according to JiJi Fan at Brown University in Rhode Island. “It gives rise to a wealth of signals that could be searched for at different experimental frontiers.” Plus, a higgsino detection event is predicted to be unaccompanied by a host of lower-energy collisions, matching the signal detected by the LZ group.

However, the higgsino has its problems. The most basic model of that sort of particle that could explain the LZ detection seems to be ruled out by constraints from other experiments. This doesn’t mean the particle couldn’t have been a higgsino, but it does suggest the higgsino in question would need to have had a much higher mass than expected.

Many other models have been proposed to explain the detection, though. Among them are several models of dark matter particles originating in extra dimensions. While this may seem an unnecessarily complicated line of enquiry, these models were already being studied to solve other problems in particle physics, says Lisa Randall at Harvard University, a co-author of one such paper. “In some sense, the data looks like it’s calling out for something like this: it avoids the pre-existing constraints and fits quite naturally.”

Particle collisions are inherently quantum, but much of that character is lost when we turn them into classical data. Sarah Alam Malik explores whether preserving more of it could help us spot signs of dark matter and other new physics

An extra-dimensional dark matter candidate could both fit the LZ detection and explain why the fundamental particles have the masses they do, a long-standing puzzle, she says. Other models propose a whole dark matter sector, with multiple types of dark particles.

Right now, there is no way to tell which, if any, of these models might be correct. “I don’t think the data currently justify saying one of these is ‘the’ explanation,” says Smirnov. Some of them do come with additional predictions, though, which will be particularly useful when trying to pick through so many ideas, he says.

As the LZ team and other teams at detectors around the world continue to analyse their data, looking for additional events to confirm that the dark matter particle was real, all of these ideas could help them know exactly what it is they are looking for. “Anomalies could come and go, as we all know,” says Fan. “My take is that they provide us with some concrete targets to think: is this expected? Are there new territories/questions in theory or experiments we should cover? No matter whether the LZ event is confirmed, some of these topics would lead to long-term research.”

Fishapod fossil shows early elbows came in a variety of forms

New Scientist September 18, 2026

An ancient fish that lived just before the first four-legged animals walked on land had a pointed forearm bone and a hinge-like elbow joint, adding to the growing evidence of trial and error in early arm formation.

The 350-million-year-old animal was one of several “fishapods” – creatures with fins that had evolved some limb-like features. It might have used its fins for actions other than swimming, such as moving along the bottom of rivers.

“We keep uncovering more and more variation in the shapes and geometries of these bones,” says Thomas Stewart at Pennsylvania State University. “The more we study the diversity, the more we realise there’s just a range of unusual forms of animals living in and exploring their ecologies.”

Advertisement

Extraordinary ichthyosaur fossil shows its last meal was a pterosaur

In the past two decades, scientists have found fossils from dozens of distinct species of finned tetrapodomorphs, or fishapods. These animals lived in water and had fins that contained bones similar to those found in the limbs of today’s four-legged animals. The most iconic fishapod – Tiktaalik roseae – has been nicknamed the “crawling fish” because it could probably use its fin-limbs to crawl out of water, capturing an important step in the evolution of vertebrates.

But the story of how fish evolved into land animals is anything but a straight line, Stewart says. For instance, Qikiqtania wakei, which he and his colleagues described in 2022, was a fishapod that appears to have initially evolved weight-supporting fins but then evolved to be a full-time swimmer.

Now, the team has analysed another unusual fishapod. So far, the animal is known only from fossils of a single isolated fin that was discovered on Canada’s Ellesmere Island. The researchers CT-scanned the fossil and compared its arm-like bones with those of 16 other known fishapods. The isolated fin didn’t quite match any of them, suggesting it came from a distinct species.

Subscriber-only newsletter

The radius – which, in humans, runs from the elbow to the thumb side of the wrist – was long and triangular, coming to a sharp point at its far end – where the wrist would be in a tetrapod. Other bones and tissue would have led from here to the fin’s tip, but the shape of the radius itself would have provided little support for pushing against the ground, says Stewart.

At the elbow end, the radius lacked the rounded knob seen in other fishapods, but instead was narrow and “shaped like a bean”. The upper arm bone was missing, but the radius’s shape suggests the joint between them would have worked like a simple hinge that largely bent back and forth in a single plane. This is more restrictive than the elbows of other fishapods: they could twist and rotate their elbows, like we can, to provide greater flexibility of movement.

The fossil also contained the intermedium, a small bone seen in fishapods that scientists suspect eventually evolved into part of the wrist. In the fossil from the unknown fishapod, the intermedium was relatively longer than in Tiktaalik and its close relatives.

Hidden fossils reveal secrets of oceans before major mass extinction

Exactly what the animal was doing with its unusual fins isn’t clear, says Stewart. The restricted movement of the elbow might have been a kind of experiment in evolving appendages that could have served this particular animal’s needs, in its environment. But this doesn’t necessarily mean the elbow joint was perfectly suited for its role.

“When animals begin to explore new kinds of movements, they might be kind of awkward,” he says. “They might not be the best at it, but they’re still good enough. It’s a matter of sufficiency, not optimality.”

Julia Molnar at New York Institute of Technology, Long Island, says she was excited to see the new specimen. “The question of when and why the fin-limb and water-land transitions occurred is still very much up for debate,” she says. “I would not be surprised if this wide variation in radius shape represents different approaches to the problems and opportunities of this changing world.”

Palaeontologists have found new evidence that the early ancestors of amphibians, reptiles and mammals did not have a larval stage with external gills like modern frogs or salamanders

Importantly, the variations shouldn’t be interpreted as different attempts to evolve limbs for a future life on land, but rather to suit their own current environment, says Brian Swartz at the University of California, Berkeley.

“A fish like this one might use its fins to ‘walk’ in shallow water or push through vegetation,” says Molnar, “allowing it to escape large aquatic predators and prey on smaller fish and arthropods at the water’s edge.”

Our brain evolved from two primitive nervous systems that merged

New Scientist September 18, 2026

Our brain may be a hybrid of two ancient nervous systems that were packaged together hundreds of millions of years ago. This is based on the finding that the front and back brain regions in people and several other species develop from two distinct cell types in embryos, instead of sharing the same developmental origin, as previously thought.

“Our research suggests that evolution took two existing neural systems and pushed them together spatially,” says Kyle Loh at Stanford University in California. “Having the brain as one organ would probably be more efficient, but we rely on this primordial way to make the brain as two separate pieces.”

Human brains may have got bigger for no particular reason

Loh and his colleagues studied early stages of mouse embryo development and found its brain develops from two types of early progenitor cells, proliferative cells with a limited capacity of self-renewal. One type expresses a gene called OTX2 and turns into the neurons found in the front part of the brain, comprising the forebrain and midbrain. The other expresses a gene called GBX2 and becomes the neurons in the back part of the brain, the hindbrain.

Advertisement

The researchers then conducted experiments using human cells in a dish and found that the neurons of the hindbrain and those of the forebrain and midbrain also develop from different progenitor cells. “We’ve shown for the first time that the front of the brain arises from a totally different progenitor cell than the back of the brain,” says Loh.

This explains why it has been so hard to grow human hindbrain tissue in a lab. “It was actually a summer student’s failed experiment that got us into this,” says Loh. Researchers have typically tried making hindbrain neurons from the progenitor cells that are destined to become forebrain and midbrain neurons, which doesn’t work, he says.

Subscriber-only newsletter

Armed with this knowledge, the team was able to grow functional human hindbrain motor neurons in a dish for the first time by starting with the correct type of progenitor cell.

The hindbrain coordinates fundamental, life-sustaining processes, such as breathing, sleeping, eating and the beating of the heart, whereas the forebrain is the centre of higher-level thought. Conditions like amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), the most common type of motor neuron disease, and spinal muscular atrophy cause speech and swallowing difficulties because they affect the hindbrain. Recently, scientists also discovered that GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy suppress appetite in mice by acting on the hindbrain.

Now that it is easier to grow human hindbrain neurons in a dish, it should assist ALS and spinal muscular atrophy research, and allow us to investigate the precise mechanisms of how GLP-1 drugs work in people, says Loh.

When does your brain reach adulthood? We’re now understanding the many ways the organ continues to mature decades after society first deems you an adult

The researchers also studied early-stage embryos of chickens, zebrafish and acorn worms, and found their nervous systems are similarly derived from two different types of progenitor cells. This suggests our shared two-origin brain system arose at least 550 million years ago.

But jellyfish, which we diverged from around 600 to 700 million years ago, have two separate nervous systems. These may have joined up in our distant ancestors because it improved their overall processing power, says Loh. “You get more efficient communication when things are closer together,” he says.

Having our brains develop along two separate pathways might also have facilitated the evolution of complex thought, says Loh. While the hindbrain was taking care of all the basic functions for keeping us alive, “evolution could play around with the forebrain, and make mistakes and give rise to all the fancy things like memory and creativity”, he says.

Nature Neuroscience DOI: 10.1038/s41593-026-02433-7

Chinese visitor numbers increase as South Island tourism market rebounds

New Zealand Herald September 21, 2026

Chinese tourists are returning to the South Island as increased flight capacity and changes to visa requirements help drive the recovery of the visitor market.

China is New Zealand’s third-largest visitor market, according to Tourism New Zealand, with 238,000 arrivals recorded in the year to June 2026 – a 40% jump compared with the previous year.

Contact our South Island newsroom

Of these visitors, 82% visited the South Island, 61% travelled to the North Island and 43% visited both islands, spending a total of $1.5 billion.

Christchurch Airport head of tourism and trade development Scott Callaway has witnessed the Chinese market’s “strong growth”.

He credited increased flight connectivity and capacity and visa changes as three of the main drivers.

Callaway said international airlines like China Southern have created direct flight links between New Zealand and China since 2015.

The airline is based in Southern China and offers direct flights from China’s five major cities: Beijing, Shanghai, Wuhan, Guangzhou and Shenzhen. This creates a connection which draws from “a huge pool of people”.

But increasing flight capacity “is a huge part of us being successful”, Callaway said.

Over the past year until June, China Southern brought 65,994 passengers to Christchurch Airport – a figure it aims to increase by a further 57% this northern winter period, from October to March.

“It’s one thing to have a plane with lots of seats on it, but to actually be able to fill those seats is really good,” Callaway said.

Callaway said that changes in New Zealand’s visa policies also provided a “huge boost”.

In November 2025, the Government launched a 12-month trial allowing Chinese passport holders to travel to New Zealand visa-free if they have an eligible Australian visa and arrive directly from Australia.

Instead of applying for a visitor visa, eligible tourists can travel to New Zealand for up to three months with a New Zealand Electronic Travel Authority (NZeTA).

Callaway said this “was a relatively minor change in position that had a really strong result”.

He said since the visa-free scheme’s introduction, Christchurch Airport has seen a boost in travellers from China, as well as indirect travellers from over the Tasman. These include Chinese passport holders in Australia, such as university students and those on working visas.

“It’s all doing well, but that was the cream on top.”

Many South Island tourism operators have also experienced this boost from the Chinese market.

Elijah Robinson from Lake Tekapo’s Dark Sky Project said the company has “definitely had an increase” in Chinese visitors.

The stargazing company saw the biggest change over the past two years, where “we’ve been looking at the same numbers as pre-Covid”.

Robinson said he had seen a shift towards the outdoor experiences Dark Sky offers, as New Zealand’s natural environment appeals to Chinese travellers.

“They’ve always been into the outdoors, but we’ve also historically had groups coming through and doing an indoor experience as well, which is more culture-focused,” he said.

“But recently, over this past year, we’ve seen a bit of a decline in that area.”

Robinson said advances in technology meant the company could not necessarily compete with attractions in China on technology alone, but New Zealand’s natural night skies were difficult to replicate.

“They’ve got an admiration for the outdoors, for the multicultural and for the night sky, because they don’t get that over there.”

Robinson said their presence on Chinese social media platform RedNote has helped push business. Some of their experiences, including visiting the Astro Café at the summit of Ōtehīwai/Mt John have gone “viral”.

Multiple RedNote users have posted photos of Astro Café, featuring panoramic views of Lake Tekapo alongside coffees topped with planet-inspired latte art.

This growing interest in outdoor experiences is also being felt further West, where glacier operators are seeing Chinese visitors return to the ice.

Rob Jewell, who manages Mt Cook Glacier Guiding and is CEO of Fox Glacier Guiding, has been involved with the China market since 2007.

He said up until Covid-19 China was New Zealand’s second-largest visitor market, accounting for about 35% of visitors to Fox Glacier.

Since the pandemic, the Chinese market has made up 30% of the business.

Jewell said it continues to increase, but has been a “little bit slower to return since Covid”.

He said Southeast Asian visitors account for 65% of Fox Glacier Guiding’s heli hike visitors, and 80% of Mt Cook Glacier Guiding’s visitors.

“Glaciers aren’t easily accessible for them, and neither are helicopters.”

The most important part of attracting international tourists is “being China service friendly”.

Websites translated into Mandarin Chinese, Mandarin marketing material and a social media presence on Weibo and RedNote are just a few initiatives the glacier guiding companies have.

Jewell also has a dedicated Asia business development manager, two Mandarin-speaking frontline staff, and a basic Mandarin training programme for his guiding team.

“It just goes to show with that market that it’s important, we value them, and we like having them in our business,” Jewell said.

“Just make your business China service friendly, keep them happy, and they’ll keep spreading the good word, and they’ll just keep coming,” he said.

For Chinese visitors, the decision to visit New Zealand can be made long before they arrive, with recommendations and advertisements on social media.

Ivy Zhang, visiting Christchurch from Shanghai, said online recommendations helped shape her family’s itinerary.

On a girls’ trip with her daughter and cousin, Zhang said, “There are some commercial advertisements. They recommend everything for us. We just follow their decisions.”

The group had seen a lot of recommendations on RedNote for things to do in the South Island and Queenstown.

“A lot of people follow these recommendations,” she said.

But while social media can help Chinese visitors decide where to go, the experiences themselves remain the biggest drawcard.

The Li family, visiting Christchurch from China, said New Zealand’s natural beauty and outdoor experiences appealed to them.

“New Zealand is a beautiful country and has a lot of wild spots,” Sean Li said.

“We can see a lot of stars in the night, the air is fresh, and we can see a lot of different kinds of animals.”

Huge swordfish caught off Hawke’s Bay coast smashes club record

New Zealand Herald September 21, 2026

A huge swordfish caught off the coast of Mahia in Hawke’s Bay has smashed a club record.

Veteran fisherman Doug Cushing caught a 234.6kg broadbill swordfish on Saturday, in deep waters about 50km off the coast of Mahia’s Portland Island.

It set a new club record at Hawke’s Bay Sports and Fishing Club for a swordfish, and marked an early birthday gift for Cushing, who turned 46 the following day.

“They are not easy fish. So it’s pretty special to get one at home.”

He said it was a real team effort and he was supported by crewmates Aaron Smith, Davey August, Adam Stoddart and Nick Dorward on board First Edition.

Smith, who was the skipper, held the previous club record with a 162kg swordfish catch last year.

The five-strong crew set off from Napier on Friday afternoon.

“We fished all night for swordfish and didn’t get any bites, just a couple of sharks, and then 10.30am on the Saturday morning we hooked that one,” Cushing said.

“We had a couple of lines in and I just happened to be on the rod.”

He said it took him about two and a half hours to reel in.

“We didn’t see the fish until maybe two hours and 15 in,” he said.

“It jumped out of the water about 20m away from the boat – so quite close – and we knew when it jumped out how big [a fish] we were dealing with.

“We got a couple of gaffs in, and it took all five of us to pull it on board.”

Cushing said he’d caught a bigger fish in the past while overseas, a tuna, but this was the biggest fish he’d caught in Hawke’s Bay.

“It means a fair bit. My [late] uncle, Kevin O’Keefe, he was the club president for years and his name is on the heaviest swordfish trophy for the year.

“The family donated it, so, if I can win that trophy, it would be pretty cool.”

Cushing said swordfish was good eating, and it would be shared around ”the village” once it had been processed.

Club operations manager Neil Price said the catch had created excitement around the fishing club, and garnered interest around the country.

“Everyone is keen to know where it was caught, and they start getting ready to go out there.”

He said Cushing had been a long-standing member, and his son actually held a junior world record for a tuna catch.

As for swordfish, he said they were rare.

“There has not been a lot of them over our scales.

“There has probably only been six or seven over the history of the club, and we have been around for 62 years.

“They are a deep-water fish. They are not on the surface, they live on the bottom of the ocean.”

Earlier this year, a Northland angler caught a 279kg swordfish, while the New Zealand record appears to be a 404kg swordfish caught in 2012 off the Karikari Peninsula.

Leaked video shows top education curriculum official telling staff not to put information about minister’s office in writing

New Zealand Herald September 21, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

A senior official working on a secondary school curriculum update has been filmed telling staff not to put information in writing showing material had “gone backwards and forwards” with the Education Minister’s office.

The leaked video, obtained exclusively by the Herald, shows Dr Catherine Law, also principal of Avonside Girls’ High School in Christchurch, reminding workers their comments are “OIA-able”.

“This is them helping us. What we do not need is anything in response in writing that shows that this stuff has gone backwards and forwards between them and us,” Law said.

The OIA refers to the Official Information Act, a freedom of information law allowing New Zealanders to request official information about activities and correspondence within government.

The video raises questions over adherence to transparency and record-keeping rules, which a Ministry of Education (MoE) spokesperson told the Herald were staff responsibilities.

“Meeting obligations under the Official Information Act is a responsibility of all ministry staff and must be reflected throughout their work. This includes creating and maintaining appropriate records as work is developed and before it is submitted.”

The response did not say whether Law’s comments were appropriate or in line with ministry expectations.

Education Minister Erica Stanford told the Herald that regarding the OIA, “my expectation is that the law is followed”.

Labour is calling for a Public Service Commission investigation, with education spokeswoman Ginny Andersen saying the video raised “serious questions about instructions given to Ministry of Education staff to keep political matters out of emails and avoid OIA scrutiny, following conversations with Erica Stanford’s office”.

She said “any breach of public service obligations must be properly investigated and the public deserves answers”.

Andersen called on Christopher Luxon to also explain what had occurred, adding “this is not how a transparent government should operate and the Prime Minister cannot simply brush it aside”.

“Parents and teachers deserve better than political interference and secrecy when it comes to our children’s education.”

The Government is progressing development of a “knowledge-rich curriculum”, drawing on sector expertise.

Work began last year on the Phase 5 Year 11-13 component of the programme.

Last November, Law was seconded from her high school principal role to be programme lead on the senior curriculum update. This involved engaging people in the sector as subject advisers, who would help with the design.

Consultation was undertaken on draft curriculum subjects throughout mid-2026, with public communications emphasising how hundreds of subject advisers and others in the sector had contributed to their development.

The video shows an online meeting the Herald had been told was held recently between Law and curriculum writers. The footage does not capture the entire meeting.

In it, Law talks about how staff in the minister’s office may provide feedback on material from the ministry, such as raising “red flags” or suggesting something “isn’t clear”.

This process allows two staff members in Stanford’s office to get “well across it” before providing the subjects to the minister to get signed off, she says.

She says that, the night before, a staff member provided her “with most of the subjects in a bundle for me and we are keeping them here in the office”.

“Whilst I communicated a few things out to a few of you, most of it was absolutely great. Again, we won’t spend time going ‘it was great’, we will just give you the quick bits we want to ask about or get some information on.”

Law then conveys a message about how to respond to any such communication.

“What I just need to say to you all, to make sure I have said it and it is really clear, is: I will communicate to you saying, ‘this is a bit of informal feedback’, ‘could you just, da da da da’.

“Please don’t respond with anything that references the minister’s office. Remember all of this is OIA-able. This is them helping us.

“What we do not need is anything in response in writing that shows that this stuff has gone backwards and forwards between them and us.

“You can feed back to me in a reply with a piece of information, like ‘here yup’, ‘this is’, or ‘done’, or nothing, or if you want to talk about it, can you let me know, I am happy to talk it through and I am happy to chat.”

Law says to be “really mindful” during this “process”, which she says comes “before we start the formal one, which is through the bags and that is all formal and public and transparent”.

“You will notice I will just use passive verbs and just say this, so as far as anyone is concerned it is just some feedback from me.”

She says the writers have done “great work” and there were “small things” to follow up.

“It doesn’t guarantee an automatic tick-off, but it gets us a long way towards an automatic tick-off,” she says.

Law says Stanford’s “new chief adviser is highly political, is really aware of the coalition, is really aware, and if anything was going to be picked up, he would pick it up”.

“So the fact he is happy as he looks at them is a really good thing.”

A MoE statement said staff had responsibility for “creating and maintaining appropriate records” and its commitment to responding to multiple OIA requests “demonstrates its dedication to transparency”.

It did not say if it believed Law’s comments about not putting information in writing were in line with this.

In response to further Herald questions, a spokesperson said: “We are not seeking to draw conclusions from individual comments contained in a transcript of part of an internal meeting provided by a third party.”

The issue of officials not putting information in writing due to OIA concerns has previously been commented on by former Chief Ombudsman Peter Boshier.

He wrote last year that while the OIA allowed not only for written information, but any information known to officials, to be requested, he had heard allegations public officials were pressured to avoid creating records for fear of them “being OIA-ed”.

“Sound information management practices require good record-keeping and the effective management of that information once it is created or gathered,” he said, noting requirements under the Public Records Act.

“In light of such unambiguous legal obligations, the suggestion made by some commentators that officials and ministers may sometimes keep things off the written record to avoid discoverability is deeply troubling.”

These comments don’t relate specifically to the MoE or Law’s remarks.

Stanford said the law must be followed.

“In terms of staff members at MoE, that is a matter for the Secretary of Education.”

Considering Law’s request for staff not to put in writing anything that “shows this stuff has gone backwards and forwards” with the minister’s office, the Herald asked about what was shared and the process.

Stanford said senior curriculum documents had been sent to a MoE staff member seconded to her office. She said they were “the only person in the office who has reviewed it”.

“As part of the normal process, this staff member checks for spelling mistakes, duplication, plain language, any obvious errors and asks questions to ensure the papers are of an acceptable standard before I review them.”

The MoE spokesperson said the videoed meeting was held as officials were managing feedback and workload across 74 subject drafts due for release in Term 4.

They said ministry staff in the Beehive office work with officials “while material is prepared, which allows questions to be raised and information to be clarified before final drafts are submitted for the minister”.

“This is a normal part of preparing material for the minister, not a separate decision-making process. The ministry remains responsible for its advice to the minister, and the minister considers and signs off the final versions.”

They said none of the subjects had yet been provided to the minister or her political staff.

Jamie Ensor is the NZ Herald’s chief political reporter, based in the press gallery at Parliament. He was previously a TV reporter and digital producer in the Newshub press gallery office. He was a finalist in 2025 for Political Journalist of the Year at the Voyager Media Awards.

New Zealand Herald September 21, 2026

The Te Awamutu railway station, where a person was reportedly struck and killed by a vintage train on Sunday night. Photo / Dean Taylor

A railway trust says it’s fully cooperating with authorities after one of its trains struck and killed a person on the weekend.

The Glenbrook Vintage Railway Charitable Trust’s board was “shocked and devastated” by the person’s death on Sunday night at Te Awamutu train station, chair Glenn Deed said in a social media post.

“Our thoughts are first and foremost with the whānau and friends of the person who died. We are providing support to our staff and volunteers and remain in contact with our passengers who were onboard the train.

“The wellbeing of everyone affected is our immediate priority at this difficult time.”

Deed’s post said the empty train had been blessed and returned to Auckland on Monday with KiwiRail’s assistance.

A passenger aboard GVR’s “Spiral Steam Spectacular” told the Herald she heard people yelling “stop” seconds after the train left the station. The words “Stop stop stop” then came across the staff radio in her carriage and the train stopped moments later.

“We weren’t told what happened but looking at the trauma of the bystanders, the trauma of staff ... something I’ll never forget,” she said.

Hundreds of people, including many families with children, were reportedly on the vintage train at the time of the incident.

Both police and the Glenbrook trust have encouraged any passengers or local community members who were at the station at the time to reach out to Victim Support on 0800 842 846 if they need it.

Deed thanked the emergency services, staff who had cared for passengers, and the passengers themselves “for their patience and support in extremely difficult circumstances”.

“On behalf of everyone at the Glenbrook Vintage Railway, I want to thank the community and the wider heritage rail sector for their ongoing care and support.”

The South Island’s Mainland Rail service was also cancelled yesterday to give crew members time to process the tragedy.

Steam Incorporated, which runs that service, said the heritage sector was “a small and tight-knit community where everyone knows each other and last night’s tragic accident will be widely felt”.

The decision was made to “give our crew the time and space they need to process what happened and support one another”, it said.

Police and WorkSafe are both investigating, while the Transport Accident Investigation Commission (TAIC) has also launched an inquiry. The commission said it would be looking for safety lessons rather than trying to assign blame or liability.

Deed said the railway trust was cooperating fully with relevant agencies.

“While those investigations are under way, we are unable to comment further.”

Climate change could push many Melbourne women out of work. This app aims to keep them in it

Sydney Morning Herald September 22, 2026

As temperatures rise, Melbourne will shift towards a nighttime economy. We trial a new app which makes walking more comfortable and safer.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

The morning has just turned light when Lisa Nicholson’s alarm sounds.

She taps her phone screen to turn it off, before sitting up and stretching muscles still tired from the day before.

After saying good morning to her teenage son, she walks out to her carport, where she hauls a lawn mower, whipper snipper, leaf blower and hand tools into the back of her little green Mazda 2.

Peering above the pile of metal in her rearview mirror, she backs out of her driveway, and sets off to create lush sanctuaries in Melbourne’s neighbourhoods of concrete and brick.

Tomorrow, she’ll do it all again – but as the city heats up, her days are getting earlier.

“I’ll try to get out and get all my work done in summer by midday,” says Nicholson, owner of gardening business Petite Gardens. “It’s a killer in the afternoon.

“Once the weather starts to really crank up – sometimes it’s earlier in the year, sometimes it’s later – it does affect the business.”

Gender and urban design expert Nicole Kalms says that, as temperatures rise with climate change, cities including Melbourne will shift their work, commerce and recreation to the nighttime economy.

Prioritising green space is a focus for Kalms, but she knows the shift to an after-dark economy also comes with an unintended cost for women. If women don’t feel safe out at night and in unlit areas, will they be excluded?

The topic of healthy places and people is one of the key pillars of Melbourne Assembly, a civic forum The Age is hosting in October, bringing together the world’s brightest minds, industry leaders, key decision-makers and the community to shape the city’s future.

Nicholson says that, if she didn’t have the agency to work around the heat, “I certainly wouldn’t do the work I’m doing”. “I’m not averse to being out there and working hard, and being sweaty and all the rest of it,” she says.

“But I will also not work in really extreme conditions because honestly, my clients don’t expect me to either.”

Escaping the heat isn’t just a matter of comfort. It’s a matter of health.

And, as the city looks to its future ahead of Melbourne Assembly, tree canopy experts are keeping a dogged watch over the state government’s plan to densify suburban transport hubs through designated “activity centres”.

Tree canopy has a direct correlation with all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease mortality, and fatal or non-fatal heart attacks, an Australian study has found.

The activity centres run vast lines through Melbourne, with one in four concentrated in the Stonnington council area, in the leafy east.

But they also trace a path over sparse tree canopy hotspots, including West Footscray, Seddon, North Essendon, Brunswick, Thornbury and Preston.

RMIT University urban planner Thami Croeser, who helped compile tree canopy data for The Age, says experts are waiting to see whether developers prioritise good tree cover across the suburbs.

Historically, they’ve taken up almost entire parcels of land with apartment buildings, leaving little space for gardens or trees. Suburbs earmarked for Suburban Rail Loop stations could also bring in tens of thousands of new homes in towers of up to 20 stories across Melbourne.

“There is a bit of concern in the tree canopy space that it’s all housing-focused, and not on the vital tree canopy that needs to make that housing liveable,” Croeser says.

“As we densify, we want to ensure we don’t crush every tree in the neighbourhood.”

As Melbourne’s skyline pushes outward and upward, urban designers say the environment below has never been more crucial. Among them is Kalms, whose app is putting that premise into practice.

At the top of a tree-lined suburban street in Melbourne’s outer south-east stands an unassuming green metal fence.

Taking a few steps beyond it reveals a ridge perched over a vast valley, where turtles crane their necks to break the surface of a lake cradled in its centre.

Rabbits burrow near the banks of the lake. And, up on the ridge at Wilson Botanic Park in Berwick, a kookaburra hops alongside the footpath, gobbling up a worm before it flies back to the oak tree from where it came.

This is a daytime route on the YourWalk app, created specifically with women and vulnerable people in mind.

Its walking routes prioritise tree cover, shade and accessible footpaths during the day, as well as adequate lighting at night – when many women don’t feel safe.

Rubina Nawabi is one of them – a 55-year-old mother of four living in the City of Casey, where the local council has partnered with Monash University XYX Lab and spatial data studio CrowdLab to pilot the YourWalk app.

After dark, the Hallam-based social worker rarely goes out, unless she’s driving (not a given for women in Casey, where many families share a single car).

She refuses to take her usual low-lit shortcut if she is out walking after sunset and fears for her teenage daughter, who recently walked home for three kilometres with friends from Westfield Fountain Gate at about 6pm.

“If I knew, I would have really gone and picked them up,” Nawabi says.

“It becomes really scary.

“Towards the Fountain Gate area, there is quite a lot of light. But as we come towards this way [Hallam], it becomes isolated with not many people on the roads, and there is not much light.”

Women consistently cite an absence of lighting (namely quality, warm lighting) as the biggest factor stopping them from going out at night, Kalms says.

That’s alongside the unpredictable behaviour of violent men.

Then there’s the lack of public toilets (which you can filter for on the YourWalk app), and accessible footpaths for prams – all of which create an inhospitable environment, excluding women from a growing economy.

Kalms says that councils have an excess of data mapping the safety and comfort of their suburbs. They know their tree canopy coverage and ground temperatures, and every streetlight they own, but they seldom use the data holistically.

“We know where all the CCTV cameras are. We’ve got crime data. We’ve got our own data about women’s safety for a lot of these communities,” says Kalms, director of Monash’s XYX Lab.

“All of this information is really about understanding quite stark statistics around how women and girls navigate cities.”

The Age tested two routes on the YourWalk app, which integrates council data to map the most comfortable and safe daytime and nighttime routes.

The app is being piloted with a view of being rolled out across Melbourne, incentivising councils to invest in more foliage and better lighting. The first route The Age took cut through the Wilson Botanic Park, simulating a journey a resident might take from Coles in central Berwick to a home on Bournevale Drive.

The second, with the app on night mode, avoided the park, instead taking the well-lit and higher-traffic Harkaway Road.

More than 4.1 million Australians – or almost 30 per cent of the workforce – regularly work at night, according to University of Melbourne urban studies researcher Anna Edwards.

In that workforce, there are slightly fewer women than men (27 per cent, compared with 29 per cent) – many of whom Kalms says don’t feel safe catching public transport at night.

Almost a third of night workers have at least one child at home aged 14 or under, Edwards says.

If governments don’t do more to accommodate women, they risk them falling further behind. Edwards points to the NSW government, which last year launched Australia’s first dedicated night worker “action plan” to improve safety and amenity after dark.

“If we’re to participate in the nighttime economy, we need to feel safe, and so we need to be planning for the 24-hour economy,” Edwards says.

That includes, experts argue, acknowledging how climate change is pushing Australian cities to later work. Extreme urban heat exposure has tripled since the 1980s, and the greatest impacts are falling on low-income and marginalised communities, Kalms says.

In Spain’s Barcelona, which just recorded its hottest summer on record (with a 61-day heatwave), the city’s council has built designated climate shelters to give locals and tourists respite.

Melbourne could become akin to some European cities, shifting more work and recreation into the evening and nighttime as temperatures rise, Bupa chief health officer Nic Woods says.

The health insurer is a major partner of Melbourne Assembly, where Woods will be a panellist in October.

“Climate change is increasingly impacting not only our physical environment, but also our mental wellbeing,” Woods says.

“As we plan the cities of the future, it is vital that we work together to create spaces that balance health, safety and equity alongside increased green spaces and healthier urban environments.”

More than 46 per cent of Australian women experience climate anxiety, according to research by the health insurer. The rate is almost 5 per cent higher than men.

Melbourne Assembly will be held from October 19 to October 21. More information is available on the Melbourne Assembly website.

The UK has agreed to provide defensive air support to Saudi Arabia to help counter Houthi fighters and restore stability in the Middle East while driving down the cost of living at home, Andy Burnham has said, ahead of his first meeting with Donald Trump.

The prime minister said he had agreed to a request for air-to-air refuelling of Saudi jets to defend energy infrastructure against the Iran-backed rebels and help keep oil flowing from the Gulf to ease global economic turmoil.

Burnham also revealed he will use his first meeting with Trump on Tuesday to urge the US president to de-escalate the conflict in Iran, warning that “dark clouds of global instability” are directly affecting people’s lives all over the world.

The turmoil in the Middle East has pushed up global energy prices, putting the UK economy under intense inflationary pressure and increasing government borrowing costs to multi-year highs just weeks before a crucial first budget for the new government.

On the flight to the United Nations in New York, Burnham told reporters that an RAF Voyager would help refuel Saudi jets for several weeks, in his first military deployment since taking power, after the Houthis advanced to areas adjacent to the crucial Bab al-Mandab strait.

The key Gulf ally has used the waterway as an alternative route for oil exports bypassing disruption in the ⁠strait of Hormuz. The RAF operational support is in addition to the UK Sky Sabre air defence system already operating.

“We have received a request from Saudi Arabia for military support and … I agreed to that request for defensive air-to-air refuelling. On cost of living pressures and acting to secure the interests of Britain, the wider region … we need to keep those pathways open,” Burnham said.

The prime minister also plans to press Trump to wind down US action in Iran, which has destabilised the region, blocked key supply chains and unleashed global economic volatility, including in the UK, where the government will struggle to drive down the cost of living as a result.

“Of course the message is that we want to see an end to the conflict as quickly as possible and we stand ready to play our part,” Burnham said when asked if he would raise the issue in talks with Trump.

As well as the focus on the Middle East, other major international challenges, including the war in Ukraine and artificial intelligence, are expected to dominate Burnham’s meetings at the UN general assembly.

The global security backdrop to the summit is bleak: European leaders have warned that Russia could launch a drone or missile attack on Nato territory within months to test the strength of the alliance.

Burnham’s speech to the UN is expected to focus on harnessing the power of AI, amid concerns at home over the safety of the rapidly advancing technology. He will be accompanied on the trip by his AI minister, Kanishka Narayan.

The prime minister’s first face-to-face meeting with Trump is a significant moment, with the US president still said to be angry over the UK’s refusal to support his military action in Iran, and ongoing tensions over levels of defence spending.

Burnham will attempt to highlight the importance of the security partnership after the UK and US launched a heavyweight torpedo, designed to sink ships and deep-diving submarines, in British waters last week from a Plymouth-made drone named Excalibur.

Government insiders, however, are taking some solace from Trump’s low-key response to UK sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, after weeks of diplomacy with the White House over the summer.

They are also hoping to avoid a clash over energy policy. The prime minister is expected to signal to Trump that he is in favour of more drilling in the North Sea, including the Jackdaw gasfield that is likely to get the green light within weeks.

Analysts believe the balance of risk for the bilateral relationship has shifted since Keir Starmer was in office, given the Republicans face a difficult set of midterm elections and the US president’s personal ratings are plummeting.

Trump is also likely to be more focused on his meeting with the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and his address to the UN, which comes shortly before the talks on Tuesday.

Government sources told the Guardian that Burnham would try to pursue a “third way” in his relationship with the US president, neither as adversarial as the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, nor as publicly fawning as Starmer’s early approach, and relying on the strength of his personality.

Asked whether he felt he could trust Trump, Burnham said: “Yes, of course, we trust our allies. Of course, we do.” Pressed whether this applied to the US president personally, he repeated: “Yes.”

Downing Street said the prime minister wanted to use his UN meetings – which will also include the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen – to “drive opportunity and deliver hope”, making progress on areas with the potential to deliver for people at home.

Burnham has focused on domestic issues since his arrival in No 10, despite Starmer warning that it would be impossible to separate them from global affairs, given how the Ukraine war is weighing heavily on UK security and the Iran conflict on the economy.

On the flight Burnham acknowledged they were inseparable. “[Starmer] was right to say it’s about how we deliver back at home and the situation in the Middle East is a very clear example of that. It is a very big driver of the cost of living pressures that we’re currently facing,” he said.

Before the trip, Burnham’s official spokesperson said: “The British people at home are at the forefront of the prime minister’s mission in New York this week. Because to deliver at home, we must ensure we are leading international efforts to brighten a darkening global picture …

“To give people the breathing space they need, he is clear we must work with our international partners to face up to the biggest challenges of our generation. So this week at [the UN general assembly] he will be leading the charge on the global issues that impact people’s lives at home.”

Burnham will tell world leaders the UK will focus on AI and climate change when it hosts the G20 in Manchester next year, potentially causing ripples with Trump, who has previously criticised the UK’s stance on global warming.

The meeting gives Burnham an opportunity, however, to host international allies on his home turf, although the location of the summit was chosen under the Starmer administration.

Burnham has been accompanied on the trip by his wife, Marie-France van Heel, who No 10 said would be meeting her international counterparts and supporting the prime minister, whose father, Roy, died last week.

Davey is expected to lay out plans in his speech on Tuesday for a new international AI safety agency – modelled on the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and headquartered in the UK, after numerous warnings from AI researchers that artificial intelligence could wipe out humanity within the decade. “We didn’t leave the atom bomb to a few billionaires to police themselves,” he will say.

Davey is expected to call for a new global movement to work together to protect humanity from the risks of super-intelligent AI, saying that the IAEA was built by nations “working together to control a technology that could destroy us all”, but warning that the future of AI is being decided by “a tiny number of the richest and most powerful in California and in Beijing” with no guardrails to slow down development.

On Monday, the prime minister announced a new AI partnership with the US ahead of Trump’s address to the UN general assembly on Tuesday.

It comes after the Lib Dems’ home affairs spokesperson, Max Wilkinson, on Monday announced that the party proposed a big tech levy and promised to create a new online crime agency focused on offences including child sexual abuse material, trafficking in drugs and weapons, and deepfake AI-generated pornographic images.

Wilkinson said the Lib Dems would properly regulate use of Meta’s smart glasses, which he called “perv goggles”, telling the conference that the glasses “are more than a benign piece of tech that provides a bit of fun” and that people – especially women – were being recorded without consent or warning. “This is becoming the new norm, because this government won’t stand up to big tech to protect our civil liberties,” he said.

Davey defended himself in a series of interviews on Monday about complaints his party lacks vision, saying it was pointless to try to compete with the attention-grabbing ideas of the likes of Reform UK and the Greens.

“It’s a very noisy environment at the moment,” he told the BBC. “But let me tell you, some of the noise generated by the populists are things that divide our country, that are nasty, or that are just completely crazy. I don’t want to do that. I want to tell people that we have really well thought through policies that will cut their taxes.”

Asked if he would propose further tax cuts in the wake of the pledge to slash 10p from fuel duty for three months, Davey replied: “Absolutely.” These would, he said, be financed by higher economic growth due to the Lib Dem proposal to seek entry to the EU’s single market.

“I think it’s good when other parties start talking about Liberal Democrat priorities,” he said. “We have led the debate on social care and carers because it’s so important for our health service. We’ve led the debate on political change because we need to change our political system, and Mr Burnham seems to be up for that.”

Celia Birtwell ‘humanises’ Burberry in London fashion week closing show

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 21:30:07 GMT

Textile designer brings florals, vines and smiley doodles to brand’s luxury checks for one-off paired collection

Burberry and Celia Birtwell are both national treasures of sorts. One is Britain’s grandest luxury name, the other the textile designer who dressed bohemian 1960s London in her prints and has a place in art history as David Hockney’s favourite muse.

Burberry’s designer, Daniel Lee, has always loved Birtwell’s prints. When the two met this spring, he fell for “her energy, and her zest for life”, and a one-off Burberry meets Birtwell collection that closed London fashion week was born.

Burberry’s calling card is a graphic check; Birtwell is all blowsy doodled florals and psychedelic snaking vines. “The check is so dominant and so brilliant that at first I thought: what can I do here?” Birtwell said before the show. She hand-painted a less regimented version, which Lee loved. “She made the check more human. If you are buying a luxury product it’s not a necessity, it’s an emotional purchase, so it needs to feel human.” A doodle of round, Smartie-bright faces from her archive, drawn 20 years ago but never produced, became another print of the season.

The mood of the show, held around the corner from Burberry HQ at Chelsea School of Art, was buoyant: charming prints, soft silhouettes, and the eclectic guest list that is as much a Burberry signature as the check itself: actor Fiona Shaw and footballer Djed Spence on the front row, with rapper Central Cee making a cameo on the catwalk.

Burberry is bouncing back from its crisis years, steered by its chief executive, Joshua Schulman, and designer Lee. This summer, the brand reported its first revenue growth in three years, as retail sales rose 5% year-on-year in the second quarter. Schulman’s strategy is offering “value for money in a luxury context”, which translates as pivoting from an ill-fated attempt to sell Burberry handbags at Hermès prices to more realistic price tags. Lee has brought a youthful, gen Z inflection to the Britishness that is Burberry’s calling card.

A successful element of its turnaround has been Burberry zeroing in on the outerwear market, where Burberry has bona fides to best every other name. British heritage is a trump card when it comes to coats, and the appeal of the Burberry name reaches from arctic explorers to football fans. For this summer collection, trenches came in slinky silk taffeta, with puffball hems and ruched collars; one model carried an embroidered umbrella, against summer showers.

To amplify its London fashion week message, Burberry is staging a small display in an upstairs gallery of the V&A museum in South Kensington, which will be open to the public until 3 January. The Burberry Trench: Crafting an Icon includes a military overcoat worn by a lieutenant colonel in the British army in 1939, designer Hardy Amies’ own Burberry trench, as well as metallic leather and gold snakeskin runway trenches from recent catwalk shows.
