Infantino proposes an ‘independent external review’ of Fifa governance

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 21:05:26 GMT

President writes to council and member nations

Infantino says he is ‘fully committed to leading Fifa’

The Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, has agreed to commission an independent governance review after coming under mounting pressure to do so in the wake of the World Cup sale debacle.

The Guardian revealed last month that several members of the Fifa council had been lobbying for an external review of both the proposed Fifa Forward Enterprise sell-off and the Folarin Balogun controversy – with the Football Association chair, Debbie Hewitt, increasing the pressure last week by writing to Infantino demanding the release of all documents relating to both issues.

Infantino opted not to engage with the disgruntled members of the council, but in a letter sent to all 211 of Fifa’s member associations he has indicated his willingness to submit to external scrutiny for the first time.

In addition, Infantino also invited proposals to review Fifa’s internal decision-making processes, which he said would be discussed at the next Fifa council meeting in Zurich on 15 October.

“First, I will ask the council whether it wishes to commission an independent external review of Fifa’s current governance framework for major strategic initiatives and recommend potential improvements,” Infantino wrote.

“Second, I will propose that the council establish a direct, structured and time-limited consultation with confederations, member associations and relevant stakeholders on how Fifa’s decision-making can be further strengthened.

“The consultation would invite specific proposals on earlier institutional involvement, the respective roles of the president, the bureau, the council and the congress, and practical ways to strengthen transparency, participation and accountability in major strategic initiatives.”

The Fifa Council, which comprises 28 representatives of the six confederations, eight vice-presidents and Infantino, is certain to approve the commissioning of an external review, although its terms of reference will be crucial in determining whether the world governing body is open to significant change or whether this represents the latest attempt by Infantino to shore up his power base before the presidential election in March next year.

The Wargame review – Michael Gove is awful at pretending to be PM in this mind-warping reality show

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 21:00:25 GMT

The premise is an imminent attack on Britain by Russia in a world in which Michael Gove is prime minister and Nicola Sturgeon his deputy. It’s enjoyably terrifying – and the politicians’ stiffness is huge fun

Trigger warning: this review contains the phrase “Michael Gove cosplaying as PM.” There is no helpline.

The Wargame is mind-warping. On the one hand, it posits an imminent nuclear strike on Britain by Russia. Bad! On the other, it posits this happening in a world in which the government is composed of Michael Gove cosplaying as prime minister, Nicola Sturgeon as his deputy, Harriet Harman as home secretary, Sayeeda Warsi as attorney general and Penny Mordaunt as defence secretary. So, you know, there’s a competing “Come, friendly bombs …” vibe too.

How does it happen, you wonder? Is there a long process of producers wooing, cajoling and making increasingly tempting offers to their putative cast members while these sober adults thoughtfully weigh the pros and cons, and the risk to professional reputations that any foray into the entertainment sphere represents (and The Wargame is essentially a heavily scripted reality show) before eventually signing on the dotted line? Or – politics being showbusiness for ugly people and all that, and large numbers of modern politicians being BoJo-type vortices of insatiable need and ego rather than the public servants of yore shaped by ancient notions of faith and duty – did they all come running? Were they begging for parts, flashing teeth and thighs and playing coquettishly with their lapels as soon as rumours of the commission made their way down the hallowed corridors of Westminster? We may never know. We may have our deeply held suspicions. But we will never know.

The four-part double-faceted nightmare that is The Wargame is set nine months in the future. Is this a coded warning to have your affairs in order and a stockpile of beans to hand by next summer? Given Channel 4 also recently aired televisual urban prepper manual Apocalypse, we cannot rule out the possibility that somebody, somewhere is trying to tell us something.

Here, we begin with a Cobra meeting, convened after the assassination of two RAF pilots and a malware attack on regional ambulance services. Which hostile force is behind them and are they linked? Hmm. The politicians all agree that they should wait for more information. The intelligence services and military brass round the table roll their eyes and go off to get it. News comes that a Russian spy ship has been found in Blighty waters, hovering over the undersea cables upon which 93% of our national infrastructure depends, and that everything can probably now be connected to Russia.

The programme starts off relatively slowly: people spend a lot of time telling each other that “This is straight out of the Russian playbook!” and you can see Gove straining to appear statesmanlike when there is nothing yet to be particularly statesmanlike about, which would be endearing if it wasn’t risible. But soon the twists and turns begin. Developments start gathering pace by the end of the first episode and the momentum builds to enjoyably terrifying proportions by the end of the third (the finale, alas, was not available for review).

When does a hostile act become an indisputable act of war? Can you hope for the best but prepare for the worst without giving the wrong signal to your enemies or your electorate? Can the electorate usefully be informed of anything in the social media age, or is everyone essentially a dysregulated toddler now? Can we depend on our allies? What about the one that is led by a dysregulated toddler now? Is there ever a point at which you have to stop thinking about optics and just do what you think best? Is there anyone left who can do that?

All these big questions are interestingly gestured at. But of course the real entertainment – and The Wargame rapidly becomes almost too much fun for something resting on the threatened annihilation of millions – lies in seeing who works well on camera and who doesn’t, and, on that basis alone, working out who you would actually want in place when the motherfunking shit hits the motherfunking fan.

Gove, Harman and Sturgeon are fabulously awful. Stiff, self-conscious, self-important, entirely unable to give any portion of themselves up to the purported reality or the flow of the thing. Sturgeon is an alternately whining and furious goblin, Harman a disappointed schoolmarm and, though I suspect he is desperate to do so, Gove cannot modulate his perma-condescending tone – whether he is addressing his fellow cabinet members, his military advisers or the nation.

Meanwhile, Mordaunt, Jim Murphy (Foreign Office minister in real life 2007-08, foreign secretary here) and Gen Richard Barrons (joint forces commander IRL 2013-16, chief of defence staff in TV land) are like MGM movie stars by comparison. Swift, decisive, plain-speaking (Murphy is the first to swear and he times it beautifully) and – yes, in an uncrowded field – charismatic, these are the people I want deciding my fate. Within The Wargame, sure. But also, at this point, maybe out here, too. If this is not just a warning to us but an audition for them, consider this trio through to the next round.

The Wargame aired on Sky One and is available on Now.

Airlines urge action after UK flights delayed and cancelled again

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 20:45:05 GMT

Nats says fault at Prestwick has been ‘fixed’ after airports in Scotland, northern England and Northern Ireland are hit

Airlines have called for “action and accountability” over the UK’s air traffic control services after a technical issue led to flights being disrupted for the second time in a fortnight.

Dozens were cancelled and others severely delayed after a fault on Monday morning at National Air Traffic Services (Nats), this time at its second control centre at Prestwick in South Ayrshire.

The fault, predominantly affecting Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England, was fixed by about 10.30am, but only after airlines including British Airways and easyJet were forced to make cancellations.

A Nats spokesperson said it had been “working with airports and airlines to safely lift air traffic regulations as quickly as we can to minimise any further disruption”, and apologised for the disruption. They said the problem was “unrelated to the issue two weeks ago”.

Despite the relatively quick fix, at least 200 flights in and out of UK airports were expected to be cancelled by the end of Monday, according to the analysts Cirium.

The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, posted on X just after 10.30am, notifying that the latest technical issue had been resolved.

She wrote: “I know this will be deeply frustrating for passengers after the previous issue. There may be some delays as things reset.”

The incident came less than two weeks after a serious problem at the Nats control centre in England disrupted travel for hundreds of thousands of passengers, and only three days after the company released an initial report that promised to “continually improve the critical service we provide”.

Nats said Monday’s incident had been caused by a connectivity issue at its Prestwick centre.

Among the stranded passengers at Glasgow were a bride and groom who had expected to fly to their Las Vegas wedding with family and friends. Their BA flight to Heathrow was cancelled, meaning they would miss their connection to the US on Monday, and they rebooked for Tuesday.

The bride-to-be, Barbara Ann Stoddart, said: “I’m completely stressed out. I have still to go to the county court in Vegas to go and get the marriage licence, and I’ve got to be there three days in advance … If there’s any hiccups I might not be getting married on Saturday now.”

The Civil Aviation Authority said it had reminded airlines of their responsibilities to look after passengers whose flights were delayed or cancelled, but that passengers were unlikely to receive compensation for delayed or cancelled flights.

“We consider that disruption caused by the technical issue at Nats Prestwick centre in Scotland on 21 September is likely to be considered the result of ‘extraordinary circumstances’ under passenger rights rules.

“This means that although passengers should be looked after by airlines, they are unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays or cancellations that were directly caused by the incident,” a CAA spokesperson said.

Airlines called for action to address repeated failures, with Ryanair reiterating its calls for the Nats chief executive, Martin Rolfe, to resign.

EasyJet, one of the most-affected airlines on Monday, said the latest flight disruption “once again calls into question the resilience of Nats’s systems and demonstrates the need for firm actions to prevent these repeated failures”.

BA described it as “yet another technical fault with Nats” and said it was disappointing.

Jet2’s chief executive, Steve Heapy, said it was “simply not good enough for this critical national infrastructure to keep letting customers down”.

Alexander has commissioned the CAA to conduct an independent review of Nats and check the findings of its initial report into the 8 September breakdown. She said the government still needed “to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos”.

Andy Burnham, asked whether the head of Nats should be sacked, said Alexander would have to “get to the bottom” of the problems.

Come back soon Premier League, the endlessly moreish mega-product

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 20:30:24 GMT

Brighton have impressed in a goal-laden start to the season, in a league that remains a brutally strong attraction

Get ready for the dopamine crash. And this one really is a proper autumn nosedive. The past 17 days up to and including Sunday’s cut-off gave us 30 Premier League games and 79 goals. Which, if you take Spurs out of it – and this is fair because Spurs are now post‑goal, an entertainment concept unrelated to goals or even football itself – is really quite a lot.

Are your pathways stimulated? Are the neural connectors flickering? Well get ready for cold turkey, for 19 blank days of shivers and shakes until the Premier League show resumes in October. Maybe it really is time to buy one of those powders off the internet.

The international break will provide its own intrigue. There will be discussions about whether Thomas Tuchel is or isn’t responsible for the inherited cultural weaknesses of English football. There will be rage at Tuchel’s inability to coach the players to keep the ball as never before via his few short hours on the training pitch. And yet more rage at the real issues, basically the fact he continues to be German and looks like a scurvy-ridden Napoleonic naval commander powered solely by ship’s biscuits and morphine.

This is unlikely to fill the hole. There will be an unavoidable “contrast effect”, the rush of adrenaline that only serves to deepen the low when it is gone. But there are also some familiar autumn rituals to help us through. One of these is the state‑of‑the‑nation Premier League address, pegged out around key questions such as “where are we?”, “what are we?” and “where is it all going?”. This time around these are relatively easy to answer.

Five rounds into the Premier League season this is pretty much a cut-and-paste job. The big news: there is no big news. Events continue to happen at great volume. But in terms of teams, style, stars, energies and potential outcomes, not much has changed. Roll back one year and this was the broad situation. A powerful team with a bald, irascible manager had won all five games, but also looked defensively fragile. The team that would win the league was second. That team was also Arsenal.

The middle classes were the most interesting story, those functional, well-run teams beginning with B, an entity you might call Brightonmouth. Erling Haaland was scoring goals. Bruno Fernandes was generating hair‑tearing anguish, like a young Elvis, but based more around shithousery and risky attacking passes.

As ever there are still some key questions doing the rounds, but luckily these can all be answered easily. Is Michael Carrick the man to take Manchester United to the next level? No. Is Michael Carrick the reason United are not at that level, but in a state where they must now employ Michael Carrick? Also no.

The reality for United is that there are no other levels. This is the level, a club that instead acts as a grand, angst-ridden but very accurate metaphor for modern‑day Britain, furiously retailing its own heritage, run by fill-ins and opportunists, a mobile waxwork museum living on tourism and memories.

Are Tottenham doomed? Probably not. They have enough semi-interested players to retain a solid hold on 17th place. Although frustratingly for Premier League content addicts, even this has been degraded by repetition. Spurs could get relegated now and you would just keep scrolling.

Are Liverpool on the verge of a renaissance? Probably not. The Jürgen Klopp golden era is beginning to look quite distant, surrounded on all sides by something a bit like the present. And, yes, Florian Wirtz is a very good footballer. He just can’t resist contact very well, which is non‑negotiable in the Premier League. He is going to be really good at Paris Saint-Gemain/Bayern Munich/Inter.

Otherwise, it is a case of stasis and a reliable, entertaining, homogenised product. Tactically, we can still get excited about small changes. If you analyse it deeply you may find a little more counterattack, Anthony Elanga running fast, an inverted winger discovering almost by accident he can also cross with his strong foot.

It is a mark of how standardised the game has become that these are deemed things worth getting excited about. There is still only one elite level style, the Omniball template of the Cruyff-Michels-Guardiola-Gegenpressing school.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

This is skewed towards physicality over control in England, but it still produces football that can feel at times a bit like driving a brand new electric car: fun, high‑grade, but also endlessly repeatable. It seems possible some time soon that a robotic bait‑the‑press system will meet a robotic bait-averse system and in that moment football will just cease to exist, reduced to two banks of human units staring at each other across a strip of empty grass.

There are two things the Premier League could really do with in the remaining 87% of its season. The nudge into greater physicality is exciting and distinct. It is notable how many games have been decided by duels, collisions, a sense of greater wanting-it. Or perhaps not so surprising when the players are at roughly the same technical level, where the only real point of difference is sustained physical power and competitive will.

This is one reason why Brighton’s defeat of Arsenal on Saturday seemed so interesting. It is rare to see any reigning champions not just beaten, but outskilled and outmuscled. For 90 minutes, only one of these teams looked like genuine contenders for every trophy on offer.

This is the second thing the league could really do with. Is it possible for one of the well-run middle class to sustain this level over a season and give us another Leicester or something close? Can Brighton just play like that every week?

There are obvious answers why not. One very good game against an ambushed Arsenal is not a 38-game slog. Brighton have a good squad, but also regular midweek football. Other teams will react and nullify your strengths. Also, and this is not a throwaway detail, Fabian Hürzeler is going to be on TalkSport for an hour on Tuesday just chatting football, which will now include how did you beat the champs and why are you third in the league.

Nothing wrong with this. But it is an indicator of where we are. Hürzeler is 33. The entire job is essentially reinventing himself, just as all of the very good players at those middleweight clubs are auditioning for bigger clubs rather than dreaming of hauling them in, playing for the life-changing money a Champions League-level club will throw at them, motivated by a breezy and entirely logical collective individualism.

Perhaps this is why one of the themes of the season has been a suspicion among fans of bigger clubs that their players don’t want it enough, that being outrun or outworked is a sign of soul sickness or debauched management. But it is also what keeps the league brutally strong, state of the art, and endlessly moreish for all its repeated story arcs. Come back soon Premier League mega-product. The comedown is already hitting.

A coalition of four other networks – ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC, who with CNN form part of a “pool” which take turns providing television coverage of presidential events – said they would not cover events in solidarity with CNN.

“Effective today, the TV pool will not be covering events designated as pool coverage of the President,” Bryan Boughton, Fox News’s Washington bureau chief who also serves as TV pool chair, wrote in an email to pool members. “This follows the White House’s position preventing CNN from fulfilling its assigned pool duties.”

As a result, viewers tuning into the White House feed on Monday could not hear Trump’s remarks during a midday ribbon-cutting ceremony unveiling the new White House helipad. Without proper audio, viewers were only able to watch the president’s mouth move while listening to the sound of the helicopter’s engine running.

In a show of support with the banned outlets, several outlets, including the Washington Post, the New York Times and the Associated Press, said they would not publish or distribute images taken as part of the White House photography pool on Monday, including the president’s departure on Marine One and his events at the United Nations in New York, until midnight eastern. In a statement, the Washington Post described the action as part of a “collective effort”.

The five news networks, including CNN, wrote in a joint statement: “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”

Although the broadcast networks said they would withhold televised coverage, the print, radio and wire service press pool continue to provide reports detailing Trump’s movements throughout the day.

Hours after the broadcast networks’ announcement, the Washington Post said it would also withhold its photographs of presidential events from being published until after midnight eastern time to support banned outlets.

On Friday, Trump abruptly announced he was banning CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House because, he believes, they “constantly write or report FICTION and LIES”. On Saturday, reporters and other staff from the news organizations were denied access to the White House.

Other media outlets and first amendment advocacy groups responded by condemning Trump’s ban, calling it an infringement on the right to a free press.

On Monday, CNN, Politico and MS Now filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration, asking a federal judge to temporarily block the enforcement of the ban and restore the reporters’ passes to the White House.

On Truth Social, Trump defended his decisions, insisting that his ban was not “instituting an assault on the Free Press”, but instead addressing “national security” threats – a claim the US president has recently used to justify building a triumphal arch and the White House ballroom.

Is it true that … cycling affects fertility?

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 19:00:23 GMT

Saddling up is only likely to be an issue for elite athletes – and those with low sperm counts

“Cycling isn’t big on the radar of fertility doctors,” says Prof Colin Duncan, a fertility expert at the University of Edinburgh.

For women, he says, the only time cycling is likely to affect fertility is when it’s done at extreme levels, such as the kind of training undertaken by elite athletes.

“Doing huge amounts of physical activity can lower body fat, and that can switch off the ovaries,” he says. “Elite athletes may stop having their periods and reduce their fertility.”

For men, things are a little different. Sitting on a bicycle saddle for prolonged periods can increase the temperature around the testicles, “almost incubating them”. This can affect sperm production, because sperm develop best at a cooler temperature – one reason the testicles are located outside the body.

But for most men, Duncan says, this isn’t something to worry about. “The testicles produce way more sperm than is actually required for fertility.

“If you cycle a normal amount, it’s still going to make absolutely no difference at all. But if you’re doing extreme cycling, it will change your sperm count a little.”

Even then, he says, the impact is more likely to matter for men whose sperm count is already borderline. “If you’ve got a really good sperm count, it probably doesn’t make an awful lot of difference. You’ve still got a lot of sperm there that are swimming.”

In fertility clinics, Duncan says he’ll consider lifestyle factors when assessing a patient’s sperm sample. “If there are abnormalities I’ll get a sense of what their lifestyle is like and talk about changes,” he says. “If you’re doing certain things to excess – smoking, drinking, saunas – it’s probably worthwhile moderating that.”

Ten lessons from Jakob Ingebrigtsen, one of the world’s most beguiling athletes

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 19:00:23 GMT

Norwegian is meticulous in his training regime – ‘if there’s anything that’s out of my control, then I’ve not done my job properly’

On a snowy Norwegian morning in January, Jakob Ingebrigtsen was on his treadmill, shooting the breeze about his running philosophy before our more formal interview. I should write something on this, I told him. Sure, came the reply.

In recent weeks, the 26‑year‑old has added to his legacy with a European 5,000m gold, the World Ultimate 5,000m title and a world road silver medal despite achilles surgery in February and a flu that lingered through May and June. So now seems as good a time as any.

Some of Ingebrigtsen’s opinions were a little hardcore. Others reiterated basic truths. But whether you are a runner or not, there are certainly some life lessons from one of the most beguiling athletes around.

1) To be the best it helps to be a control freak

Ingebrigtsen runs a lot, around 175-180km in a typical week. Apart from his family, that is his sole focus. “I prioritise the absolute crucial,” he says. “That is to wake up, to eat, to train.” It is, he concedes, not a life most would enjoy. “A lot of people could never be in my shoes, having my responsibility. They just wouldn’t handle it. But that’s how I want to be. If there’s anything that’s out of my control, then I’ve not done my job properly.”

2) No days off

“If you have a day off, you lose 20-25km of running,” he says. Counterintuitively, perhaps, he believes the risk of injury goes up too and tries to run even when he is moderately poorly.

“Having one week off if you are sick, injured or travelling, or even just doing easier training, that’s probably the worst thing you can do in terms of risk of injury. Because you are taking your body out of a consistent load. When you get back again, you will have sore legs because your body is not adapted to that load and when you compensate, or just change symmetry a little bit, that’s when something snaps.”

3) Consistency is king

Ingebrigtsen runs twice a day, in the morning and afternoon, with hills on a Saturday and a longish run of 20km on a Sunday. He supplements this with drills, mobility and core work on Monday and Wednesday and weights every Friday and Sunday. He does this week after week after week unless he is injured. Consistency, and gradually increasing load, is a lesson he says amateur runners should apply.

4) Be prepared to work very hard

Ingebrigtsen is famous for his double threshold runs on Tuesday and Thursdays – two runs each day that aim for the sweet spot between hard, but not brutal, fatigue, but sustainable. A morning session, for instance, might involve 5x6 minutes effort with a one‑minute jog for recovery between repetitions. In the afternoon it could be 25 times around a 400m track at 5km-10km pace with 30 seconds recovery.

Ingebrigtsen says that while he runs more miles than his 1500m competitors, “the biggest difference is how often we train and the size of our sessions – we very rarely do more than 10km-12km of quality in one session”. He adds: “With having more sessions you can spread the volume out a lot more without having spikes and peaks in load.”

5) No slacking even on Christmas Day

“Last year, I ran twice and did 22k. I think that counts as an easy day,” he says, although he had to watch for digestion problems. “Christmas dinner in Norway is very rich in fat because we have pork ribs. I just had to be a little bit careful with the amount because we have different sausages, sheep and meat cakes too.”

6) The treadmill is your friend, whatever time of year

“I’ve always used treadmills, not only because of the conditions in Norway, but also to control a lot of the variables,” he says. “I put it on a certain speed, at a certain incline, and it’s always the same. It doesn’t matter if the wind is from the north or if it’s raining or cold.” He also does a morning threshold session on his treadmill, even in the height of summer, with punk and rock bands Green Day, Blink-182 and Black Sabbath topping his playlist.

after newsletter promotion

7) Fast shoes help with recovery too

Ingebrigtsen wears speedy and bouncy shoes for most of his running, with the Nike Zoom Fly 6 among his favourites. “You can decrease the load and impact by the amount of cushioning that’s now available in shoes,” he says. “So if I can get out of my Monday to Sunday programme 95% fatigued, that is enabling me to do the same the next week with the same amount of quality … just with 5% extra intensity.”

8) Training in mud is a waste of time

Ingebrigtsen sneers at the old-school approach of lots of running on trails and cross-country. “It is pointless. Training in mud or grass is not something I believe in. Let’s say I was going into a field and all of a sudden I’m doing 1k reps in mud and stones. Think about the extra risk that I’m taking, not only in terms of load and training but also tripping and snapping my ankle? Why would I risk it?”

9) Always question what coaches can teach you

Perhaps this is explained by Ingebrigtsen’s relationship with his father and former coach Gjert, who he ended up facing in court in 2025. But he is adamant that discussing everything with his brothers Henrik and Filip is better than a top-down approach.

“With a lot of coaches, it’s more like a priest. You can get really attached to them and it’s almost dangerous in the way it takes away responsibility from the athlete. If you have an ex-professional runner as a coach, it is always going to be ‘I did this, I did that, this is what worked for me, this is something new and revolutionary’. I don’t believe in it.”

10) You always have to keep yourself accountable

Some truths are universal when it comes to running and life. “You have to take responsibility for yourself,” he says. “Each individual and every athlete needs to build their own toolbox regarding their qualities and maybe lack of qualities. Responsibility, I think that’s the key word. And accountability.”

Venezuelan man shot by ICE agent as enforcement surges in Austin

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 18:41:11 GMT

The shooting of Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez comes months after increased federal immigration enforcement across the Texas capital

The shooting of a man by a federal officer on Sunday in Texas ruptured an ostensibly quiet afternoon amid an immigration enforcement surge in Austin.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has been very active in the Texas capital of late, although less showy than the militarized federal violence in Minneapolis this January, helping keep the operation effective but flying under the national radar. Then shots rang out.

Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was in the process of delivering a DoorDash food order on the city’s north side when ICE encountered him shortly before 1pm. Video posted online appears to show an ICE officer getting out of his car and shooting at Garcés Pérez’s car three times.

His car, as later visible at the scene, had a large dent on the front passenger side. Garcés Pérez, who was hit once in the back between his shoulder blades, is a Venezuelan national who has lived in the United States for two years, according to his lawyer, but had been ordered removed from the US. Garcés Pérez told onlookers who rushed to the scene that he had been shot because he hadn’t stopped.

Austin police officers who arrived could be seen in bystander footage rendering first aid to the bleeding man, while ICE officers stood back. Garcés Pérez was taken to a downtown hospital for treatment but, according to lawyer Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, was whisked away from there by ICE late Sunday afternoon.

For a few hours, his partner and the lawyer could not locate him, then on Monday morning Lincoln-Goldfinch told the Guardian he’d been located at the South Texas ICE Processing Center, located 140 miles to the south-west, in Pearsall.

“Bullet still lodged in his back. No pain meds,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said by text on Monday.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, did not respond to questions about the circumstances leading up to the shooting, or Garcés Pérez’s whereabouts and condition.

Austin, the politically liberal capital city of conservative Texas, has repeatedly found itself at the crossfire of the immigration debate.

The state’s Republican leadership has often sought to make an example out of the city, forcing local leaders to weaken Austin’s policy of not collaborating with ICE.

For more than a year, state police have handed countless unauthorized immigrants over to ICE during traffic stops, but the city police had not joined in.

Cooperation between state or local law enforcement and federal immigration enforcement is arranged under so-called 287(g) agreements, which have been proliferating in the second Trump administration, especially in states such as Texas and Florida.

But even with that, some local leaders said this summer has marked a low-profile but aggressive surge in immigration enforcement in the region, spurred by a jump in ICE acting alone rather than relying on state troopers to stop people and pass them on. Lawmakers reported ICE stopping cars in traffic or asking people about their immigration status in public sites like parking lots and gas stations.

“I think it needs to be said that as mayor of the city of Austin, I’m very angry about this,” Kirk Watson, the city’s Democratic mayor, said on Sunday during a press conference after the shooting. “A person being shot on the streets of Austin by someone purporting to be law enforcement, particularly when it’s ICE, is something that causes me to be unhappy and angry. And while I’m unhappy and I’m angry about it, I’m not surprised at all. It’s happened in other cities, with the nature of ICE and the way ICE is doing its business these days.”

In an initial statement issued shortly before midnight on Sunday night, DHS said Garcés Pérez was in stable condition and that he was “in federal custody pending removal” out of the US.

The agency also said that it was leading the investigation into the shooting, alongside the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). However Austin leaders have called on city police and the Texas Rangers, part of the state’s Department of Public Safety, to aid with the investigation, citing public distrust in DHS. They have also demanded that the agent involved in the shooting be kept in Texas as the investigation continues.

The exact details leading up to the shooting remained unclear on Monday.

Video posted on social media shows a man running out of the black SUV and shooting at Garcés Pérez’s mostly stationary blue sedan from behind it. Three gunshots ring out. The car moves up a few feet and then stops.

Nedavia Bolaños and her husband were the first witnesses on the scene. The couple, owners of a Mexican ice cream shop just off the intersection of the shooting, ran outside after they heard the shots. For several minutes, they pestered the only ICE agent on the scene about what had happened.

The agent, masked in what appears to be a black balaclava, stood there, saying only that he wanted the couple to stay at a distance. He did not render aid, a video Bolaños provided exclusively to the Guardian shows. They acknowledge that an ambulance has been called, as the man sits in the driver’s seat, clearly in pain and clutching his chest.

That video then shows Austin police arriving at the scene minutes later. After helping federal agents handcuff Garcés Pérez and seat him on the ground, they cut off his black T-shirt to reveal a bullet wound between his shoulder blades.

About 10 minutes later, an ambulance arrived and carried Garcés Pérez away, Bolaños said.

Within an hour, more than a hundred protesters had gathered at the site. State and local police formed a barrier around the dozens of federal agents, who based themselves under the highway median. The protesters chanted expletives and waved Mexican, American and Guatemalan flags, some of which had been bought on the spot for $20 from a hawker who set up shop nearby. Several protesters could be seen washing their eyes and mouths in pain, after they were sprayed with what they said was teargas or chemical spray.

The protests grew and lasted late into the night, resulting in several arrests, according to local news reports.

The shooting comes after several months of increased immigration enforcement, particularly in the immigrant-heavy north side neighborhood where the shooting occurred, as well as several predominantly Hispanic suburbs and exurbs.

Austin city council member José “Chito” Vela, who represents the neighborhood where Garcés Pérez was shot, said that he has heard constituents describe an increase in immigration arrests since the start of the summer, an enforcement bump driven by a rise in unilateral action by ICE. While ICE was largely seen making immigration arrests after Texas Department of Public Safety traffic stops for the first year or so of the second Trump administration, they have begun to act increasingly on their own, Vela said.

City leaders had previously raised concerns over the increased action. Congressman Greg Casar, an Austin Democrat who leads the Congressional Progressive Caucus, has sent a letter to DHS demanding cooperation in an “immediate, independent investigation” into the shooting, the full release of any footage the federal authorities have of the shooting, and “accountability for any wrongdoing by the agent responsible”.

Rwandan man charged with crimes linked to 1994 genocide in first case brought in UK

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 17:38:14 GMT

Dr Vincent Brown will appear at Westminster magistrates court charged with seven offences

A man has been charged with crimes linked to the genocide in Rwanda in 1994 in the first case of its kind to be brought in the UK.

Dr Vincent Brown, formerly Dr Vincent Bajinya, 65, who used to live in Kigali, the capital of Rwanda but now lives in Islington, north London, will appear at Westminster magistrates court on Tuesday charged with seven offences.

The charges are one of conduct ancillary to genocide and six offences of conduct ancillary to murder as a crime against humanity, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said.

Frank Ferguson, the head of the CPS special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “The charges relate to allegations that Dr Brown took part in the genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda in 1994.

“He is alleged to have directed and incited acts of murder and genocide carried out by others.

“The Crown Prosecution Service made its decision after reviewing a file of evidence submitted by the war crimes team at the Metropolitan police.

“We concluded that our legal test for bringing criminal charges had been met.

“The Crown Prosecution Service makes prosecution decisions independently of police and government, on the evidence available and in accordance with the law. Criminal proceedings against Dr Brown are now active.

“The defendant has the right to a fair trial, and it is extremely important that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information online that could prejudice those proceedings.”

The charges arose after an investigation by the Metropolitan police war crimes team, which began in September 2019 after a request from the Rwandan government.

This was to investigate those allegedly involved in a genocide in the Rugenge district of Kigali in April 1994.

Commander Helen Flanagan, the head of counter-terrorism policing London, said: “To secure the first-ever UK charges related to a genocide has involved a huge amount of work and determination from officers in the war crimes team.

“This case demonstrates the UK is not a safe haven for individuals suspected of committing international crimes.

“The war crimes teams remains committed to ensuring those suspected of involvement in genocide and other atrocity crimes are held accountable through due legal process.

“A number of other investigations remain ongoing into other individuals in the UK for similar offences related to the genocide in Rwanda.

“Our thoughts remain with the people of Rwanda, particularly those who lost family members and loved ones during the genocide against the Tutsi.”

The Guardian view on Friedrich Merz: Germany’s chancellor must change course to halt the rise of the AfD

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 17:34:09 GMT

A failure to address widespread economic insecurity, and a crisis in living standards, is allowing the far right the harness a growing protest vote

After less than a year and a half in office, Germany’s beleaguered chancellor, Friedrich Merz, is already looking like a lame duck leader. Anticipating dire results in two state elections which were held on Sunday, Mr Merz cancelled a planned speech at this week’s United Nations general assembly in order to plot an emergency response. A night of extraordinary humiliation for his conservative Christian Democratic Union party (CDU) must have confounded even his own low expectations.

In the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the far-right Alternative für Deutschland party (AfD) won its second regional election this month with 38% of the vote. The CDU meanwhile recorded its worst result since the second world war, failing even to meet the 5% threshold for representation in the state parliament. Mr Merz took over the leadership of the CDU promising to see off the threat of the AfD. Instead it has ascended to a menacing and unprecedented position of electoral strength, and enjoys a comfortable lead in national polls.

In the other regional contest, the CDU ceded control of the mayoralty in Berlin and finished second behind the radical Left party, which campaigned on a platform to address the capital’s soaring housing crisis. These were seminal reverses, but Mr Merz shows no sign of learning the lessons from either defeat. Defiantly dismissing speculation over his future, he insisted that his coalition government was “determined to live up to the historic responsibilities our country is facing”.

Without a change of political direction that seems improbable. Suffering from depopulation and persistent inequalities relative to the west, Germany’s eastern regions have been particularly vulnerable to the rise of one of Europe’s most extreme far-right movements. But as the continent’s powerhouse economy struggles with Chinese competition, US protectionism, and a cost of living crisis, there is nationwide disillusionment with the chancellor’s abrasive style and “tough love” prescriptions. Mr Merz’s personal poll ratings hover at a record low of around 13%.

Doubling down on a programme which includes raising the retirement age, cutting health insurance benefits, and making it much more difficult to claim sick leave, is hardly likely to turn those numbers around. The Social Democratic party (SPD), as the junior coalition partner, has attempted to act as a partial brake on the chancellor’s pro-austerity instincts. But as one of its despairing MPs acidly observed of Mr Merz: “He constantly asks people to work more, while tens of thousands of jobs are currently being cut in German industry!”

The constitutional obstacles to removing a chancellor – and the reality that neither the CDU nor the SPD want a new election given the state of their respective polling – mean that Mr Merz is likely to stay in post. But if the government’s fortunes are to revive, a radical rethink is required. The chancellor’s unsuccessful strategy for spiking the AfD’s guns has been to ape its draconian positions on immigration. But it is the failure to address a crisis in living standards and widespread economic insecurity which allows the far right to channel a growing protest vote.

That is deeply worrying. On Monday, Mr Merz emphasised that Germany’s “democratic future” must be defended. He was right to emphasise how much is at stake. But it is becoming increasingly and alarmingly clear how ill-suited he is for that task.

The Guardian view on rape courts: ministers know that victims deserve better

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 17:33:34 GMT

New facilities for witnesses who have been sexually assaulted are a step towards halving violence against girls and women

The creation of specialist courts to try rape and serious sexual offences in England and Wales is a welcome recognition from the government that the status quo is unacceptable. Victims, the vast majority of whom are women and girls, are being failed by a system that too often appears blind to the obstacles in the way of anyone who wants to see a perpetrator brought to justice. In 2025, rape cases took an average of 424 days after they had reached the crown court. Added to pre‑trial delays, this means thousands of lives being placed on hold for years.

Long waits are simply unendurable in many cases; a rape review ordered by Conservative ministers in 2021 found that the proportion of complainants dropping out of cases had risen from 25% to 43% in five years. As well as the harm caused to individuals, there is an obvious impact on public safety when perpetrators go unpunished, and chances to rehabilitate them are missed.

Plans for clearer scheduling, so that rape trial dates are fixed in advance, ought to make the whole experience easier to manage. A funding boost for victim support services, and commitment to greater continuity, will strengthen the framework around them. This follows other recent changes, including an extension of the period during which a sentence can be reviewed, included in the Victims and Courts Act.

Ministers have already committed, in their violence against women and girls strategy, to specialist units in every police force. This week’s announcement signals that an important argument has been won, about the need for dedicated training and tailored approaches in the courts as well. But implementation of both commitments will be a huge challenge. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has set an ambitious timetable. Specialist police units are due to be in place by the end of next year, with the courts given slightly longer to prepare facilities including separate waiting rooms for victims and links to observe sentencing hearings remotely.

Two new taskforces have been unveiled in recent days. One will bring together experts to focus on rape justice. The other, chaired by Bridget Phillipson, the women and equalities minister, will focus on misogynistic attitudes. This twin-track approach is promising in that it addresses the underlying causes of violence against women and girls, as well as the criminal justice response. But having pledged to halve such violence in a decade, ministers will need results to convince the public that they are on track. This is all the more important given past failures, and the eagerness of rightwing parties to exploit the issue of violence against women at every chance.

The backlog in the courts is a problem that goes wider than sexual offences. Restricting jury trials was the wrong solution, but a bigger role for magistrates has the potential to bring down waiting times. Court hours should be increased where this is feasible. Scrutiny of the Crown Prosecution Service’s decisions on rape cases must also continue, along with efforts to tackle the disturbing rise in online sexual offences, including image-sharing. The criminalisation of pornography featuring strangulation should be viewed as a step on a journey towards making the internet a safer place. This is a daunting agenda that stretches across government. But with concrete changes to the courts and victim support, ministers have shown an intention to grasp it.

Another day, another Reform Wales leader. Grumpy Nige seems to miss the old one

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 17:08:43 GMT

At a low-key event, Helen Jenner replaces Dan Thomas, who was arrested on suspicion of assault and gets warm words from Farage

Twenty-five or so Reform members of the Senedd were lined up against a wall. Almost as if they were in a police identification parade. Reform’s need to find a new leader in Wales is becoming habit-forming.

First, Nathan Gill was banged up for 10 and a half years on eight counts of taking £40K in bribes to make statements in support of Russia. Easily done. Who among us hasn’t been tempted by the Kremlin? And then last week, Dan Thomas chose to stand down after being arrested on suspicion of assault and coercive behaviour, leaving the Welsh leadership spot open once more. He denies the allegations.

It’s almost as if there’s a pattern emerging. That the job of Reform leader in Wales is somehow cursed. Otherwise law-abiding men and women suddenly find themselves accused of all sorts of things. So much so that it’s now the job that no one really wants.

Yet politics abhors a vacuum, and someone has to do the job. So it was a decidedly grumpy-looking Nigel Farage who turned up in Cardiff on Monday morning to pretend to be interested in announcing the next Reform Senedd leader. Perhaps he reckoned he had better things to do.

The event – if you can call a five-minute announcement that – was supposed to kick off at 11.45. Nige was booked on the 12.18 back to Paddington and had hoped to be in London for a late lunch. No champagne and oysters. There were no undercover reporters posing as Americans trying to make a potentially illegal donation this time. Instead, there was a 20-minute delay.

Nige really was going through the motions. He was thrilled by the results in Wales at the May elections, he began. He didn’t sound thrilled. Though that could be because Reform has been shedding support in Wales – as elsewhere – ever since. They have lost seven points in the opinion polls over the course of the summer and are looking less and less likely to challenge Plaid Cymru.

“Dan Thomas has been doing a brilliant job,” Nige continued. “I am sorry for his personal difficulties.” This was just weird. Almost as if he hadn’t even considered what Thomas had been alleged to have done. Yeah, Dan. Great bloke. Brilliant Reform leader. Always buys his round in the pub. It’s just unfortunate that he’s been arrested on suspicion of assault and coercive control. But it’s no big deal. He’ll soon be sorted.

Nige doubled down, calling the arrest a “bump in the road”. Not a word of sympathy or support for the person he is accused of having assaulted or subjected to coercive control. Besides, he was clear that Dan would come back soon. There would always be a welcome in the Reform valleys for Dan. We all need someone like Dan.

After the Song for Dan, Nige made the briefest of introductions to the new leader. Best to skip over the bit where almost half the Reform members of the Senedd had preferred a different candidate. The party in Wales is a hotbed of backstabbing. Not literally, mind. The job was going to Helen Jenner, the former deputy leader and Nige’s old-time Ukip mucker. “I’ve known her for years and I trust her,” he said.

Helen mumbled her thanks and said she would build on the good work done by others. It wasn’t clear if Dan would take over from her if he is cleared of the allegations, which he denies. It sounded like a possibility. In which case, I guess Dan might then only be keeping the seat warm for Nathan when he gets early release in 2031. You have to admire Reform’s loyalty.

And their amnesia. Because you also can’t help wondering if Nige is beginning to lose the plot somewhat. How else do you explain his recent Substack post in which he claimed that “British politics is awash with dirty money”? I mean, he’s obviously not entirely wrong. But why would he want to draw attention to it when questions remain over money received by Reform and figures associated with the party?

There’s the £40K that went to Gill from the Russians. There was the apparent eagerness on the part of Dan Jukes and James Orr to accept overseas donations. A meeting at which Nige was present. Though not listening, apparently. There’s the dosh from Ben Delo, a man convicted of failing to comply with anti-money-laundering legislation in the US.

There’s the cash from Posh George and his mum that is somewhat opaque to say the least. There are the police and parliamentary investigations. The £5m gift that went undeclared. With the best will in the world, none of this seems the model of transparency. But what do I know? And it’s good to know that Reform operates in a world where any transgressions are so readily forgiven.

Race to be next UN secretary general could rest on US and China trade-offs

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 16:56:29 GMT

Numerous possible last-minute entrants being discussed as current field of seven candidates struggle to garner support

Numerous last-minute entrants in the race to become the new UN secretary general are being discussed amid concerns that the world powers may not be able to agree a successor to António Guterres from the current field of seven candidates.

Three rounds of secret ballots have so far not produced an obvious frontrunner, with probably only three candidates regarded as still having a realistic chance of gathering the required support.

The new leader, due to take office in January, will face an organisation at the start of a cost-cutting overhaul programme and seen as marginal to the major global conflicts.

But surveys still show strong international support for the institution among a public that blames world leaders as much as the UN itself for its recent failing.

A survey by GeoPoll for the UN Foundation published last week found six out of 10 people trust the UN to deliver on the issues that matter to them, but 85% said they had heard nothing or little about the process to choose a new secretary general.

The successful candidate must win the support of nine current members of the 15-strong security council with no veto by any of the five permanent members of the council – France, the UK, China, Russia and the US.

Achieving consensus among the permanent five is fraught given the breadth of political divisions. Guterres’s term ends on 31 December.

Names being mentioned as potential late drafts include Lana Nusseibeh, the minister of state at the United Arab Emirates and a former UAE ambassador to the UN, and Sigrid Kaag, a former UN under secretary general and Dutch centrist politician. She was briefly the senior humanitarian and reconstruction coordinator for Gaza before joining the advisory committee to Donald Trump’s Board of Peace.

Other candidates mentioned include Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, the polyglot president of Kazakhstan, and, in deference to the US, Viktor Orbán, the former prime minister of Hungary, who is still much admired by Trump but reviled as a disruptive populist by many European leaders.

Vuk Jeremić, a Serbian former president of the UN general assembly who came second behind Guterres in the 2016 race, has also been mentioned.

None of the speculated candidates have given any public indication they wish to be drafted.

A communique at the end of this month’s Brics summit attended by 21 countries, of which 10 are full members, said: “We note that no woman has ever been elected for the role of secretary general, and only one national from Latin America and Caribbean, and only two nationals from Africa and Asia each have ever occupied this position.”

Some would also resent a late candidate, regardless of their origin, entering the field since strenuous efforts have been made to democratise the selection process by holding regional and global hustings. The last general assembly president, Annalena Baerbock, has helped spearhead the attempt to open the selection process.

But the need to avoid alienating any of the five, internally divided, veto-wielding security council members inevitably incentivises the candidates to issue slightly bland consensus-seeking statements at a time when the organisation needs firm leadership. All the candidates have said they would like to see the UN return to an active role as a peacemaker – a task often demanded by amateur US diplomats close to Trump.

In the third and last straw poll of the 15 security council members on Friday, Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica regained the lead after receiving nine “encourage” votes from the security council. She got five “discourage” votes and one “no opinion”. Her fear is that the discourage votes came from Russia and China, an opposition she would need to overcome.

In the second straw poll on 21 August she had dropped behind Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, a Guyanese politician who then came first – receiving eight encourage votes, three discourage and four no opinions.

Last Friday, Rodrigues-Birkett maintained the eight encourage votes, but her discourage votes had risen from three to six.

A third candidate, the Ecuadorian former finance minister María Fernanda Espinosa, is just about still a viable contender despite the numbers discouraging her reaching six last week, up from three in August. She has been calling for an early warning system inside the UN to help prevent wars, and for a secretary general more willing to take risks in mediation.

It will not be until later in the process – when colour-coded balloting reveals if a vote is from a permanent member of the security council or not – that it will be clear whether a candidate faces an insurmountable barrier.

In reality the decision may turn on the horse-trading between the US president and the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and whether Trump accepts that China cares more about the UN’s future than him, and that may mean accepting a candidate that China wants and the US can tolerate.

The Trump administration appears to have softened some of its scepticism towards the UN under the US ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz. The US not only provided $1.8bn (£1.35bn) in additional humanitarian funding in March but also recently sent $827m in dues, admittedly less than a quarter of what it owes the cash-strapped organisation.

Michelle Bachelet, a former president of Chile and a human rights campaigner, became the first candidate to drop out of the race at the weekend after she received only one encouragement in last week’s poll.

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 16:54:14 GMT

President to meet Ukrainian counterpart in New York as Ukraine steps up attacks on Russian energy sector

Donald Trump is expected to press Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy on an energy ceasefire during a face-to-face meeting this week during United Nations high-level week, as world diesel prices have soared due to the war in Iran, as well as Russia’s war in Ukraine.

Ukraine stepped up its attacks on Russia’s energy sector over the weekend, launching its largest reported strike yet on the Moscow region in a barrage that struck a major Moscow oil refinery and killed three people.

On Monday, Trump said the whole world was suffering due to an energy shortage that he said was being exacerbated by the war in Ukraine.

“Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine,” Trump said in a Truths Social post on Monday morning. “A large number of their Diesel refineries have been blown up and are, at least temporarily, out of commission.”

“This ridiculous and never ending War with Ukraine must be ended,” Trump said. “The whole World suffers as 25,000 people, mostly soldiers, are being killed each month. What a shame!”

Trump had earlier blamed Kyiv for the escalating energy war even as Russia has decimated Ukraine’s economy and launched night barrages of drones and ballistic missiles against Ukrainian cities.

Zelenskyy on Monday said negotiations were continuing and that that there are “ideas on the table for bringing peace closer, starting with strong de-escalation steps”.

“Ukraine’s energy sector, critical infrastructure, and our food exports must stop being targets for Russia, and this will lead to matching de-escalation steps on our part,” he said in a statement. “Solutions are possible.”

The two leaders are expected to meet on Tuesday during a rare sitdown on the sidelines of the high-level week of the United Nations general assembly. Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov will also be in Washington this week, and is expected to meet with secretary of state Marco Rubio.

During a trip to Ireland last week, Trump directly addressed Zelenskyy, saying he has to do “one thing: he has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia”.

“Let him go after targets but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage,” he said.

Trump spoke with Zelenskyy on Sunday in a phone call that one senior Ukrainian official told the Financial Times was about “diesel, diesel, diesel”.

Average diesel prices in the United States hit a record $6.50 per gallon on Monday, up from $3.19 per gallon this time last year before the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran and Tehran responded by closing the Strait of Hormuz to most international trade. The rise in prices is seen as a liability for Trump’s Republican party in the US midterm elections, which will take place in November.

Trump is expected to deliver a speech to the UN general assembly on Tuesday morning, and is expected to meet with major energy producers including the Gulf Cooperation Council and Venezuela’s recently installed leader Delcy Rodriguez.

In a preview, Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, said Trump would speak about how he has “confronted complex problems head-on around the world. Many of the peace deals that he has driven to conclusion, or is in the process of driving to conclusion.”

Trump last week prematurely announced an energy ceasefire under which Ukraine had agreed not to hit Russian energy targets and that “Russia has agreed to do likewise!” The deal had not been agreed, however, and Russian strikes against Ukrainian energy and other critical infrastructure have continued.

Britain loves its underdogs. We should be celebrating our Eurovision flops, not investigating them

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 16:51:39 GMT

The digital, culture, media and sport select committee is to explore why the UK’s entrants are frequently ‘dismal’. Surely such a trifling matter is not worthy of the House of Commons

The State of Play inquiry, which is run by the UK House of Commons’ digital, culture, media and sport select committee, recently announced the five areas on which it will focus in 2026-27. One of these is: why are our Eurovision entries so bad? The word used by the chair, Dame Caroline Dinenage, was “dismal”, which is parliamentary speak for “shit”.

The evidence is all around. With the exceptions of Sam Ryder (second in 2022) and Jade Ewen (fifth in 2009), the UK has bumped along the bottom of the table in recent years, coming last in 2021 and 2026, second last in 2023 and 19th and 18th in 2025 and 2024 respectively. In four of those cases, the artist received no public votes at all.

Mindful that parliamentary inquiries always take roughly 10 times longer than seems reasonable and cost whatever number of pounds they ought to multiplied by a million, I’m going to suggest a couple of sub-categories. Why do all the other countries hate us, irrespective of the entry?And why do we seem to enjoy it so much that they do? Some of this is about core British values and some of it is about geopolitical orientation. Sometimes those things interact in such a white-hot and contradictory way that it’s amazing no one has devised a way to give us minus points.

A national underdog fetish drives the selection. Whomever we send, they cannot take themselves too seriously; they have to be self-mocking. But that’s not enough: they have to be so absurd that they can’t generate the level of ridicule required alone. Our entry this year – by Sam Battle, AKA Look Mum No Computer – was no less catchy and flamboyant than many Scandinavian entries past, but some combination of trying too hard for the laugh (which was knowing and ironic) and trying too hard to speak German (“look, Mum, I – a Briton – can count to three in a foreign language”) did not translate into popularity. While we love an underdog, we also hate sincerity, which presents confusingly. Come on, Britain, do you think you’re inferior or superior? Make your mind up!

Our refusal to pick a lane on this matter is another core British value. But however you articulate that – a love of ambiguity for its own sake? A reflexive, historical rebellion against being asked to emote sincerely? – other people don’t like it. Ryder is an interesting counterpoint. He slipped through the net by which we typically exclude anyone who can hold a tune, having garnered fame on the socials with his acoustic balladeering during Covid. The year in which he competed, 2022, was the tail end of a poignant time during which we briefly admitted to the experience of real feeling – loved each other, loved the NHS, loved society. That didn’t last, unfortunately.

Leaving aside the music, the UK is often awarded nul points to signal disapproval of its foreign policy. This seemingly began in 2003, because we had jettisoned European values (looking for evidence, considering consequences) in favour of American ones (going to war because, heck, we could). In 2008, our next brush with the dreadful zero, bestowed by 38 of the 42 voting countries, the objection was to the “big four” – the UK, Germany, France and Spain – getting automatic entry into the final stage of the contest. Eurovision was being used to symbolise the arrogance of these dominant countries after the financial crash. (No, I don’t have to prove that. It’s obvious.)

I want to say that the more recent low scores may be down to Brexit, but that would raise the question of why we did so badly in the years directly before it (17th in 2014 and 24th in 2015). It may just be collective muscle memory: “Hey, I remember these guys! They’re the ones we always give nul points.”

If I were involved in Eurovision, I would put together a counterinquiry to ask why the digital, culture, media and sport committee is so dismal. Alongside the cultural crises worthy of its attention this year – the structure of the football academy system, the role and funding of arts centres, the protection of journalists in conflict zones and inclusion in football management – it has chosen this matter of no consequence, this trifle, this contest we actually enjoy being bad at. It has managed to produce the inquiry equivalent of one of the UK’s Eurovision entries, which is, now I think about it, quite a British thing to do.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

‘Half my day’s pay goes to filling up my car now’: diesel crisis ripples across Britain

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 16:29:25 GMT

Small traders and drivers bear the brunt of a refining shortage taking forecourt prices towards £2 a litre as wars wipe out about a fifth of global supplies

The smoke rising from the Kapotnya oil refinery to the south-east of Moscow marks one of Ukraine’s biggest air raids on the Russian capital since the start of the war, and the latest salvo in an energy crisis that threatens to affect households and businesses across the globe.

More than 1,500 miles away, British motorists are braced for the ripple effect from that conflict, and the US-Israel war on Iran. Average UK diesel prices are expected to reach record highs within days – while across Europe and the US, pump prices have already surpassed all-time highs.

In a call on Sunday, Donald Trump pressed Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian refineries over concerns that the attacks were pushing up global fuel prices, the Financial Times reported. On Truth Social, Trump said Russia has “unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry” and called for an end to “this ridiculous and never ending war”.

While the price of Brent crude oil – which briefly fell below $100 a barel on Monday – remains in flux, already hard-pressed households and small firms face a far greater cost threat at forecourt pumps as the combined impact of Russia’s war-damaged refineries and the Middle East crisis has erased about a fifth of the world’s diesel supplies.

“Around half my day’s pay goes to filling up my car now,” says Jon Barden, a former humanitarian adviser turned handyman, who says his fuel costs have doubled. His diesel Ford estate, once used for camping trips, is now used to carry heavy tools to jobs around Tottenham in north London.

Across Britain’s forecourts, the average price of diesel has climbed by 54% to 196.28p a litre since the Middle East crisis began in late February. It is expected to reach a record £2 a litre within days, with some forecourts already charging above the psychologically important mark.

In Europe, pump prices have already hit record highs in recent weeks, leading to unrest and growing calls for government leaders to protect consumers from the surge in cost.

While the popularity of fully electric and hybrid petrol vehicles may be on the rise in the UK and Europe amid attempts to move away from polluting fossil fuels, diesel remains the overwhelmingly dominant fuel. It is the single biggest cost for many independent traders and small business owners, powering transport, tools and services. It is also the economic lifeblood for farmers, and logistics and haulage businesses, layering costs on to grocery bills and consumer purchases.

“I’ve had to put my prices up,” says Barden. “I don’t want to because the people around here don’t have a lot of money. But when fuel prices go up everything else follows. The things I need to buy from Wickes to do a job will cost more before I even fill up,” he says.

In part, the surge in fuel prices is due to the rise in global oil prices following Iran’s effective blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, a vital trade route for Gulf oil. The price of Brent crude has climbed to a four-year high, raising the cost of refined oil products such as diesel and gas oil.

Yet the most pressing energy crisis is not a shortage of crude, but a shortage of the refining capacity to turn crude into the fuels consumers need. The Middle East crisis has severely damaged many of the region’s refineries, which once supplied 10% of the world’s fuels. What little can be produced has struggled to circumvent the blocked trade artery.

Output from Russia’s war-damaged refineries has fallen by almost a third over the past year to reach a 20-year low following sustained drone attacks by Ukraine, according to the International Energy Agency. The latest strike on Kapotnya came after a similar attack by Ukraine in June.

Although Russian oil exports have been subject to toughened EU sanctions since 2022, a reduction in exports to other parts of the world, including Asia, is likely to push up global prices.

In China, which hosts the world’s largest refining capacity, and had been the largest importer of Iranian crude, exports of refined oil products have been capped since March to safeguard the country’s domestic supply.

The global refining slump has helped to keep oil market prices down by dampening the demand for crude. But this is cold comfort for economists who warn that the ‘crack spread’ – or the price difference between crude oil and its refined products – has climbed above $100 a barrel on the continent for the first time and is likely to rip through the economy by raising the cost of all transported goods, as well as household bills.

Diesel in particular is “the workhorse fuel that powers business, haulage, deliveries and rural communities”, according to Luke Bosdet, the AA spokesperson on fuel prices. “Increased fuel costs are passed on to customers, and then on to consumers, which adds to inflation.”

While sales of new diesel passenger cars have plummeted over recent years as motorists increasingly opt for petrol, hybrids, and electric vehicles, the UK’s consumption of diesel has continued to climb because of its role as a crucial industrial fuel.

“Almost everything on supermarket shelves got there on a lorry,” Richard Smith, the managing director of the Road Haulage Association said. “When diesel goes up that cost has nowhere to go but on to the price of goods.”

The AA’s chief concern is for “small businesses, such as taxis and vehicle-based services, and rural communities who already do higher mileages even before diesel costs went through the roof”, Bosdet adds. “They don’t get to add diesel surcharges to invoices, like many of the big companies, for fear of losing customers.”

Mehmet, from Clacton, began driving black cabs in central London 35 years ago. “When I first started, diesel cost 10 bob a gallon,” he laughs. In modern terms this would be 11p a litre, or a fraction of the looming £2 a litre average expected nationwide within days, while cab fares remain capped.

Diesel taxis are easily outnumbered by EVs in London, but they still make up about a third of the black cabs. Drivers were told in February that they would be allowed to raise their fares by 4% this year. At the time, the rise was above inflation – amid concerns over an exodus of black cab drivers. However, the US-Israeli bombardment of Iran ignited a war that has caused fuel costs to surge and inflation to remain well above the Bank of England’s 2% target, at 3.1% last month.

“We’re stuck with it,” says Mehmet. “We don’t want the meter price to go up, because then we lose custom. But we can see oil companies making billions in profit while we take home less. How can that be right?”

The UK may be acutely exposed to the global squeeze on road fuel supplies. The number of refineries in the UK has dwindled since the start of the century from nine to four, causing the UK’s reliance on diesel imports to climb from 14% of the UK’s diesel consumption in the early 2000s to 54% last year, according to Fuels Industry UK.

Elizabeth de Jong, chief executive of Fuel Industry UK, said: “Our latest annual statistics, published earlier this week, show that UK demand for petroleum products increased by 1% in 2025 to almost 61m tonnes, while the closure of the Grangemouth and Lindsey refineries reduced UK refining capacity by almost a quarter.

“We are currently having to import about 55% of our road diesel, meaning a growing dependence on overseas supply. Global events such as the conflict in the Middle East demonstrate the vital role that UK refineries play and why they are crucial to our economy,” she said.

The continued deployment of Jofra Archer and Josh Tongue at the end of a long, all-format summer for the pair is also notable. The next 12 months are about building towards the 50-over World Cup in southern Africa, meaning full-strength ODI XIs where possible and T20 series likely to involve more squad rotation.
