Get tested and talk to your partner: how to have safer sex after age 50

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 16:00:19 GMT

At 51, I want many more years of a healthy, happy sex life. So I decided to compile my own guide

When I got divorced after 28 years of monogamy, I was excited to be having sex again, but had concerns. I was 48, and the last time I’d been single was in the 90s; terrified of pregnancy and hyperconscious of HIV/Aids, I hadn’t considered condomless intercourse an option back then.

Now, at 51, I’ve been wondering how important barrier protection is for me. Though I haven’t hit menopause, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) says that “by 45 getting pregnant naturally is unlikely”, and HIV/Aids prevention and treatment have improved significantly in the last three decades.

When I consulted with my physician, she said I should still “be careful” but didn’t provide specific guidelines.

Frustrated, I started researching. I found books on safer sex for older adults, such as Never Too Late: Your Guide to Safer Sex after 60 by Dr Shannon Dowler. But I wanted something more concise, like the pamphlets we saw as teens. I want many more years of a healthy, happy sex life. So I decided to compile my own guide, with expert advice about how to have safer sex as an older adult.

No sex is totally risk-free – at any age. This reality is reflected in the American Medical Association (AMA) using the term “safer sex” since the mid-90s, rather than “safe sex”.

So it’s certainly important for people in their 50s and beyond to think about safer sex practices – not least because they are having more sex than ever.

“People are living longer,” said Dr Tyler Evans, infectious disease physician and CEO of the public health organization Wellness Equity Alliance. If you add sex-enabling factors like dating apps for older adults and medical advancements in sexual longevity, you get a more sexualized older population, he said.

It’s true that pregnancy becomes far less of a concern at this stage. During the years leading up to menopause, a woman’s fertility steadily diminishes. After menopause, which happens at 51 on average, according to the ACOG, natural conception is no longer possible.

But sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are another matter. “While STI rates have stabilized in younger people, the rates for 55 and up are increasing,” said Dr Sarah Berg, a board-certified OB-GYN, Menopause Society-certified practitioner, and founder of Selfority, a menopause education platform. “The chlamydia rate for this age group has more than tripled the past decade, gonorrhea has gone up sixfold and syphilis has increased even more.”

(A quick note: the term STD, or sexually transmitted disease, used to be common. Educators and healthcare providers consider “STI” a less stigmatizing term.)

Older adults can contract the same STIs younger people can. But they may overlook infections, as symptoms can be mistaken for those of other age-related conditions like menopause, arthritis or urinary tract infections. As a result, people may delay treatment, causing STIs to fester.

An age-related immune system decline can also make STIs more severe. “As adults age, their ability to mount a response to any microbial load decreases,” said Evans.

“A sexually transmitted infection might increase your risk for mortality,” said Dr Renee J Flores, professor of medicine at the McGovern medical school of UTHealth Houston and a certified sexual counselor and educator, “but only if left untreated.” She emphasized that communicating with partners, using barrier protection and testing regularly can significantly decrease risk.

There’s a straightforward reason: more sex in the over-55 population has not coincided with an increase in preventive measures.

This is partly because of a lack of information. “Many didn’t have sex education in school,” said Dr Janie Steckenrider, associate professor at Loyola Marymount University whose teaching and research focuses on gerontology, ageing and sexuality. “They don’t know the risks or the symptoms.”

There’s also a misconception among sexually active older adults that their partners aren’t sexually active. “They don’t see a need to screen,” said Flores. “They think they are the rare ones having sex, though they may be having unprotected sex with multiple partners.”

Online dating has also contributed to increased sexual activity with less social vetting. “It’s not like you’re dating the person you grew up with or who went to your church,” explained Steckenrider. “Somebody that you’re meeting on a dating app – you get whatever information they’re willing to tell you, and a lot of people don’t feel comfortable asking.”

Further, general practitioner often assume older people are not sexually active and often have “little to no medical training on sexual health and ageing”, Steckenrider said. “You fill out a questionnaire about your bowel movements and whether you have fallen, but there’s nothing about whether you’re engaging in unprotected sex.” A geriatric doctor or geriatrician may be more likely to ask or raise sexual health than a GP, said Steckenrider.

It sometimes falls to the patient to bring up the subject. Steckenrider referenced a University of Michigan study that found only 17% of older adults had discussed sexual issues with their doctor in the last two years – and in 60% of those discussions, the patient initiated it.

Get tested regularly: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s STI testing recommendations vary depending on age, sexual history, sexual practices, location and symptoms. If you’re over 50 and sexually active, your doctor may not recommend regular testing. “Bring it up if they don’t bring it up,” said Berg.

If you and a partner want to stop using barrier protection, “get tested together before you stop using condoms, not after”, Berg added. “And know that some infections take weeks, occasionally months, to show up on a test, so one clean result on day one isn’t the finish line.”

Communicate with partners: “It’s important to ask questions if you plan to get intimate with another person,” said Steckenrider. “This needs to be talked about beforehand – not in the moment.”

She gave some examples: have you had unprotected sex in the last six months? How many partners have you had in the last six months, including oral sex and any kind of intercourse?

Use barrier protection: According to the CDC, condoms provide the highest level of protection against fluid-based STIs, though they only offer partial protection against those that can spread via skin-to-skin contact. Dental dams and condoms can be used during oral sex.

Take prophylactic medications and get vaccines: Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for HIV is available as a daily pill or long-acting injection. After a suspected exposure to HIV, PEP is “very effective” if taken within 72 hours, according to the National Institutes of Health.

The HPV vaccine is FDA-approved up to age 45.

Sign up to Well Actually

Practical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good life

after newsletter promotion

Avoid sex when STI symptoms are present: Planned Parenthood recommends avoiding sexual contact, even with a condom, during active herpes outbreaks or when you have visible syphilis sores or genital warts.

Fluid-based infections, including chlamydia, gonorrhea and HIV, are transmitted when infected bodily fluids (such as vaginal fluid, semen, rectal fluid or blood) come into contact with mucous membranes, according to the CDC. They can also enter the bloodstream during vaginal, anal or oral sex.

STIs that spread through the blood might present a higher risk for post-menopausal women as “vaginal dryness at this age can cause bleeding, increasing the risk of sexually transmitting infections, particularly viruses”, said Evans.

Infections like syphilis, genital herpes and HPV spread primarily through direct skin-to-skin or mucous-membrane contact; fluids need not be exchanged. Transmission can occur even when an infected partner has no visible symptoms.

It depends – on whether you have symptoms or whether you are getting routine testing, and what you’re testing for.

Your doctor can administer a standard STI panel via urine samples or blood draws. The makeup of the panel may differ depending on your doctor or lab – common tests include chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis and HIV. Check with your doctor if you’re not sure what’s included.

For women in or beyond menopause, it is important to remain up to date with cervical cancer screenings with Pap testing, HPV testing or both. This is because they may see an unexpected rise in HPV either due to new infection or the reactivation of an old one, according to the NIH.

Genital herpes (HSV) testing is recommended by the CDC for individuals with active symptoms, such as genital sores, or who know they have been exposed. It is not always included in a standard STI panel, so you may need to request it specifically.

You can also request a swab in certain circumstances. “Swabbing is actually best practice for some anatomical sites,” Evans said, specifying that if you suspect vaginal, anal or oral exposure to gonorrhea or chlamydia, a swab may be more sensitive than a urine test is. You should also ask to have any active herpes or syphilis lesions swabbed; lesion swabs may detect these two infections before they show up in the bloodstream.

Genital warts from HPV infection are typically diagnosed visually, rather than swabbed, per the CDC.

Hepatitis A, B and C can all be passed by sexual contact, although the latter is rare. The CDC recommends that adults be screened for both hepatitis B and C at least once in their lifetime, but hepatitis A testing is not recommended for asymptomatic people. Many older adults may be vaccinated against A and B, but there is no vaccine for hepatitis C.

STIs can result in many symptoms, per the Mayo Clinic. For instance:

Burning with urination, unusual discharge, pain with sex and testicular pain are common signs of both chlamydia and gonorrhea.

Gonorrhea may cause spotting between periods (premenopausal women) or spotting (post-menopausal women).

Syphilis may present as a firm, round and painless sore at the site of infection.

Genital herpes can cause painful fluid-filled blisters and flu-like symptoms if it’s your first outbreak.

HPV is typically symptomless but can eventually cause genital warts or precancerous cell changes.

HIV often causes a temporary flu-like illness within two to four weeks of exposure, according to the NIH. Because HIV symptoms can be nonspecific and clinicians may not consider HIV in older patients, infection may be diagnosed late, per HIV. gov.

Many STIs can be asymptomatic, according to the Mayo Clinic; for instance, chlamydia in women is commonly asymptomatic. This is why getting your and your partner’s test results before engaging in unprotected sex is important.

Prevention and testing have improved significantly in the past three decades.

Many STIs are highly manageable and often curable if treated early. Gonorrhea, chlamydia and syphilis are treatable with antibiotics. For viral STIs, early intervention is very effective, according to the CDC: antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV makes the virus untransmittable once undetectable, suppressive therapy can reduce the transmission of genital herpes and early screening for HPV allows infected individuals to remove precancerous cells before they become cancer.

“There are risks, but the good news is there are a lot of prevention and treatment options,” said Evans. “The most important thing is to get educated, to become informed and talk to your medical provider.”

Amanda Zuckerman Klarsfeld is a freelance writer in New York City

Chancellor vows to stay on for Germany’s ‘democratic future’ after latest loss to far-right AfD

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 15:38:22 GMT

Merz seeks to shore up support after CDU loses two state elections and is ejected from Mecklenburg parliament

Latest German election humiliation puts Merz on borrowed time as CDU unrest grows

Germany’s beleaguered leader, Friedrich Merz, has vowed to keep his fractious coalition government together for the good of the country’s “democratic future” after his conservative party suffered a drubbing at the polls in two state elections.

Merz, who has vowed to plough ahead with an unpopular reform agenda, dismissed speculation over his position, saying it was vital that he and his coalition government remained in place.

“We are determined to live up to the historic responsibilities our country is facing,” Merz said on Monday. “It is about nothing less, and nothing more, than the democratic future of our country.”

Germany faces political uncertainty in the aftermath of three hefty defeats for Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) this month, with it ousted from a state parliament for the first time, and the far right and far left making strong gains at its expense.

On Sunday the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) emerged victorious in the coastal northern state ofMecklenburg-Western Pomerania for the third time in a German state, securing 38%. The anti-immigration, pro-Russia AfD party’s leaders predicted Merz would be out of office in months, as they set their sights on securing victory at the next federal election in 2029.

“The chancellor certainly won’t make it to the end of the year,” Leif-Erik Holm, the AfD’s top candidate in Mecklenburg, said. “I think the twilight of the chancellor’s era has begun.”

Merz described the results as a “disaster”, in particular the CDU’s ejection from Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania’s state parliament, where it failed to reach the 5% barrier needed after losing more than half of its voters to the far-right AfD and centre-left Social Democrats. The result was all the more shocking as Mecklenburg was once a CDU stronghold.

In Berlin on Sunday, the CDU fell to second place behind the far-left Linke party, which is on track to lead the next government in the city-state and could give Berlin its first Turkish-born mayor in its lead candidate, Elif Eralp.

In Mecklenburg, the SPD under its existing state leader, Manuela Schwesig, is expected to lead a three-party coalition government. Her campaign had focused almost wholly on presenting herself as a buttress against the AfD, as well as distancing herself from the federal government’s reform agenda. The SPD is Merz’s coalition partner in the federal government.

Although the CDU’s poor performance had been predicted, Sunday’s outcomes only added to the extreme pressure on Merz already after the CDU’s crushing defeat to the AfD in the state of Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago, which triggered the first serious speculation over his future as leader.

Last week, the CDU’s powerful regional leaders governing in eight states gave their backing to Merz, but questions remain as to how sustained their support will be. At the same time there appear to be few candidates willing to step up to the post, which is increasingly being viewed as a poisoned chalice.

On Monday, Merz dismissed the idea that the outcome was a personal rebuke. “The reasons for these election results go far beyond my own person,” he said. “We are witnessing a profound transformation of the political party system in Germany as well as in many other countries around the world.”

Karin Prien, the education minister and deputy CDU leader, accepted accusations that the government was failing to take voters’ fears seriously enough. But she said the government had no choice other than to continue trying to reform Germany from within, at a time of chronic economic weakness and global instability.

“Without support and steadfastness we will not be able to achieve the necessary reforms, which are by no means a given. Nevertheless, not everything can remain as it is,” she told the broadcaster Deutschlandfunk.

“The chancellor knows he will have to change, at least in how he addresses the people … We are a strong country, we have every chance of mastering this challenge together, but I believe that cooperating with each other will be crucial for this, and for the party it means we must broaden our appeal.”

Doubts over the efficacy and fairness of the government’s agenda – which includes an overhaul of the pension system, a reduction in overbearing bureaucracy and cuts to income tax for the less well-off – played heavily into both election campaigns.

On Monday, SPD leaders said they remained confident in their coalition with the CDU, but said that changes to the agenda were necessary.

Lars Klingbeil, the deputy chancellor and finance minister, said: “Saying we will ignore what the voters said to us in three state polls won’t work.”

While the country needed reforms, he said, they “must be fair and they need support in the population”. The labour minister, Bärbel Bas, also of the SPD, said the plans needed a “reality check”, but said “nothing would be more lethal than letting this coalition break apart over some technicality”.

Rubbing salt into Merz’s wounds, the Kremlin on Monday waded into the election analysis, calling the AfD’s win in Mecklenburg a response to Berlin’s refusal to buy cheap Russian gas, which has jolted the economy and caused prices to soar, contributing to voter dissatisfaction.

The Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said: “Naturally, Germans, ​or at ​least some of them, are looking for an alternative to the current authorities in order to improve their situation. That is a natural process.”

Europe is under attack from three sides – but the EU and Nato are unfit to defend us

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 15:37:32 GMT

Ursula von der Leyen’s outreach to Canada and new security proposals are wise – but she may not be the right messenger

Europe’s strategic predicament is ever clearer, and ever darker. The continent is at war, which is being fought militarily in Ukraine, but is escalating rapidly across Europe through hybrid attacks. Germany’s disclosure that it blames Russia for the drone attack at Leipzig airport; a Russian drone strike on a train near the Ukraine-Poland border; an Italian jet shooting down a Russian drone over Lithuania; flares fired from a Russian warship at a Danish helicopter – all within the space of a couple of weeks – tell a coherent story. Whether because Russia is bogged down and unable to advance in Ukraine, or because it believes the US will not come to Europe’s rescue, Vladimir Putin’s regime is ever more bent on escalating its aggression in Europe.

Putin’s calculus is not irrational. Trump never misses a chance to lash out at Europe – the latest example being his threats of further tariffs on the EU if Brussels proceeds to offer Canada “associate membership”. Europeans have grown numb to Trump’s insults and threats, but these threats do underline his deep antipathy, suggesting that if a Russian attack warranted a response, Trump might look the other way. The US certainly can’t be relied on to have Europe’s back.

This is the context in which Ursula von der Leyen caused surprise last week by proposing associate membership of the EU for Canada. To bolster Europe’s defences, the European Commission president also wants a “European security council”, and a mutual solidarity mechanism to respond to hybrid attacks.

While they have distinct rationales, these ideas fit into the same strategic logic: in a world of predatory powers, the “rest of the west” must huddle together.

The threats are not only external. Along with Putin’s Russia and Maga America, the rise of the far right in Europe completes a triangle of threats. The far right is a threat to liberal democracy. But by instigating internal division and pushing for disintegration, it also supports the divide-and-rule designs of predatory external powers, representing a challenge to Europe’s independence and sovereignty. It has taken the earthquake of the AfD’s successes in German regional elections for von der Leyen to acknowledge openly that Europe’s threats are also homegrown. Better late than never.

Faced with this unprecedented convergence of threats from three sides, leaders are scrambling for a response. Nato has what it takes to defend Europe against Russia. But if its majority shareholder – the US – is unwilling to step in, the question of its plans, structures and capacities is moot. If a hybrid attack on a European country caused civilian casualties, would Nato be bypassed if Washington signalled its unwillingness to act? Collective defence would not even be invoked if the anticipated result were the US’s betrayal of its European allies.

This is where von der Leyen’s emergency protocol comes in, filling the gap between the high-water mark of mutual assistance – article 42.7 of the EU’s founding treaty, which covers armed aggression – and nothing at all. The attacked state would activate the protocol, an emergency European Council would convene, and the commission and EU high representative would propose responses, including evacuation and medical support, stockpiling and energy security, economic coercion, military mobility and more. The mechanism could extend to like-minded non-EU partners, starting with Canada, Norway, the UK and Ukraine. The proposal to offer Canada associate membership, while still undefined, can be read in this light as well.

On paper, it all makes sense. In practice, it is hard to see such a mechanism operating seamlessly, let alone rapidly, given the EU’s organisational complexities, its slowness to act and its internal divisions.

Hence the proposal for a European security council, consisting of those countries willing and able to contribute to the defence of Europe, without the US if need be. Some of these countries would be EU members, but not all – again, Canada, the UK, Ukraine and possibly Turkey.

Both the problem and the solution are clear. To protect itself against predatory powers, what remains of the west must cooperate ever more closely. But the existing multilateral organisations – Nato and the EU – are unfit for purpose. Nato will remain anchored to the US, while the EU is slow and cumbersome, built for peacetime. Its membership, while large, is not wide enough, excluding key players in the wider European space.

Sign up to This is Europe

after newsletter promotion

Developing alternative forms of EU membership could be of interest not just to Canada, but to the UK, too. The idea was first raised by Berlin for Ukraine, in fact, but Kyiv turned down the offer, seeing it as second-class. Ukraine deserves full EU membership, but if a substantial associate membership is on the table in the short term, it should take that, while continuing to press for more.

The rise of far-right nationalism means that reaching consensus within the EU will become harder, not easier – which is precisely where the proposal for a smaller, more agile European security council comes in, provided far-right governments do not simultaneously come to power across major European countries.

Von der Leyen’s security proposals are sensible and urgently needed. The potential pitfall lies not in the message, but in the messenger. In her years at the helm of the commission she has grown a reputation for centralising power and overstepping boundaries, irking other EU officials in Brussels as well as European capitals. When it comes to security and defence especially, sovereignty is jealously guarded by the EU’s nation state governments. It would be tragic if European governments ended up killing off a set of good ideas because of Europe’s institutional turf wars. Rearranging the deck chairs on the Titanic is the last thing Europe and its partners need right now.

Nathalie Tocci is a Guardian Europe columnist

The Washington press corps needs to boycott White House events

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 15:21:19 GMT

CNN, MS Now and Politico accurately call last week’s sudden lockout ‘a direct assault on the first amendment’. That’s right

On Monday, the three news organizations that had been kicked out of the White House because of Donald Trump’s latest fit of pique sued the president and three top advisers.

An accompanying statement by CNN, MS Now and Politico accurately calls last week’s sudden lockout “a direct assault on the first amendment”.

The legal action is the right move, of course, and one that may prevail since the ban seems to be a clear case of what press-rights lawyers call “viewpoint discrimination”. In other words, Trump didn’t like their stories so he removed their access.

The president has been in a bad mood lately, for obvious reasons. Retaliating against the press is his favorite way to let off steam.

But something else, beyond legal action, is necessary, too.

“Time for the New York Times, Washington Post and Wall Street Journal to report on the White House from off campus,” wrote Richard J Tofel, an attorney and the longtime president of the investigative news organization ProPublica, who writes a press-related newsletter, Second Rough Draft.

In other words, the biggest and most influential “print” news organizations – along with the major broadcast TV networks – should take collective action by boycotting that briefing room and similar White House events until their journalistic colleagues get their credentials back.

The major TV networks took a commendable step in that direction on Monday by deciding to suspend “pool coverage” of presidential events, since CNN was assigned to the duty of recording events and sharing them with the broader “pool” of news organizations.

“There will be no replacement pool put in place,” stated Bryan Boughton, the Fox News Washington bureau chief and chair of the TV pool in a memo to the White House press corps.

It’s especially good to see because the White House press corps often talks a good game about solidarity and press rights, but they’ve mostly kept doing what they’ve always done – treating Trump like any other president.

He can ban the Associated Press from the briefing room for refusing to use the term “Gulf of America” instead of “Gulf of Mexico”. He can respond to a reporter’s question with the disrespectful command “Quiet, piggy.” He can (through his defense secretary) try to revoke journalistic access to the Pentagon and fire top staffers at Stars and Stripes, the military newspaper. His weaponized justice department can subpoena New York Times reporters or show up at a Washington Post reporter’s home and seize her devices.

He can even trash as the “worst” his loyal rightwing media outlet, Fox News, for its recent polling that showed Americans’ deep dissatisfaction with his handling of the economy. He’s an equal opportunity media-basher.

But, no matter, Trump still gets that annual invitation to the White House Correspondents’ Association’s fancy DC dinner, where he can insult the press and make personal attacks on reporters whom he finds displeasing or those he simply wants to single out for abuse.

He still gets treated with deference.

And the reporters who are not in particular disfavor continue to go to White House briefings and press gaggles.

In other words, he mostly gets away with it.

This most recent ban is one of the most serious actions yet, as the scholar of authoritarianism, Ruth Ben-Ghiat, declared, calling it “a moment of reckoning for America”.

It’s not only, she said, “part of the autocratic playbook, but the timing is no coincidence. Trump is well into the autocratic backfire process, thus entire media outlets he sees as threats must be banished.”

To put it bluntly, Trump is a bully. And bullies will keep bullying until they get a punch in the nose.

As much as he professes to hate the mainstream media, Trump depends on it. He wants the constant attention. He loves being in the spotlight, where his every utterance – no matter how unhinged or false – is blasted out to the public.

It will get through to him if that kind of attention is withdrawn, as it was on Monday with the pool suspension.

Back when the AP was banned last year, a former Washington bureau chief at the news service, Ron Fournier, had some broader advice for the press corps.

“No self-respecting journalist should attend a White House briefing while the White House bans the AP for not accepting state-mandated language,” he wrote on social media, using the hashtag #BoycottTheBriefing.

Yes, media organizations may issue strongly worded statements, and may join in lawsuits, but solidarity is too often a theoretical thing, not a practical action with real-life consequences.

They offer a rationale, of course. It’s of utmost importance, journalists and their bosses will tell you, to cover the president. Not doing so would be a dereliction of duty and would stoop to the president’s level. It would be, God forbid, unprofessional.

But here’s the thing: reporters do not need to do their journalistic duty from inside the White House, or in an impromptu gaggle with Trump.

“We don’t need our journalistic watchdogs to have ‘access’ to Trump,” as former CBS News justice correspondent Scott MacFarlane put it. (He is now the chief Washington correspondent at MeidasTouch, the progressive media company.) “Everyone in the press room should walk out in protest … and source up.”

In other words, don’t abandon the job. Report aggressively from “off campus”.

It is a matter of principle at this point.

And principle should trump access. Especially at a time when American democracy is teetering on the brink.

Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture

The last two seasons were grim for Spurs. This is as bad as it’s ever been

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 15:20:18 GMT

Pre-season thoughts of European qualification are already beginning to look bafflingly optimistic for Roberto De Zerbi’s team

Sign up for our free newsletter here

In March, Tottenham, fearing possible relegation, spent big to bring in Roberto De Zerbi, who will probably never go into a negotiation with a stronger hand. There was obvious improvement and they stayed up on the final day of the season. Since then, Spurs have spent a net £175m ($234m) on improving the squad. The message seemed clear: the fiscal caution of the Daniel Levy era was over and this was a club willing to spend. Yet Spurs go into the first international break bottom of the Premier League table.

To an extent, the issue is confidence. On the opening weekend at Brentford, with a weird mishmash of a side, a team that was clearly undercooked, they were hammered 3-0 by much better-prepared opponents. That was not hugely surprising given how sensible Brentford’s transfer dealing had been and how early they had done it. More worrying was what happened the following week as Spurs, starting well before fading, lost 2-0 at home to Newcastle.

Goalless draws against Nottingham Forest and Everton seemed to have steadied the ship. Their biggest problem seemed to be a lack of confidence. They were tentative in possession, indecisive when chances did come. The two goals they managed in their 3-2 defeat to Aston Villa on Saturday mean Spurs climbed above Coventry to second-bottom of the goal-scoring charts, but they are ninth for shots. That should be reason for frustration rather than panic; the goals will come eventually.

But there are more concerning things to have come out of Saturday’s game. The lack of confidence in front of goal seems to have curdled into something worse, a more general mental degeneration. Again, they started well. The Villa keeper Zion Suzuki made a string of saves. And then just before half-time Villa scored a shambolic goal. Micky van de Ven was off the pitch receiving treatment. Andy Robertson, in preventing the ball running out for a corner, gifted possession to John McGinn. A cut-back, a scuffed shot and Johan Manzambi was unmarked in the six-yard box to score. It was a horrible goal to concede.

The second goal they conceded was just as bad. A long punt not dealt with, Nicolas Jackson bringing the ball down, Van de Ven not getting tight enough, a shot that bounced in off Antonin Kinsky’s hand. The third Villa goal was whipped brilliantly into the top corner by Emi Buendía, but he had space to line it up before James Maddison, who had been marking João Gomes, got out to him. Perhaps Maddison could have been more aggressive, and the slight turn of his back as Buendía struck his shot is never a good sign, but this was at least as much a failure of structure.

To an extent Spurs were unfortunate. Robertson might have cleared that ball for a throw-in, or at least got distance down the line, and Boubacar Kamara’s mishit cross could have gone anywhere. Jackson will not always be so deft in taking down a chest-high ball. Buendía, enormously technically gifted as he is, will not always pick out the top corner. But equally, each goal followed some sort of error: the Premier League is full of high-class players who will take advantage of any slip.

Sign up to Soccer Desk

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

after newsletter promotion

De Zerbi spoke of Spurs being “too fragile”, by which he seemed to be talking both of their physicality and mentality. They have players returning from injury. Like so many clubs, they brought in players late. Preseasons have been curtailed, perhaps inadequate.

Where the initial instinct was to be impressed by the numbers and the change of policy, doubts are now emerging about the nature of those summer signings. Is Sandro Tonali really worth £100m? Mateus Fernandes played for a relegated side. Jan Paul van Hecke wouldn’t be the first player to leave Brighton and find his level dip outside that precisely configured environment. Sávio and Omar Marmoush struggled to get into the team at Manchester City. Sávio’s finishing brought just two league goals in two seasons at City and the evidence of Saturday is that it has not improved.

The sense had been that this season couldn’t be as bad as the last two for Spurs. There is no Europe to distract them. The injury crises couldn’t be as bad again. De Zerbi has proved his worth in the Premier League before. They have spent money. And yet this is as bad as it’s ever been. Once a club of Tottenham’s stature could have dismissed this as a blip, the kind of thing that would inevitably sort itself out as the season went on. After the last two seasons, nobody can be quite that confident again.

It’s still implausible Spurs could be relegated, unlikely even that they’ll be in another fight, but those preseason thoughts of European qualification are already beginning to look bafflingly optimistic – and that will inevitably slow the rebuilding of the club.

Paper trail of protests: José Mourinho plays the hits in Madrid derby defeat

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 15:13:40 GMT

Facing Diego Simeone 13 years on, José Mourinho brought a print-out and paranoia. Some things don’t change. Some people don’t, either

There were many questions to emerge from the Madrid derby, which Atlético won 2-1 in front of 70,514 very, very noisy people at the Metropolitano on Sunday afternoon, even if not the one José Mourinho was asking. Like: what year is this? Or: what was Dean Huijsen thinking? Why always Arda? And whatever happened to Vinícius Júnior? How come Koke is still the best? And how long before Giuliano Simeone actually bursts, his atlético insides exploding across the pitch? Above all though, you were left wondering: where did Real Madrid’s manager get a printer from? And how did he get the bloody thing to work?

You could still hear the singing outside when Mourinho turned up in the press room, laid down his glasses and sat. In his hand was a piece of paper. Thirteen years after his last derby, on the Santiago Bernabéu night when Madrid lost the Copa del Rey final and a 13-year unbeaten run against their neighbours, Diego Simeone had defeated him again. The stage was new – this stadium didn’t exist then – but his adversary was somehow still the same man, still dressed in black, and the scene was a bit like old times, a classic. Mourinho unfolded the paper and held it up. “We can save ourselves the bother of the press conference,” he said, “because the story is right here.”

Printed on the back side of an Atlético info sheet were two screen grabs from the first half, one on top of the other. Someone had been sent to run off a copy, some footballing Natalie Harp or the manager himself coming back with a couple of gory, freeze-framed, full-colour closeups of tackles. The first showed Cuti Romero’s studs catching Jude Bellingham’s knee; the second showed Kang-in Lee on Fede Valverde’s ankle. Both should have been red, Mourinho insisted, and he was probably right, but neither was. It should have been nine against 11, he said; instead, it was 11 against 10 because early in the second half Huijsen dragged Giuliano Simeone down for the penalty that gave Atlético the lead and got him sent off. And that, Mourinho said, was that. End of story.

At which point he could have got up and gone, saved everyone the bother of the press conference like he promised, but no one wants that, least of all his president, and that’s the bit he does best so he carried on. Five questions he faced. Four of them were about the referee; so was the answer to the one that was not about the referee. And when he had finished, leaving the paper there for Diego Simeone to have a look at, most agreed: now Mourinho is back, and he’s playing the greatest hits, a hint of the nostalgia that had brought him “home” in the first place, a hint of the conspiratorial mindset too, echoes of him reading out 13 “errors” made by the referee Clos Gómez 16 years earlier.

The “poor ref” – just 41, not an international, and named in advance rather than 24 hours before kick-off – couldn’t handle the pressure, which was “like the 1980s”, Mourinho claimed. The coach, who had already revived his famous “por qué” (why?) line after they lost at Betis, also ran through a list of decisions made by the referee in the VAR room, Daniel Trujillo Suárez – a man supposedly with history – which “make you laugh”. There was talk of “strange things” happening. He insisted he didn’t want to think ill of officials, didn’t want to say the league has been “set up” for others to win, didn’t want to think that these were anything other than honest mistakes – of course not. He congratulated the referees’ committee and vowed to fight for the title despite being six points behind already – if they let us. “I thought I would come back to find a different league to the one I left, but [at Madrid] they told me not and explained why not,” he said.

What Mourinho didn’t say was anything really about the actual football, which might be because there wasn’t much football. The cards might have conditioned the game – of course they might – and he was entitled to insist on the reds, although you could debate Romero’s. But it was hard to avoid the feeling that Mourinho purposely missed a deeper point and revealed a deeper reality, that there could be no escaping the reality he sought to escape: that Madrid are just not very good. That too many questions were avoided and another could be asked: is that it? There was little evidence to back his brief claim that they played well in the first half and were set up to win it in the second – how? – and even if true, it pointed to something limited: wait, counter and it will come.

With the players Madrid have, often it will, but Atlético were aware of that, planned for it; they were aware too of where the damage could be done, overloading Madrid’s left. Simeone’s side took more than twice as many shots and had two-thirds of the possession. They had done so cautiously, it is true, but they, not Madrid, had exercised control. Mourinho’s team had offered little before the potential reds, their first shot on target coming on 39 minutes and from 25 yards, and even less after the actual red, Atlético’s half unoccupied for most of the period except by a pigeon. With Guler withdrawn, their reaction didn’t exist. It’s not easy with 10 men, but there was barely a spark. Even the goal they did get in the 89th minute was an isolated moment and, for all the nerves at the Metropolitano, was followed by more chances for Atlético.

Espanyol 1-3 Elche, Sevilla 1-3 Barcelona, Celta Vigo 5-0 Real Santander, Athletic Bilbao 0-0 Alavés, Osasuna 1-1 Rayo Vallecano, Valencia 2-3 Real Sociedad, Villarreal 3-1 Levante, Deportivo A Coruña 1-1 Real Betis, Atlético 2-1 Real Madrid, Getafe 1-0 Málaga

None of which would matter so much as a one-off, but these flaws were familiar. Madrid needed last-minute Carlos Espí goals to beat Espanyol and Elche and they’re still six points off the top already. It’s not even close to definitive just seven weeks in and Madrid’s rebuilding process has only just begun, but basic issues they have faced for the last two years remain unaddressed; Fabio Capello’s implausible 2006-07 league title win is the only time Barcelona have ever had a lead that big at the top of the table and lost it. Hansi Flick’s team are flying; and right now you wouldn’t trust Madrid to take advantage even if they did slip up. Claude Makélélé summed them up as: “Nothing, nothing, nothing.” Which leaves only this: a print-out and paranoia, a campaign. Some things don’t change. Some people don’t change much, either.

Some, though, do. The last time these two coaches met in a derby, Simeone’s son Giuliano was told he was too little to go to the final so he hung scarves around the living room and watched it from home with his brothers instead. It was late, it was a school night, and he was only 10. He is 23 now and these days he plays for them, a bundle of intensity going at it the way a fan would, and on the day these two “colleagues of war” – as Mourinho called them – met again 13 years later he decided the derby, forcing the penalty for the first and setting up the second. There is some footage somewhere of Giuliano as a ballboy racing up the touchline and leaping into his father’s arms, celebrating wildly when Atlético scored against Madrid. A decade on, another derby day, and it happened again, only this time it was his dad sprinting up the line towards him.

“We give him the ball, he scores the goals,” Fermín López said. Over and over and over again. Raphinha, who is filling in at centre forward, has now scored 12 league goals in just seven games, plus two more in the Champions League. He is five ahead of anyone else already. On Saturday night he scored an outrageously good hat-trick, the movement every inch the No 9, the touch and finishing at ridiculous speed all his, as Barcelona beat Sevilla 3-1. Sevilla went a goal up and were as good as anyone against Flick’s side so far this season but in the end just couldn’t live with them, coach Luis García calling them “stratospheric”. That’s seven wins from seven (eight from eight in all competitions), and 31 goals already, the captain leading the way. And not just with the goals, but with everything, taking everyone on a wild intense ride with him. Raphinha says that Lamine Yamal should win the Ballon d’Or but right now there’s no one quite like him anywhere. That said, Lamine Yamal was absurd at the Pizjuan.

Lucy Letby, the NHS and the rise of managerialism

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 15:06:32 GMT

Pete Dorey believes most public services are thoroughly over-managed, Michael Barrett says whistleblowing policies are essential. Plus letters from Frances Kirkham and Jenny Webb

Tom Dolphin’s excellent article on the failings of NHS management made sombre reading (The Letby inquiry report makes one thing crystal clear: too much NHS management is scandalously poor, 16 September). Yet I believe that most of our public services are thoroughly over-managed, with frontline professionals neither listened to nor respected by their institutional superiors, and at risk of damaging their careers if they speak out about poor decisions, excessive workloads and impossible targets or “performance indicators”.

Like so many of our current woes, the rise of managerialism can be traced back to the public service reforms of the Thatcher governments in the 1980s, and the mantra of “management’s right to manage”. As professionals were supposedly self-serving vested interests, the transfer of power to managers was supposed to increase efficiency and responsiveness to service users.

Yet, in many cases, the long-term result has been the rise of excessive, remote and unlistening senior management, and the parallel marginalisation or exclusion of professionals from decision-making in their spheres of expertise, coupled with plummeting morale. Pete DoreyBath

Dr Tom Dolphin’s article on the failings of NHS management raises some important points about whistleblowing and the regulation of non-medical managers. Hospital board members do have responsibility for their overall management, but how well they exercise their responsibilities depends very much on leadership and the creation of a culture committed to patient care, as well as excellence throughout all the systems delivering that care.

One of the essential assurance measures along with risk management and clinical governance is the promotion of a whistleblowing policy that encourages reporting of concerns to board level without fear of repercussions and with certainty that action will be taken if necessary. If there are still any hospital management teams out there without a clear protocol for raising and pursuing problems, confidentially if appropriate, that should be a matter for urgent action. Michael Barrett London

Yvette Cooper states: “This must be a turning point for the NHS”. The cry always goes up: “Lessons must be learned”. But the carefully considered, evidence‑based recommendations made by those who have conducted public inquiries or by coroners are invariably ignored. There is a shelf in government that’s high up – in other words, fairly inaccessible – on which every such report is placed to gather dust. So the lessons are not learned. Frances KirkhamBirmingham

In the wake of the Lucy Letby inquiry, the NHS will no doubt face a barrage of criticism. But we must also remember what a wonderful institution it still is. Earlier this month, after two agonising days and nights, my daughter died in the intensive treatment unit at Leeds general infirmary.

Throughout, the service we received was wonderful – not just the medical expertise, but the kindness and loving consideration of all staff, from the consultant to the ward clerk. We were always kept fully informed about what was happening, and in the end we were consulted on the final decision to turn off the life support.

By all means, criticise the NHS for its shortcomings. But let us also treasure its strengths, and its potential to help us through some of the most difficult times of our lives. Jenny WebbChichester, West Sussex

To minimise the risks to young football players we should ban agents recruiting under-18s

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 15:01:10 GMT

Phil Murray responds to articles about the precarious path talented young athletes face

Jonathan Liew’s piece (Raheem Sterling’s bleak tale a reminder of absurd path young footballers face, 17 September) is informative and timely, particularly when set against Jacob Steinberg’s report (‘They are very similar’: Arsenal’s Dowman reminds Merino of Lamine Yamal, 16 September) .

The tiny proportion of young footballers originally “signed” by top flight clubs at a ludicrously young age, who then achieve their dreams of a Premier League career, rather than being summarily dismissed at the age of 16 or 17 with the vast majority of their contemporaries, should be a reality check for parents/guardians of all aspiring young athletes.

For those such as Raheem Sterling, Max Dowman and JJ Gabriel, who do achieve their ambitions, the pressures, from coaches, fans, sponsors and social media must be immense. To navigate such pressures requires an exceptional degree of individual maturity way beyond their years, ideally alongside a trusted safeguarding mentor, to guide them through the many pitfalls in their path, rather than relying on cliched verbal assurances from their clubs regarding their welfare. To help minimise the many risks to such young talents, I would also suggest that the football authorities ban any agent recruiting/negotiating on behalf of any player under the age of 18, none of whom need to be exposed to such malign influences in the early stages of their careers.

Without such measures being put in place, I have no doubt that in years to come there will be regular reports of young athletes, similarly lauded in their mid-teens as the next “big thing”, only to succumb to the pressures associated with success in their chosen sport – a bleak prospect indeed. Phil MurrayLinlithgow, West Lothian

Awaab’s law is not working, say social housing tenants stuck in mouldy homes

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 15:00:35 GMT

Residents say new legislation in England forcing landlords to fix dangerous hazards is not improving conditions

Sarah Killick has been battling problems in her social home for months, including mould and damp. She says the anxiety has been insufferable and she has permanently damaged her teeth from grinding them due to stress.

She thought help would come in the form of Awaab’s law, new legislation designed to force social housing landlords in England to fix dangerous hazards, which came into effect in October last year.

But it did not. Killick said her landlord, Clarion Housing Association – the largest social housing provider in the UK – sent contractors to do a mould wash, but claimed they did nothing to address the root causes of the damp. This was despite surveys showing outside cracks, as well as guttering and drainage problems that could be contributing to the issue.

“We have to leave the mould on the walls, because if they turn up and we’ve wiped it, they say there’s no mould, so you have to start the process again. You have to leave the mould growing until it’s really furry and it’s awful,” she said.

The housing ombudsman has just concluded maladministration and service failure on the part of Clarion in Killick’s case, and said the landlord “did not recognise that it failed in its duty to fully comply with Awaab’s law”. Clarion said it did not agree with the ombudsman’s conclusion and would appeal against the decision.

Social housing residents living in homes managed by a number of providers, as well as campaigners, have raised concerns that Awaab’s lawis not working and people are still stuck living in mouldy, damp and dangerous homes.

The law was named in memory of two-year-old Awaab Ishak, who died in December 2020 from a severe respiratory condition caused by prolonged exposure to black mould in his family’s social housing flat.

Suzanne Muna, a co-founder of the Social Housing Action Campaign (SHAC), said that while Awaab’s law had introduced timelines for hazards to be fixed, it was difficult for tenants to enforce this.

If landlords do not adhere to the law, tenants can take them to court for breach of contract, and the housing ombudsman can publicly name noncompliant landlords, order apologies, repairs and compensation.

But Muna said many tenants struggled to navigate the complexities of court action, especially when up against housing associations with a team of solicitors.

“We haven’t really seen any improvement, because it’s no easier now for people to enforce their legal rights than it was prior to Awaab’s law,” said Muna. “The law says landlords have to make things fit for human habitation within these timescales, but it did nothing to address the enforcement gap.”

She believes some landlords would rather pay compensation than spend potentially larger amounts of money on repairs to make properties compliant with Awaab’s law.

In Killick’s case, Clarion was ordered to pay her £1,175 in compensation, provide a formal written apology, and complete the full repairs by 9 November. If it does not do so, it must explain to the ombudsman why.

“I just don’t think it’s going to happen, it’ll have to go to court,” said Killick, who is a full-time carer for her disabled son and also struggles with mental health issues.

Clarion claimed that Killick had repeatedly denied it access to the property. The ombudsman found that Killick’s temporary refusal to allow access contributed to delays, but there was no evidence “the landlord took steps to obtain access to complete any of the other outstanding repairs”.

The ombudsman said that, as of 15 July 2026, it had received more than 400 cases where Awaab’s law was relevant, and there was a finding of maladministration in 97% of completed cases.

Damp, mould and fungal growth accounted for the largest number of cases, and the most common failings were not realising that Awaab’s law applied, failure to investigate emergency hazards within the set timeframe, and not keeping records.

Complaints to the ombudsman take an average of nine to 12 months to be resolved, although its interim head, Andrea Keenoy, has said the organisation is working hard to reduce the backlog, including hiring 77 new case workers.

Muna said it was hearing multiple reports of landlords doing minor fixes, such as applying mould washes and mould-resistant paint, to meet Awaab’s law deadlines but failing to stop problems recurring.

“People are still having to throw out clothes, worrying about the impact on their children – all of the things that were happening before are still happening,” she said. “Landlords might do things a bit quicker now, but that’s no comfort if they’re not solving the problem.”

Khayriya*, a single mother with five children living in Sheffield, has struggled with serious problems in her council home for years, including living without a working shower and toilet.

She said the mould and damp in the property was so severe that she believed it led her children to become ill with respiratory conditions, and addedthat they were bullied at school because of hygiene issues caused by the faulty shower.

Even after Awaab’s law came into effect, she said it took months for problems to be addressed. Local campaigners at the community union Acorn confronted Sheffield council’s housing policy committee chair at a Green party event in July to spur them into action.

Repair work then took place, but Khayriya said she was concerned mould had just been painted over in some places.

“Awaab’s law doesn’t feel like it’s made any difference yet,” she said. “[Landlords] have still got the money, the power, the responsibility, but there’s not enough accountability. Tenants still need more protection.”

A spokesperson for Clarion said: “Resident safety is our top priority, and we take all reports of damp, mould and repairs needed within properties seriously. We are sorry that Ms Killick has been experiencing issues with her home and have been working hard to provide a resolution.

“Over the last nine months, five senior colleagues have been focused on Ms Killick’s case with a dedicated single point of contact liaising with her to try to resolve her concerns. We have attempted to make multiple appointments with Ms Killick to complete works, and have repeatedly been refused access. We have also paid for an independent survey and facilitated an inspection by the local authority’s environmental health team when she remained dissatisfied with our assessments.

“Whilst we acknowledge that Ms Killick remains dissatisfied we do not agree with the ombudsman’s recent determination and will be taking up our right to appeal this decision. We remain confident we have complied fully with Awaab’s law, and have tried to provide a range of options for third-party support to allow Ms Killick to be confident in the safety of the approach that we are taking.”

A government spokesperson said: “Everyone has a right to a safe and secure home, free of damp and mould, and it is completely unacceptable for any social landlord to ignore fixing these issues.

“If social landlords fail to meet the proper safety and quality standards for their property, they can face strong punishments including an unlimited fine, and Awaab’s law aims to further empower social tenants to hold their landlords to account using the full force of the law if they fail to investigate and fix hazards on time.

“We’re ensuring that these rogue landlords cannot dodge their legal responsibilities by working with councils to ensure they know how to enforce Awaab’slaw, and investing up to £50m to modernise courts so that it’s simpler to hold landlords accountable.”

Sheffield city council has been contacted for comment.

* Name has been changed for anonymity.

Sense and Sensibility review – Daisy Edgar-Jones leads sober-minded next-gen do-over of Austen romcom

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 15:00:35 GMT

With Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles as the Dashwood sisters, this fresh take on a beloved classic is not to be confused with Ang Lee’s

There’s no reason for anyone working on a new adaptation of Jane Austen’s Sense and Sensibility to be intimidated by the celebrated 1995 movie by director Ang Lee and screenwriter Emma Thompson, any more than they should be or overawed by Austen’s original novel. Sacred cows are there to be … not slain, but re-invented. The decision to bring out a next-gen Sense and Sensibility, with a new young cast – as opposed to, say, a new Northanger Abbey or a new spin on the unfinished The Watsons – might bemuse some and at first it bemused me, like hearing about a Love Actually remake starring Millie Bobby Brown. But this turns out to be a more downbeat, ruminative version, happening in much cloudier weather than 30 years ago and without the sugar-rush final wedding scene. The mood is cooler, but interestingly austere, sober and thoughtful. There are also some strange casting decisions.

The sisters at the heart of the story, Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, played in 1995 by Emma Thompson and Kate Winslet, are now played by Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles, and frankly don’t look and sound much like the sisters we thought we knew. They look like young women who knew each other reasonably well at uni and are now in a flatshare in London. It is a story of financial and romantic crisis. Mrs Dashwood and her three daughters, having happily occupied a handsome Sussex estate, are forced to move to humble Barton Cottage in Devon when Mrs Dashwood’s stepson John Dashwood inherits their property and effectively evicted them.

Before this can happen, Elinor meets and falls for young Edward Ferrars, a shy and decent young man of a well-to-do family, reticently portrayed by George MacKay. Here, in fact, it should be said that Diana Reid’s script and Georgia Oakley’s direction put into valuably sharper focus something left unstressed in 1995: that Mrs Dashwood (Caitríona Balfe) is pointedly insisting on moving away to the west country rather than endure the indignity of her daughter seeming to be a gold-digger.

It is in the wilds of Devon that Elinor broods unhappily on why Edward isn’t proposing marriage, and where the headstrong, romantic Marianne twists her ankle while out for a walk and is carried back to the cottage by dishy dreamboat-cad Mr Willoughby. The latter is played by Frank Dillane with a certain amount of insidious charm, but also a sort of Uriah Heep smirk. And Marianne does not see the integrity and all-round loveliness of the gallant ex-soldier who is poignantly in love with her: Colonel Brandon, heavily and inexplicably played behind hefty facial hair by Norwegian actor Herbert Nordrum.

Now, no actor would want to follow Alan Rickman from 1995 in the role of Colonel Brandon. But Nordrum, genuinely great in Joachim Trier’s Oslo-set comedy drama The Worst Person in the World, is just an eccentric, stolid outlier in this context; his line-readings feel unengaged and he doesn’t seem to be that moonstruck by Marianne, or particularly enthused by anything much at all. Of course, some of the film’s (worthwhile) intention is to push against envelopes and stereotypes and I quite enjoyed the gender-challenging casting of Eliot Sumner, icily playing Mr Palmer. But Brandon feels uncomfortable.

The scene-stealer is the mischievous, gossipy and forthright Mrs Jennings, marvellously played by Fiona Shaw, who brings up the voltage every time she comes on and effectively makes of it a far bigger role than Elizabeth Spriggs in the same part in 1995. Overall, the movie always looks and sounds perfectly good, though some of the sensibility is lacking.

Sense and Sensibility is out on 25 September in the UK, 15 October in Australia and 16 October in the US.

The AfD thrives in the absence of mainstream parties that speak to people’s daily lives

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 14:59:40 GMT

Readers respond to Carolin Würfel’s article on the reasons behind Alternative für Deutschland’s recent electoral success in Germany

Carolin Würfel is right to see the success of AfD in the eastern states of Germany as a way to protest against west German dominance (I know why many east Germans vote AfD. And no, it’s not an inherited longing for dictatorship, 15 September).

But she overlooks the fact that the “takeover” of 1990 could not have been done much differently. Any path more resembling those of other east European nations would have led to mass migration to West Germany. In that sense the current situation is not the fault of western politicians and industrialists. One thing could and should have been done differently, though. An attempt to build a conservative-centrist party representing the east would have been important, instead of just transferring the western parties. Die Linke fulfilled such a role for some time, but from the left, not the centre. Now AfD fulfils this role from the right.

In Bavaria, the Christian Social Union has exactly such a role and has helped to keep that state a stable member of the federal republic. A similar “Ost-Union” would have been important, but for that the 5% threshold in the federal voting laws would have had to be replaced by a state-based threshold. A new local party in one state, “Thüringen. Gerecht”, formed by former members of BSW, a split from Linke, could develop into such a role, but without federal representation it will be a very long road. Jürgen SchwarzBerlin

Carolin Würfel’s article highlights a dynamic that is not confined to Germany. The same forces are reshaping politics across Europe and the US, and they all begin with a widening gap between political leaders and the people they are meant to represent.

In much of Europe, that gap produces cynicism. Many citizens feel that leaders are driven by party interests, media pressures and broad national narratives rather than the realities of daily life. When people sense that distance, they become receptive to parties like the AfD, which present themselves as the only ones willing to listen.

In the US, the emotional response is different. What I see is not just cynicism but a deeper hopelessness – a belief that no leader or institution can address the problems people face. This is the environment in which Donald Trump rose to power. Like the AfD, his appeal comes from exploiting the disconnect between political rhetoric and lived experience.

Across democracies, people are responding to the same underlying pressures: deindustrialisation, rapid technological change, climate‑driven disruption and large migration flows from countries experiencing severe poverty, state fragility and deep social fragmentation. These are human problems, not ideological talking points. When leaders fail to engage directly with individuals, frustration and hopelessness become political fuel for movements whose primary interest is power, not solutions. Mickey WrightUtah, US

Pakistan jails sisters of Imran Khan before protest seeking his release

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 14:48:49 GMT

Police crack down on family and political supporters of former PM who say authorities are ‘slowly killing’ him in prison

Three sisters of Pakistan’s incarcerated former prime minister Imran Khan have been arrested amid a heavy-handed government crackdown on plans for a nationwide protest to demand Khan’s release.

The lawyer for the three sisters, Aleema Khan, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, said on Monday that they had all been detained and jailed for 30 days under a warrant that accused them of being a threat to public order.

Leaders from Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) condemned the “illegal harassment” of his sisters. Since Khan was arrested and held in prison on corruption charges in 2023, his sisters have been vocal advocates for his release.

His family and party allege that Khan is being kept in solitary confinement and has been denied visits and calls from his family for six months, as well as being allegedly prevented from accessing vital medical treatment for an eye condition.

The arrest of Khan’s sisters marked a dramatic escalation of a crackdown on PTI members and supporters in the run up to a nationwide demonstration due to be held on Sunday – described as a “long march” – to demand the release of Khan and to protest an alleged erosion of democracy and the constitution under the ruling coalition government.

None of Khan’s sisters hold a political position in PTI. Since protesting against their brother’s detention – including by camping outside the prison where he is held, demanding to see him – they have been named in various court cases. This is the first time they have all been held in prison.

Aleema was arrested in Lahore on Sunday as she was travelling to a private club; her driver was also picked up by police. Uzma and Noreen were then arrested at around 3am on Monday morning, after they held a press conference to condemn Aleema’s detention at her house in Lahore.

According to their lawyer, Rana Mudassir Umar, hundreds of police officers later surrounded the family home as more than 100 entered to arrest Uzma and Noreen, as well as their children, grandchildren – who are four and six years old – and the household staff. The house was raided and all their phones were taken.

By 7am on Monday morning, the children and grandchildren had been released but the three sisters were held and charged under the country’s Maintenance of Public Order law, according to Umar.

He said: “They have not been allowed any family access, no legal counsellor access and they were not even allowed to bring clothes or basic things.

“We have challenged their arrests in the high court in Lahore and [are] hoping we will get a hearing soon.”

While Pakistan is ostensibly ruled by a civilian coalition government, the army is widely regarded as the country’s most powerful establishment, led by Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshall Asim Munir, who fell out with Khan while Khan was prime minister. The current government was brought to power in an election in 2024 which was widely documented as rigged, allegedly by military intervention, to prevent Khan’s party returning to power.

Speaking to the Guardian last week, Khan’s two sons, who are based in London and fighting for his release, accused Munir of a “personal vendetta” against their father and alleged the Pakistani authorities were “slowly killing” Khan in prison.

Interior minister Mohsin Naqvi said on Monday that the government would “find a permanent solution” to prevent to march going ahead and shutting down swathes of the country “once and for all”.

Despite Khan’s lengthy incarceration, he is still regarded as Pakistan’s most popular politician and there are fears among officials that large numbers could turn out to support PTI’s march on Sunday. It is being held as discontentment is rife on the streets amid an economic crisis and crippling petrol shortages due to the turmoil in the Middle East and the Gulf. Disgust at the alleged mistreatment of Khan is also widespread.

Khan’s party has faced constant harassment over the past three years, with most senior PTI figures either in jail or pressed to leave politics.

Sheikh Waqas Akram, a senior PTI leader, said the government feared that hundreds of thousands of people may turn out to the long march and “topple the government”, as protest movements have done recently in neighbouring countries such as Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka.

Over the weekend, the capital of Pakistan, Islamabad, was transformed into a fortress of heavy security, with barriers and heavy armed security lining the roads and shipping containers placed to block the entrances into the city.

“Punjab police are raiding houses, harassing families, bulldozing houses and arresting workers and families,” Akram said. “They are going to insane levels to crush the long march and stop it with violence and arrests. This illegitimate government know they can’t survive if people are allowed to protest and march on Islamabad in huge numbers.”

The hill I will die on: Private karaoke is the death of socialism – only a pub singalong is good enough for the people

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 13:56:40 GMT

Community, camaraderie, connection: I learned about all these things while hosting pub karaoke nights. Sticky private booths are their absolute antithesis

On a gloomy Wednesday evening, my best friend and I decided we wanted to scratch our singing itch. We searched for a pub that was hosting karaoke but couldn’t find anything in our area. So we headed to the local branch of a well-known private-booth karaoke bar instead. But it wasn’t just the astounding £18 per hour (per person!) charge or the poor sound quality that made the whole experience so profoundly sad.

Private karaoke booths are sticky little cubicles for people who like singing but don’t want to be seen. They’re places where you pay a premium to avoid rubbing shoulders with strangers or making new connections. The whole point is to avoid exposure to the real world, which fundamentally misunderstands the power of karaoke.

I grew up in a former steel town. Twice a week, my mum hosted karaoke at a local pub, and because we couldn’t afford a babysitter, my sister and I went with her. When Mum’s caring responsibilities for my dad increased, she passed on the mantle to me, aged 17, to earn a bit of cash and keep the family business alive. Sitting with strangers across generations, hearing the stories behind their song choices, sharing rounds of drinks and political opinions, I felt like a sponge, soaking up different walks of life.

This is why when I talk about karaoke I’m not picturing these private, pay-by-the-hour cells. I’m thinking about the working-class pubs and clubs of Britain, where coming face to face with your community was more than half the point.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Pub karaoke is social cohesion in action. The root of socialism is to be supportive of your fellow man, to uphold them and work collectively. While traditional performance art is often expensive, formal and ringfenced by wealth, private education and elite tastes, karaoke was always for the people.

The death of these spaces alongside the rise in private-hire karaoke booths is denying us this cohesion. Unionism was born in the pub – collective thinking comes from being with people, exchanging ideas and belting out the classics. When you hear a plumber from Kettering sing Careless Whisper by George Michael, an angel gains its wings. When an audience comes together to support a person they don’t know, the seeds of collectivism are sown.

We all crave connection, and this can’t be achieved in the cramped confinement of a beer-drenched booth in front of a tiny, curated audience of people we already know. Don’t succumb to the isolationism these corporations are foisting on us – instead, let’s get back to the pub, hand in hand, singing Sweet Caroline and hyping up our fellow strangers.

Kelli Blanchett is a freelance writer, disabled activist and musician
