‘Being in Madness kept some of them out of jail’: how the baggy-trousered nutty boys made a guerrilla cinema classic

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 13:55:06 GMT

From a jail-inspired light sabre fight to the moment a sax-player flew, Take It or Leave It brilliantly captured the hit-makers’ grimy origins. Will the film’s return see it finally honoured as a music movie landmark?

It’s March 1981 and Madness are revisiting the haunts of their recent youth with a film crew in tow. In the 18 months since releasing their debut single, The Prince, the group have become the UK’s most beloved hit-makers, their ascent abetted by inventive music videos that have left viewers of Top of the Pops and Tiswas believing a man could fly – while blowing a sax.

But this new project is something else. Instead of squandering their newfound wealth on fast cars and country piles, the seven-piece have invested in a semi-fictional big-screen telling of their origin story that tempers their trademark “nuttiness” with a kitchen-sink realism suiting their working-class roots. While Take It or Leave It sank into obscurity soon after release, a new 4K restoration has primed the film for rediscovery as a time-capsule of grimy 70s London, and perhaps cinema’s most honest depiction of the challenges involved in trying to get a band together.

The movie was the brainchild of Dave Robinson, honcho of Stiff Records. Back in 1979, Robinson triumphed in the bidding war for Madness, then in their late teens and early 20s. “There was a special connection,” the charismatic Dublin-born mogul says today. “To them I was ‘Uncle Dave’.”

Robinson recognised Madness as more than just prodigiously talented musicians and songwriters. “We were these different characters, jumping around and clowning about, like kids at school showing off,” says keyboardist Mike Barson. “Dave encouraged that.” Uncle Dave intuited this energy would flourish in the embryonic music-video format, hiring Chuck Statler – who’d made memorable clips for Devo and worked quick and cheap – to film Madness’s first promos. Dave took over the reins for 1980’s My Girl, working even quicker and cheaper. “I was also running a record label,” he says, “so we’d have to get the videos done in a day.”

But Robinson never compromised his youthful charges’ imaginative approach. Saxophonist Lee Thompson tested the label-owner’s impressive ability to “make things happen” with 1980’s Baggy Trousers. “I told Robbo I wanted to play sax while flying through the air,” says Thompson, who arrived at the shoot to find Robinson had booked a forklift and kirby wire. The resulting stunt became part of the group’s iconography.

When Robinson began work on Take It or Leave It, he says, “people told me it couldn’t be done, that we were mad”. He tapped the band members and manager John “Kelloggs” Kalinowski for £20,000 each (“the price of a fuckin’ two-bedroom in NW5 back then”, says Thompson), covering the rest of the budget himself. “I had planned to shoot it in a week,” he says. But when Robinson arrived on set the first day he was greeted by “50 guys staring at me, eating bacon sandwiches”. Unlike the videos, the movie was “a unionised shoot”, and Robinson sensed this crew would slow him down. “I had to get rid of them. I paid them all off and they never turned up again.”

Crew purged, he returned to his “typical smash-and-grab, guerrilla-film-making methods”. Frontman Graham “Suggs” McPherson remembers tracking shots being filmed “by a cameraman in a trolley or on a bicycle”; overhead shots involved “someone hanging off a stepladder”. Robinson rarely sought permission to shoot locations, guitarist Chris Foreman describing their mindset as “do it quick enough and they can’t tell you to stop. By the time some jobsworth comes along, you’ve already finished.” It was a vibe they’d learned as teenage delinquent graffiti artists.

Unsurprisingly, Madness took care of the soundtrack, covering Elvis Presley and Fats Domino tracks – often poorly, on purpose, to suggest the roughness of their first incarnations – and performing their own songs during scenes replicating early gigs. They also cut new songs such as Don’t Look Back, a funk track heard during a party scene, and co-wrote the script – what there was of it.

Before production began, Robinson interviewed the group about their early days, boiling his research down to 30 scenes that told the Madness story. On set, the band members would ad-lib these scenes with “great older actors” Robinson had hired to play authority figures. His cast were, he says, “all naturals”. McPherson remembers Robinson screening “Kes, Bronco Bullfrog, Mean Streets and some British kitchen-sink dramas, to get that vibe of just being ourselves”. He also took them to see Raging Bull, Thompson adds, which was “an eye-opener: black and white, grainy, gritty, real. Dave wanted that as our inspiration.”

Realism was paramount. Robinson filmed scenes where they’d actually happened: shabby rehearsal rooms; legendary Camden hostelry The Dublin Castle; the Crouch End home of Mike Barson’s mum, where the group first formed. “Dave used cameramen who’d worked on documentaries,” says bassist Mark Bedford, “and the film was close to a documentary – most things had really happened.”

“We’d done all these psychedelic videos,” McPherson adds, “but our aim now was to capture the dreary reality of forming a band.” The first 20 minutes of the movie are in black and white, he says, “because London felt fuckin’ black and white in the late 70s”. There’s little of the manic visual invention of their music videos, although a set-piece where Thompson drives a van into a low bridge during brief, ill-fated employment on a building site is a masterpiece of comic pacing. A plan for the streets to turn into marshmallow after a wild night out was nixed due to budget – and a worry this family-friendly band shouldn’t let on that some members enjoyed psychedelics.

Nevertheless, Take It or Leave It is a very funny film, much of its comedy coming from Barson. “Mike had a role he could sink his teeth into: the bad guy,” says Foreman. As the sardonic ringleader of this unruly circus, he excoriates band members for bum notes, bad attitudes and, in McPherson’s case, ditching rehearsal to go see his beloved Chelsea FC. Barson’s abrasive manner, which Bedford says was “slightly exaggerated” for the film, sees off McPherson, Thompson and vocalist/trumpeter Cathal Smyth for brief periods, although everyone agrees that without Barson’s “doggedness”, the band would never have made it. “Mike was the engine,” says Bedford.

Throughout, there is a sense that this beloved pop-cultural institution might easily have never happened, for all the everyday, low-drama reasons so many bands implode: internal ructions, the interminable juggle of creative ambitions and real-life responsibilities – and the eternal struggle to find a decent drummer. When the lineup finally coalesces and the artists formerly known as the North London Invaders rehearse as Madness for the first time, it makes for electrifying cinema.

Not least because of the stakes at play. Throughout the film, it’s clear the youthful Madness aren’t Brit School graduates or posh kids slumming it before taking a job at daddy’s firm. Thompson can’t get saxophone lessons because his horn is stolen and its serial number has been rubbed off. Suggs’ chronic truancy and misbehaviour solicit the unwelcome attention of social services, looking to remove him from his mum’s care. One gig ends with an ambush by skinheads in the toilets, the band narrowly escaping a clobbering in their Morris Minors.

On the commentary track for an earlier DVD release, Robinson said: “The system didn’t know what to do with young lads who weren’t nasty but were just trying to have a laugh.” Today, he reckons “being in Madness kept some of these lads out of jail”. The film reveals an edge that wasn’t obvious while the group was clowning with Tiswas’s Phantom Flan Flinger, but surfaced on grittier songs like Embarrassment, Overdone and Not Home Today.

“I was at a crossroads,” nods Thompson, whose dad had been in prison multiple times. He remembers wondering, “‘Do I stick with the band, or hang around the bus stop sniffing glue?’ The pal who got me my saxophone, he was later stabbed to death in the Music Machine.”

Barson’s crossroads moment is depicted in the film, although it’s played as fantasy, he and friend Si Birdsall discovering neon tube-lights, wielding them like light-sabres and evading the coppers. In reality, they actually got caught smashing lightbulbs by transport police and were sentenced to three weeks at Wormwood Scrubs. En route to prison, his police van passed Buckingham Palace, and he saw the bus he used to ride into central London.

“I thought, ‘If I was free, I could get on that bus, go home and make myself a cup of tea. But now I’m wondering if they’re going to strip-search us and hose us with disinfectant when we get there.’ I was scared. After that, I pulled back from hanging out with them kids who were into wild, aggressive things and put that energy into music. Years later, in 2012, we played on the roof of Buckingham Palace and the queen waved up at us.”

“We were all on a spectrum of petty criminality, growing up in an environment of violence,” says McPherson, “though none of us had that thing where you’ve been beaten into wanting to hurt other people. There was a crossroads where some in our gang were definitely going criminal, and we were the artistic side of that coin. Criminality boils down to: are you prepared to shoot someone? And no, I’m not. I don’t think I had the guts for it. The band was our way out.”

Ultimately, the shoot took longer than a week: memories vary, but somewhere between a fortnight and a month. Robinson broke his foot midway through but says: “At the end, we all clapped each other on the back and said, ‘We got away with it!’ We were thinking it’d go on the art film circuit. But it played in one cinema in Camden and that was it. We didn’t get a big campaign from the distributor, which it needed.”

Although the Guardian’s Derek Malcolm gave the film a positive review, and a VHS release sold well to the Madness faithful, Take It or Leave It was quickly forgotten. A couple of years later, after their guest appearances on The Young Ones, that show’s creatives, Ben Elton and Richard Curtis, filmed a pilot for a proposed Madness sitcom. “The premise was that we ran Britain and had to solve some big problem every week,” remembers Foreman. “ITV were interested, but we were holding out for the BBC. Then Mike left the group, so it came to nothing.”

Later, McPherson auditioned for Julien Temple’s Absolute Beginners, but broke his big toe while training with the choreographer. “So that was the beginning and the end of my film career,” he sighs, though he doesn’t really sound very disappointed. “Madness was always my priority,” he explains, “and I’m so glad. If I’d gone into acting, I’d never have achieved everything I did with the band. You can’t have it all.”

While he never made another film, Robinson is still active, organising benefit concerts for the children of Ukraine. Madness released their 12th album in 2023 and recently completed a summer tour. The restoration has them reflecting on their movie, and the passage of time. For Barson, four-and-a-half decades have caused reality and near-reality to blur. “When I try to remember what really happened, I get stuck on how it happened in the film,” he says. “The reality has become inaccessible because that film gets in the way.”

The film is now a time capsule for a bygone age: the band comment longingly on machines on the tube selling 40p tickets and the ability to park your car wherever you wanted. Other memories are more heartfelt. “Gary Dovey, who was briefly our drummer and played himself in the film, was a good friend of mine,” says Bedford. “He died a few years ago, and it’s amazing to see him on screen, speaking and being himself.”

“I was so disappointed with the film when we finished it,” adds McPherson. “I thought it was prosaic and boring. But now – it’s just so charming. We were friends, most of us, before the band started, and we are good friends now. To see our story up on screen makes me very proud. I love those guys. I fucking love them.”

Take It or Leave It is in UK and Irish cinemas from 1 October, and on Blu-ray/DVD from 19 October.

Thomas Tuchel rocked by five key withdrawals from England squad

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 13:39:28 GMT

Palmer, Rice, Mainoo, Rashford and Livramento injured

James Garner and Morgan Gibbs-White called-up as cover

Thomas Tuchel has been rocked by a host of withdrawals from his England squad, with Cole Palmer, Declan Rice, Kobbie Mainoo, Marcus Rashford and Tino Livramento all out because of injury. The head coach has called up James Garner and Morgan Gibbs‑White to boost his options for the upcoming Nations League programme.

Tuchel gave Palmer a high-profile recall on Friday for the beginning of the two-year international cycle that he hopes will end in glory at Euro 2028. England are back in the top division of the Nations League and they kick off against Spain at Wembley on Saturday. They then play Czechia and Croatia away before returning to Wembley to face Czechia.

Palmer has felt a minor muscle issue and, not for the first time under Tuchel, has been forced to make himself unavailable. The Chelsea midfielder, who has started the season in fine form, has made only three appearances under Tuchel. He was left out of the World Cup squad after his form ebbed last season and the head coach spoke at his squad announcement of a fresh opportunity for Palmer. That will have to wait. The 24-year-old has been a virtual ever‑present for Chelsea this season, contributing four goals and two assists in all competitions.

Rice’s withdrawal is not a complete surprise given his workload for a number of seasons. He needed to manage a nerve issue in a hamstring in the second half of last season which also affected his lower back and caused the midfielder discomfort at the World Cup. He has started all of Arsenal’s Premier League matches so far this season – plus their Champions League opener against Napoli. It has been decided that a rest at this point is the wisest course of action.

Mainoo was taken off after 80 minutes of Manchester United’s game at Fulham on Sunday; a move from the manager, Michael Carrick, that led to boos from the travelling support. The midfielder was in the World Cup squad but he was the only outfield player not to get a single minute on the pitch. Tuchel has said Mainoo’s lack of involvement was no slight on him, his ability or application levels. It was, instead, purely down to decisions that Tuchel took for technical reasons. The head coach had promised to give Mainoo minutes over the coming fortnight or so.

Mainoo’s United teammate Rashford was substituted in the 77th minute of the Fulham game and was seen holding the area by the front of his hip and groin as he slowly walked off.

Tuchel has always championed Rashford; he called him up when he named his first squad in March of last year when the player was struggling for form. Tuchel wanted to show Rashford that he believed in him and he has always included the 28‑year‑old when he has been available.

Tuchel seemed to lose a bit of faith after Rashford played poorly against the Democratic Republic of the Congo in the last 32 of the World Cup finals tournament over the summer. Thereafter, Tuchel barely used him until England’s semi-final exit against Argentina, giving him a couple of minutes as a stoppage-time substitute in that game but nothing more. He did play him for the first 45 minutes of the third-place playoff against France.

Livramento was named in the World Cup squad only to sustain a calf injury in training on the eve of the tournament. The Newcastle full‑back had to fly home. He underwent surgery and returned for his club as a substitute against Bournemouth at the start of the month. He had a setback in training before Newcastle’s win against Hull on Saturday and was not in the matchday squad. The 23-year-old is yet to start a game this season.

Garner comes in as a central midfield replacement for Rice and Mainoo while Gibbs-White adds to Tuchel’s options in the No 10 position in the absence of Palmer. Tuchel also has Jude Bellingham, Morgan Rogers and Eberechi Eze as No 10s. The players are due to report on Tuesday to St George’s Park.

‘Jaw-dropping’ El Niño bursts through temperature record months before peak

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 13:25:04 GMT

‘Godzilla-level’ phenomenon is supercharging the climate crisis and will have a huge impact on communities across the world

The “jaw-dropping” El Niño currently heating up the planet has burst through the highest temperature ever recorded for the phenomenon, several months before its expected peak.

The latest data shows the temperature rise at the heart of El Niño in the Pacific Ocean has now reached 3.05C. That is higher than the 3.02C set in late November 2015, the previous high set in the 150 years of modern records. This temperature is measured against the average of 1991-2020.

The preferred measure of most meteorologists uses a 30-year rolling average as a reference and so takes account of human-caused global heating. This metric, called ONI (Nino3.4), is on the brink of breaking the record, just one-hundredth of a degree below the 2015 record. Both metrics are underpinned by data from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

The most recent forecasts predict a peak of 4.0C in November and December, according to the average of 14 different models assessed by climate scientist Zeke Hausfather. That is a level so far above previous events that Hausfather called it “mind-blowing”, while others have described it as “Godzilla-level”. Any temperature rise above 0.5C is deemed an El Niño; above 2C is officially called a “very strong” El Niño – often referred to as a “super” El Niño.

The current El Niño is likely to be the largest in at least 1,000 years and will pile extra heat into an atmosphere in which temperatures are already rising rapidly due to human-caused global heating. This double whammy means 2027 is expected to “blow apart” previous records and become the hottest year ever recorded.

The climate crisis, caused by pollution from fossil fuels, is already supercharging extreme weather and killing people. The El Niño will ratchet up the impacts even further, and has already begun to affect regions across the planet as weather patterns are altered.

“Very strong El Niño events like those in 1997/1998 and 2015/2016 were associated with hundreds of billions of dollars in damages globally – this event is leaving those past ones in the dust,” said Hausfather, whose analysis is published by Carbon Brief.

Prof Friederike Otto, at Imperial College London, said: “This event is a huge redistribution of energy in the climate system and is dangerous because it is unfolding on top of a much warmer, human-influenced climate system.

“So, in many places around the world we will see never-before-experienced heat extremes, with all their consequences on health, food security and water stress,” she said. “El Niño comes and goes, but as long as we continue to burn fossil fuels it occurs on an increasingly hotter baseline, making it much more difficult for communities to deal with the consequences.”

Hot and dry conditions in Indonesia have already spurred record wildfires and fatal levels of air pollution, while India has seen vital monsoon rains curtailed. Drought conditions in Central America and the Caribbean are causing crop losses and a slowdown of trade due to low water levels in the Panama canal. The World Food Programme said in August the impacts of El Niño were likely to push about 50 million people into acute hunger and drive prices up.

El Niño years also see more intense rains and flooding in some regions, with Peru and Chile already suffering, and access to Machu Picchu is disrupted. The Horn of Africa is also very vulnerable to increased downpours, while the southern US is expected to experience fierce rains in the winter.

The southern hemisphere summer is predicted to be hotter and drier as a result of the huge El Niño, meaning greater wildfire risk and droughts in Australia and southern Africa. Typhoons in the Pacific are expected to be more intense, but Atlantic hurricanes are suppressed by El Niño and, unusually, none has yet occurred this year.

While the usual impacts of El Niño are well known, scientists are concerned that the multiplying effect of the climate crisis could shift these patterns. This would make it harder for countries and communities to prepare. The UN World Meteorological Organization said it has launched the biggest mobilisation in its 50-year history to support national weather services to deliver “life-saving” forecasts.

The UN secretary-general António Guterres said earlier in September: “El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters and the world is in the danger zone of extreme weather. The race now is between rising risks and our commitment to take climate action and protect people.”

In the Guardian on Tuesday meanwhile, Prof Bill McGuire said: “What is happening in the equatorial Pacific is jaw-dropping and could well mark one of the biggest global weather upheavals in a millennium.

“It will spawn a string of weather catastrophes around our world.”

He said strong El Niños can have a devastating effect on the global economy: “While the great recession of 2008 resulted in global GDP reducing by around $2tn, the 1997–98 super El Niño resulted in losses of $5.7tn.” That El Niño has already been surpassed by the current one.

Recent research shows global heating is now intensifying El Niño cycles, which then in turn intensify the impacts of the climate crisis. Data from analysis of corals, tree rings and historical documents suggest no El Niño has reached this level in the last millennium, added Hausfather.

“All effects from El Niño are magnified by global climate change,” said Prof Kevin Trenberth, at the National Center of Atmospheric Research in the US. “The northern summer of excess heat and wildfires in Europe, North America and Asia are but a sample of what is to come.”

‘My whole identity was wrapped up in Ally McBeal’ – Calista Flockhart on her smash hit 90s comedy rollercoaster

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 12:12:30 GMT

‘In the street or at restaurants, people still come up to me and say, “I became a lawyer because of you.” But I just went to work and said my lines!’

I was doing a play in New York, Three Sisters by Chekhov. We regularly got scripts sent to us. One going around was written by David E Kelley. I flew out to Los Angeles to screen test, and I got the part right in the moment. It was a difficult transition as I felt very much settled and happy in New York and I had only been to LA briefly, to shoot The Birdcage. I was such a bad driver that I didn’t get on the freeway there for a year. I was afraid of it.

Playing Ally McBeal was exciting and I was up for the challenge, but it was daunting. It was also very collaborative. Everybody fed each other and we all worked it out together. We started shooting in July and were on air in September, so there was this beautiful brief time when it was just ours. I remember that very well. Then, very quickly, it became popular.

David is a genius. What I love about his writing is his imagination – there’s no ceiling on it. At first, I thought the dancing baby was really weird. David was so excited about it but I really did not get it. Then, of course, I realised it was quite brilliant. Ally’s biological clock is ticking, and she’s being haunted by some weird, spooky dancing baby. It’s awesome. By nature, I’m a little on the shy side, so I had to find a place in myself to forget about being embarrassed. I just danced crazy and wild because it was sort of reflective of Ally’s inner life.

In one episode – Seeing Green – I was having hallucinations of Al Green. He guest-starred and I had the good fortune of dancing with him. It was filmed very late at night, with rain on the street, and it was so magical. He showed Ally the moves and I tried to do them. Then he flew away and Ally was left standing there alone. It was beautifully written. He is such a kind, sweet soul.

In terms of the music, I wouldn’t even say that it was part of the show – the music was the show. The minute you heard Searchin’ My Soul, you wanted to live in this life. I really identified with Vonda Shepard’s music and it was very reflective of what Ally was feeling. It was a way for characters to communicate with each other.

At the end of most days shooting, I was emotionally raw – I was pretty much there all day, every day. I was just so totally spent from the rollercoaster of Ally McBeal’s life and where I had to go to get there. In the end, after five seasons, it had sort of run its course and done what it set out to do, but my whole identity was wrapped up in Ally McBeal for five years. My son was about one then and I was really happy to have the time with him, but it was sad to say goodbye to everybody. There’s such a strong bond between us that will never go, even though our lives have gone in many, many different directions.

Sometimes at a restaurant or on the street, people come up to me and say: “I became a lawyer because of you.” Then I say: “No, you became a lawyer because of David Kelley.” It had nothing to do with me. I just went to work and said the lines. He had the hard job.

I had made two albums, but then I got dropped. I was struggling. I was lugging my keyboard to gigs in the rain, playing in tiny clubs. I have been friends with Michelle Pfeiffer since I was 18, before she was married to David Kelley. The two of them came to see me play one evening, which turned out to be the turning point of my life.

About a week later, I got a call from David. The songs that I was playing were from my album It’s Good, Eve and they resonated with the character he was writing about, he told me. David wanted me to sing Tell Him by the Exciters as the theme song, but my manager and I really wanted one of my own songs. So, we played them five of them, including Searchin’ My Soul, and David said: “If you can squeeze that song into one minute, that can be the theme song.” So, we just sped it up and they loved it.

Overnight, I went from playing for 30 people to 5,000 people. We won a Golden Globe, we won an Emmy. It changed my life. But I don’t care about being famous – I just want to be able to play music for people who like it and share that with them, and the show gave me that gift.

I went on to produce more than 500 songs during its five years. It was more like a musical. It was very fulfilling, watching the music come together. When I was 16, one of my favourite albums was The Belle Album by Al Green. At the end of one track, he laughs. It’s so solidly locked into my memory. We were in the studio with him recording his vocals for an episode and all of a sudden, Al Green sings a take, and he does the laugh. I thought, “Oh, my God, I’ve really made it.”

Searchin’ My Soul had the struggle and the challenge and then the breakthrough of the positive ending, the uplifting side of it. The show was a magical experience. I think back on it with such appreciation. You feel that connection and emotion, and it’s genuine.

Vonda Shepard tours the UK and Ireland from 1 October. Her new album, Nine Songs, is out on 25 September

‘I have to keep reliving it’: infected blood claimants being asked to prove eligibility

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 11:48:35 GMT

Claimants having to find decades-old medical records to prove they qualify for compensation despite inquiry’s recommendations

Suzanne Morgan will never forget the day her mother died. It was nine months after she had gone into hospital with gallstones, where she received a routine blood transfusion.

“She went downhill rapidly,” Morgan recalled. Her mother haemorrhaged in her liver, and the next day she was dead.

The family were astonished to be told that she had hepatitis C, and doubly shocked to learn that they couldn’t see her because her body was sealed due to contagion risk, leading them to suspect she was HIV positive.

Morgan, who was pregnant at the time, said: “I went into full-blown miscarriage. I was in total shock. I was hysterical.”

That was 35 years ago, and the family now know Morgan’s mother died because she was given infected blood. Yet Morgan has found herself forced to “keep reliving” the horror through the infected blood compensation scheme. Like many other victims of the scandal and their families, she has been asked to dig out decades-old medical records to prove she qualifies, despite the public inquiry’s recommendations that eligibility be determined “on the balance of probability”.

“I have been everywhere to try and get medical notes of any sort. I cannot get them,” said Morgan.

Infected blood campaigners who spoke to the Guardian shared their fury that thousands like Morgan face being locked out of the Infected Blood Compensation Authority (IBCA) payment scheme due to its stringent approach.

Rachel Halford, the chief executive of the Hepatitis C Trust, said this was “placing an intolerable burden on people who have already endured decades of injustice”.

Victims and bereaved families had been asked to prove “even the most basic of things”, such as whether they lived with their deceased spouses or siblings, she added. Some have had to show old school records, tenancy agreements, utility bills or family photos.

“People feel they are being treated as potential fraudsters rather than victims of one of the greatest scandals in our history,” said Halford, adding that there have been complaints of unfairness after different compensation awards for people with similar experiences.

Halford said the community hoped that Andy Burnham, who has long campaigned for victims of the infected blood scandal to receive justice, would offer his support. “As prime minister, we need him to live up to that reputation and the promises he has made,” she Halford.

Yet Rosie McKearney, a policy specialist at the Hepatitis C Trust, said the community was “shocked” that Burnham had moved responsibility for the scandal from a cabinet-level secretary of state to a junior minister.

Research from the Haemophilia Society suggests that two years since the IBCA’s inception just 15% of projected compensation claims have been dealt with. In a letter sent to the IBCA’s chief executive, David Foley, the campaigners said they were “concerned and angry at the lack of progress”, especially its “unreasonable and sometimes impossible bureaucratic demands”.

The Haemophilia Society is calling for regulatory change to shift the burden of evidence from applicants to the state, meaning that all applicants with a bleeding disorder would be entitled to compensation unless proved otherwise.

Kate Burt, its chief executive, said that the current system was “putting haemophilia treatment centres under intolerable pressure”, with staff “asked to sift through patients’ medical notes to find evidence”, knowing that errors could cost the applicant thousands of pounds.

“This is highly technical work, relying on expert knowledge to find fragments of crucial information, yet centres are expected to fund this themselves,” she said, adding that one consultant told her they work unpaid on Saturdays to answer the IBCA’s inquiries.

Charlotte Evans, a lawyer at Leigh Day who is representing several victims and their families in their IBCA applications, said “the balance of probabilities” was the standard of proof for medical negligence claims.

She said it represented a comparatively lower threshold, which considers a risky procedure that took place at the same time as infected blood was used as indicative that a blood product had been administered.

Instead of assessing all the available evidence to build up a picture of what most likely happened, applicants are being asked to prove beyond reasonable doubt that they received a specific blood product.

“The scheme is supposed to provide a simpler process,” she said, adding that although the government and the IBCA had an obligation to ensure taxpayers’ money was properly spent, “the question is whether those obligations, and IBCA’s understanding of the same, go beyond what the regulations actually require”.

The reasons for this disconnect remained unclear, she said. “It may be that certain individuals [assessing claims] haven’t been given the appropriate guidance or training.”

Lynne Kelly, the chair of Haemophilia Wales, observed a “tick box” approach from the claims managers she had met. “The Cabinet Office is completely controlling the Infected Blood Compensation Authority scheme. It’s meant to be an independent, arm’s length body,” she said, adding that she believed the eligibility criteria was intended to “minimise the amount of compensation paid out”.

For Zena Whittaker, that extra compensation would both give closure and a comfortable retirement, enabling her to stop worrying about putting the heating on.

She is still haunted by the memory of asking a doctor how much longer her son Andrew had to live. He replied: “We don’t know, because it depends whether the hep C takes him first, or the Aids.”

As a haemophiliac, Andrew received multiple blood transfusions, making it more likely than not that he also had hepatitis C. Yet medical records were destroyed when his hospital merged with another.

“It’s just coming up to the anniversary [of his death], which makes everything raw,” Whittaker said. “It’s 31 years since he died and it brought it all back again.”

Luke O’Shea Phillips is also struggling with a bureaucratic nightmare. He was given an infected clotting product as a three-year-old, but because he was not given a liver biopsy due to the risk of bleeding for haemophiliacs, he is unable to prove how bad his liver damage was, resulting in a shortfall in compensation he estimates at up to £1m.

“I wasn’t told I had hepatitis C until I was 15. So just as life was beginning to open up, I was suddenly told what had already been done to it,” he said. “My infection is my life, and it’s unrecognised in every way.”

A spokesperson for the IBCA said: “Missing or destroyed records will not prevent someone from making a claim. We will determine what is most likely from all available evidence.

“Our claim managers work with the person claiming to help them gather information from a range of sources to support their claim. We consider all evidence: medical records, witness testimony, and other family records can all be used to support a claim.

“Every compensation claim is unique, with individual circumstances, so they cannot be compared.”

A government spokesperson said: “The government has listened and learned through constant engagement with the community to make changes to the compensation scheme to ensure the community receive the compensation they deserve.

“The government will continue to be held accountable for its work in the usual ways across both Houses of Parliament.”

Granit Xhaka admits to receiving fake Covid vaccination certificate in 2022

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 11:46:02 GMT

Sunderland captain withdrawn from Switzerland squad

He will be questioned by prosecutor’s office in Lucerne

Granit Xhaka has been withdrawn from Switzerland’s squad after he admitted receiving a fake Covid vaccination certificate in 2022. The Sunderland and Switzerland captain – who was an Arsenal player at the time – has apologised for this “mistake” and will sit out his country’s forthcoming four Nations League matches.

Xhaka is poised to be questioned by the prosecutor’s office in Lucerne next week as it decides whether any criminal proceedings will be initiated regarding the alleged issue of a series of false Covid certificates by a doctor based in the Swiss city during the pandemic. The doctor, who was first investigated in 2023, has denied the allegations.

In a statement issued via Instagram, Xhaka acknowledged he had decided not to be inoculated against the virus. “In recent days there has been much reporting about a matter from my past. I would like to address this personally,” he wrote. “At the time, I was personally very uncertain and had serious concerns regarding the Covid-19 vaccination. I felt deep distrust of the vaccine and was plagued by fear and uncertainty.

“In this turbulent emotional state, I obtained a vaccination certificate instead of clarifying my open questions through the proper channels. Today I clearly see this was not the right course of action. It was a mistake. I am sorry. I take responsibility for this decision, am committed to investigating the matter and am co-operating with the relevant authorities.”

Xhaka tested positive for Covid in September 2022 and the 33-year-old – he turns 34 on Sunday – did not feature in Switzerland’s internationals that month.

A spokesperson for the Lucerne cantonal prosector’s office said: “The aim [of the inquiries] is to clarify whether there has been conduct relevant under criminal law in connection with the possible fraudulent obtaining of a false certification and/or document forgery.”

Should charges be brought, Xhaka could face a heavy fine or, theoretically, a five-year prison sentence. However, the imposition of the latter sanction – or any sort of custodial punishment – is understood to be extremely unlikely.

Given that Xhaka was with Arsenal in 2022, Sunderland have told the Guardian they are not commenting on the matter. The midfielder left north London to join Bayer Leverkusen in 2023 and arrived at the Stadium of Light two years later.

Xhaka, who has been capped 152 times by Switzerland, will now miss the Nations League matches away to North Macedonia and Scotland and at home against Slovenia and North Macedonia.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

The president of the Swiss Football Association, Peter Knabel, said: “Granit Xhaka approached us about the situation last [Sunday] night and told us he would admit it publicly and take responsibility. We welcome Granit taking this step and facing the consequences. We jointly concluded that it is in the team’s interests to complete the entire camp without him. Our priority now is to calm the situation.”

Although the Swiss FA possess the power to hit Xhaka with a suspension from football – something they could ask Fifa to apply worldwide – that scenario is regarded as highly unlikely.

‘I lost my children, and I’m afraid of losing my baby again’: a day in the life of a pregnant woman in Gaza

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 11:00:23 GMT

Alaa lives in a tent pitched on the ruins of her house, which was destroyed by an Israeli airstrike that killed all three of her children. In one month, she will give birth again.

As the war in Gaza approaches its fourth year, this week, the Guardian follows five ordinary Palestinians as they go about their lives. Each will tell the story of their day, revealing the terrible toll of the ongoing conflict.

Alaa Hessi takes each step deliberately: raises her foot to land heavily on the stair above, takes a breath, slides her hand up the railing. Resting atop an uneven mess of rubble, the wooden staircase judders with each motion. Her movements are slowed by the heavy melon of her pregnant belly.

At the top of the stairs, she pauses for breath, then walks on to the platform that once formed the upper storey of her family’s home. A tent is pitched where the house stood. Beneath her feet are the ruins of the house where she raised her three children, Waseem, 10, Mohannad, 7, and Khawla, 5. And where they died, all three killed by an Israeli airstrike that levelled the home.

In about one month*, Alaa will give birth again.

double quotation markThe sound that wakes me in the morning is the buzzing of flies inside the tent, and the noise of our neighbours.

Privacy in the tents is nonexistent, as is safety. Everyone here hears each other’s secrets. We hear people when they go to the bathroom. We can even hear them breathing. The window of my tent faces the yellow line directly. You can see the Israeli army positions from here, and sometimes they fire at us.

My husband and I love drinking tea in the morning, but making tea has become a challenge, because Israel has prevented cooking gas from entering Gaza and gas is extremely scarce. We still rely on firewood and open flames for cooking and preparing hot drinks. Gathering wood and making a fire is enough to exhaust me.

After I drink my tea, I tidy the tent and try to cook as early as possible before the sun becomes too intense. I also hand-wash my husband’s clothes and my own, which is physically exhausting now that I am eight months pregnant*.

Alaa opens the window – a tarpaulin flap at the side of the tent. A hole out into open air. As her eyes adjust to the brightness, it is clear that everything, as far as can be seen, is destroyed. The landscape is a mass of shattered concrete and twisted steel.

double quotation markToday, I have a prenatal appointment, to check on the baby’s progress.

The place is far away, and I walk there – usually there is no vehicle that can give me a ride. It’s 34C, and walking through bombed streets filled with rubble and insects in the heat of the day is extremely hard. The place where I get prenatal care is a tent, not a proper healthcare facility.

The doctors have prescribed me nutritional supplements for my pregnancy. I have been pregnant before, and I can tell this pregnancy is different: no matter how much I try to make up for the nutritional deficiencies and food deprivation I lived through in the war, my body remains exhausted. Food is scarce. My husband buys me fruits and vegetables and refuses to eat them himself, because he can only afford small amounts.

When I learned that I was pregnant, I felt two completely opposite emotions. I was happy that I would have a child, but I also cried constantly because I missed my children – Waseem, Mohannad and Khawla. Everything reminds me of them. When I crave certain foods, I remember Waseem, because I loved those foods when I was pregnant with him.

I do not tell nurses at the clinic about my circumstances and my children who died, because even the healthcare workers are emotionally exhausted. They are unable to offer comfort or psychological support. My story is not unusual in Gaza. Many women here have lost their children.

After the appointment with the nutritionist, I also have an appointment with the maternity psychologist. They tell me to focus on my breathing: take a deep breath, hold it and let it out slowly.

Then I walk home.

Tackling the stairs again, Alaa heaves a blue backpack up to the tent. It contains some of her dead children’s clothes, which she hopes the new baby might someday wear. Many of them were damaged by the bomb blast – ripped, their edges burned, but still wearable. She carefully unfolds a Snoopy T-shirt and a hat with two fluffy pompoms, pulls out a scarf for Castleview AFC – a small football club in Cork – that her son Waseem treasured. “He wore it all the time, even in summer. I would say, ‘Waseem it’s too hot, take it off!’ And he would say, “No, I love it.’”

double quotation markI spend the afternoon with my brother, trying to decide how to store the clothes for the new baby.

He suggests a sturdy cardboard or wooden box. The thing that we are worried about is the rats: the rats are everywhere. We hear them every night, and they always find their way into the tent. I sewed up the place where they entered, and they chewed a new way in – today we found another hole in the side of the tent.

I wonder if we could use rat poison, but my brother fears that then the rats will die here in the tent and spread disease.

For the baby who’s coming, all I want is a safe place where the rats can’t reach. The baby will be so small, and I am terrified for him. I would like to have a proper crib for him, but cribs are hard to find in Gaza now, and the tent is already overcrowded.

What I wish the world outside Gaza understood is how humiliating life in a tent really is. It is difficult, degrading and profoundly inhumane. Death still surrounds us in every direction.

As late afternoon approaches, Alaa scrolls through her photos of her children. The smartphone that holds them, like so many in Gaza, is old, and its screen is cracked – after a long blockade, new smartphones are now being shipped in, but they are expensive, and many families cannot afford them. The children’s voices chime thinly from the speaker. Khawla and her older brother teasing each other. “Mama, I’m the sweet one!” Khawla shouts. Mohannad laughs, calls back: “No – I’m the sweet one!”

double quotation markI only really speak about my children with my husband. He is the only person who carries the same pain and truly understands what is in my heart.

When I become weak, he gives me strength. When he struggles, I try to comfort him and support him emotionally. We spend hours talking about our children – their personalities, the things they loved and the way they behaved. We even visit their graves together.

This place still holds the memories of my children. It reminds me of our beautiful life together before. When I look at this rubble, I remember my children – the life I shared with them, raising them, preparing food for them and teaching them. Everything beautiful disappeared after they were gone.

Sometimes, fear controls me because I lost my children, and I’m afraid of losing my baby again. I hope my new baby will live a better life than the one his siblings experienced, and that he will be safe.

* Shortly after this story was reported, Alaa gave birth to a healthy baby boy. She named him Waseem, after his older brother.

The Houthis’ offensive is the latest spillover from Trump’s Iran disaster

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 10:00:21 GMT

Trump’s mess has rekindled Yemen’s civil war and a years-long conflict between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia

When the US and Israel launched a war of aggression against Iran in late February, Tehran’s allies in the Middle East jumped into the fray. Lebanon’s Hezbollah militia fired rockets at Israel, while Shia militias in Iraq attacked US bases and diplomatic outposts. But the Houthis, who control large parts of Yemen, mostly stayed on the sidelines.

Over the past few weeks, however, the Houthis have changed their tactics and have entered the conflict in full force. They led a rapid advance along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, seizing a strategic port city and several islands that gave the militia control over the Bab al-Mandab strait, a vital waterway for energy shipments and other global trade. Thanks to Donald Trump’s war, Iran and its allies now dominate the Middle East’s two major regional energy chokepoints: Bab al-Mandab and the strait of Hormuz.

And Trump’s misadventure in Iran has unleashed other unintended consequences: it has rekindled Yemen’s civil war, and a related years-long conflict between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia. In recent days, the Houthis have expanded their offensive beyond the Red Sea coastline, targeting two provinces in Yemen’s eastern region, which is home to the country’s largest oil and gas fields. Those areas, including the resource-rich Marib province, are under the control of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, which is supported by Saudi Arabia. If the Houthis can capture those regions, it would be their biggest territorial advance in more than a decade.

The renewed fighting has displaced more than 100,000 people inside Yemen, and forced thousands of others to flee across the Red Sea into Djibouti. Even before the latest escalation, Yemen was facing one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, with nearly half the population – about 22 million people – needing relief aid and protection, according to the United Nations.

The Houthi-Saudi conflict will also impact global energy supplies and prices: the militia has attacked oil facilities and other infrastructure inside Saudi Arabia, in retaliation for Saudi airstrikes on Houthi-ruled areas of Yemen. After the two sides agreed to a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022, there were occasional skirmishes but the truce largely held until mid-July. That’s when Saudi airstrikes struck the main airport in Yemen’s capital, Sana’a, which is under Houthi control. The Saudi-aligned Yemeni government claimed the attack was intended to stop an Iranian plane from landing at the airport, and to enforce an air and naval blockade that Saudi Arabia had imposed years ago against Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. The Iranian plane was carrying a delegation of Houthi officials on their way home from the funeral of Iran’s supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, who was assassinated by US-Israeli airstrikes in the war’s early hours.

On 20 July, the Houthis declared a siege on Saudi ships transiting the Red Sea through the Bab al-Mandab strait, saying it would only be lifted when the kingdom removed its own blockade on Houthi territory. After Iran shut down the strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s energy supplies transited before the recent war, Saudi Arabia was forced to move much of its oil shipments via its east-west pipeline to Saudi ports along the Red Sea. That exposed Saudi dependence on both the Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab waterways.

After announcing their blockade in July, the Houthis fired on several Saudi vessels in the Red Sea, forcing the kingdom to reroute a significant portion of its oil exports to Asia through a far longer and more expensive journey. That alternative route can take ships more than 30 days, and it involves transiting through the Suez Canal, the Mediterranean Sea, and around the southern tip of Africa, before finally reaching customers in Asia, who buy the bulk of Saudi oil.

To make matters worse for the Saudis – and global oil prices – the east-west pipeline was struck recently by a drone attack blamed on Iranian-backed Shia militias in Iraq. Saudi officials were forced to shut down the nearly 750-mile-long pipeline on 11 September, and it’s unclear how long repairs will take. If the network is offline for a month, it could reduce global oil supply by 120m barrels and raise crude prices as high as $120 a barrel.

As the Houthis carried out their lightning offensive along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, Saudi Arabia’s crown prince and de facto ruler, Mohammed bin Salman, reportedly called Trump twice on 10 September, urging him to order US airstrikes against the Yemeni rebels. For now, Trump has ruled out direct US attacks against the Houthis, despite the appeals from his ally and benefactor Prince Mohammed. (After a mob of Trump supporters stormed the US Capitol in January 2021, several US banks and large companies distanced themselves from the president’s family business, the Trump Organization. But Saudi Arabia and its crown prince became a crucial source of new real estate and other deals for the family firm while Trump was out of power.)

Trump’s decision to keep the US out of the Houthi-Saudi conflict is one of the best foreign policy choices of his second term so far, although it’s dwarfed by his catastrophic decision to launch a war against Iran. Trump seems to realize that neither the US, Saudi Arabia nor other Arab states have been able to bomb the Houthis into submission – despite trying for more than a decade.

Yemen’s civil war has been a complex conflict for decades, with Saudi Arabia, Iran and the US supporting different factions at various times. The Houthis, who are officially known as Ansar Allah (the Partisans of God), emerged in the 1990s as a Shia tribal movement based in northern Yemen that fought multiple battles against the central Yemeni government and other tribes aligned with Saudi Arabia. The conflict escalated significantly in September 2014, when the Houthis overran Sana’a, and within a few months forced the internationally recognized government to flee to the kingdom, which shares a long border with Yemen.

In early 2015, Saudi Arabia led a coalition of Sunni Arab states to intervene in the war, trying to push the Houthis out of the capital and restore Yemen’s Saudi-backed government into power. Barack Obama and his administration supported the Saudis and their allies, especially the United Arab Emirates, with US weapons and extensive intelligence sharing.

Despite thousands of airstrikes and a Saudi-led blockade, the Houthis survived the onslaught. Yemen was effectively divided into two states, with the Houthis in control of Sana’a and large parts of the north, while the Yemeni government controlled much of the south and a competing capital in the port city of Aden. After seven years of stalemate, Saudi Arabia decided to cut its losses and agreed to a ceasefire with the Houthis in 2022, after which the group stopped its attacks on Saudi territory until resuming them this summer.

Negotiations over a permanent peace agreement in Yemen stalled for several years, mainly over economic incentives for the Houthis and recognizing the militia’s rule over parts of Yemen. In recent weeks, the Houthis sensed an advantage in the regional chaos and global economic turmoil unleashed by Trump’s war on Iran.

The Houthis are trying to gain new leverage by taking control of their own regional energy chokepoint and capturing more territory from their enemies in Yemen. For now, no one seems to be able to stop them.

Mohamad Bazzi is a Guardian US columnist. He is also director of the Center for Near Eastern Studies and a journalism professor at New York University

The Joy of Six: epic sporting grudge matches

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 09:00:05 GMT

From F1 feuds to tennis’s soap opera love triangle, we run through half a dozen rivalries that have defined (not so) sporting culture

A boxing rivalry so intense that their sons got to copycat it 35 years later, yet the original is simply the best. That the preening, poetry-spouting, monocle-sporting, Jodhpur-wearing Eubank would irritate the rough-and-ready ex-squaddie Benn was hardly surprising. But the depth of the animosity was remarkable.

“I personally do hate him,” intoned Benn, exuding malevolence at the contract signing for their 1990 middleweight fight, shown live on ITV. Eubank, who refused to even look at his foe, demanded “some parliamentary procedure” – but there would be none shown in the ring on fight night. Benn’s ferocity forced the unbeaten but untested underdog to fight fire with fire. Eubank, swallowing blood from a badly cut tongue, rose from a knockdown in the eighth round to stop Benn in the ninth and take his WBO title.

In truth, the two Britons, who came from tough upbringings, had more in common than they cared to admit. But Eubank’s disdain for his profession – “a mug’s game” – antagonised Benn. Their 1993 rematch, which drew 43,000 people to Old Trafford and 16.5 million viewers on UK television, ended in a draw. It was their final in-ring fight but the two have made up, then fallen out again, several times since. We wouldn’t have it any other way.

Drive to Survive would give its right axle for a modern-day Formula One feud this bitter. The motor-mouthed, hot-tempered Piquet once referred to his fellow Brazilian Ayrton Senna as “a São Paulo taxi driver”. Yet Piquet’s dislike of his 1986-87 teammate Mansell raised his insults to the Shakespearean. “An uneducated blockhead,” was his view of his Williams partner, before Piquet tumbled into the gutter when referring to the British driver’s “stupid and ugly wife”.

Mansell understandably bristled at such appalling language and the pair focused so much on their own battles throughout the 1986 season that Alain Prost snuck in to claim the drivers’ championship. In 1987, the moustachioed Mansell won six races to Piquet’s three, yet the latter was rarely off the podium and lifted his third world title. It was their final season as teammates but bridges have been built in retirement. After several TV appearances together, Piquet conceded that in terms of titles: “I should have won in 86, he should have won in 87.”

Sir Alex Ferguson v Arsène Wenger, Brian Clough v Don Revie, Diego Simeone v anyone – manager rivalries are a rich tapestry. But few burned with such intensity as Guardiola v Mourinho, particularly during their two years in La Liga. Real Madrid brought in Mourinho in 2010; the ultimate win-at-all-costs pragmatist to dismantle Barcelona’s tiki-taka idealists. Familiarity quickly resulted in contempt between the pair, who had spent four years together at Barça when Guardiola was a player and Mourinho an interpreter and assistant coach.

“I hope one day he has the chance of winning a brilliant, clean championship with no scandal,” sneered Mourinho in 2011, as he accused Uefa of favouring Guardiola after a Champions League triumph. Cuttingly, he would later claim Guardiola’s baldness was a sign he “doesn’t enjoy football”. Barcelona won most of the head-to-head battles – including a 5-0 league thrashing – but the sniping exasperated Guardiola who called Mourinho “the fucking boss” of the press room, adding: “I try to learn from José on the pitch, but I prefer to learn as little as possible from him off the pitch.” In 2012, Madrid won La Liga with 100 points and a burned-out Guardiola stepped away from management for a year.

Yet the toll was just as great for Mourinho, who left Madrid in 2013. The anticipated rematch in Manchester failed to spark, despite Mourinho’s gripes at City’s “financial sharks” and unfair league titles. Their feud has mellowed in the years since, but it is doubtful the two will be chuckling away on their own Iberian football podcast (‘Pep Talk’?) in retirement.

“I think Serena hated me for being the skinny kid who beat her,” Sharapova wrote in her autobiography, recalling her breakthrough 2004 Wimbledon final win at age 17. Well, Williams definitely hated that experience enough to win the next 19 matches against Sharapova, ending their rivalry with a staggering 20-2 win-loss record.

The American’s relentless dominance, raising her game to new heights against one foe in particular, seemed fuelled by something beyond on-court competition. That they reportedly dated the same player, Grigor Dimitrov, added personal heat. “Hey, if she wants to be with the guy with a black heart, go for it,” said Williams in 2013, while labelling Sharapova “so boring”.

Maria returned serve: “If she wants to talk about something personal, maybe she should talk about her relationship and her boyfriend that was married and is getting a divorce.” But Williams v Sharapova was bigger than any soap opera love triangle. It was a battle between the world’s best player and its most marketable; as if Williams – irked by the media attention paid to her 6ft, blond Russian adversary – had to remind everyone who the real era-defining athlete was. Happily, the two have actually become friends in retirement, with Sharapova asking Williams to induct her into the tennis hall of fame in 2025.

Cricket’s ultimate ‘Ian-off’ first began with a bar brawl in Melbourne in 1977, when England’s 21-year-old rising star Botham got into it with Australia’s former Test captain Chappell. The details have been vehemently disputed ever since. Beefy’s version is him punching Chappell to end his vile pommie-bashing. Chappell’s take is a hysterical young Botham lost the plot and pushed him off his chair, then threatened him with a glass.

They later clashed on the pitch – sledging, bouncers and send-offs – but it is away from the sporting arena that the rage has spilled over. More than 30 years of trading insults came to a head during the 2010-11 Ashes in Australia. Unable to walk past one another in a car park without some sly verbals, the two grandpas – combined age of 127 – went for each other and had to be restrained by their media colleagues. Three years ago a TV documentary, The Longest Feud: Chappell v Botham, brought no resolution with Chappell calling Botham “a coward”, while Sir Loin labelled his adversary “sad and lonely”. Sensational longevity.

Who didn’t the mercurial genius Higgins view as a loathed nemesis? Steve Davis (“I hate him”), Dennis Taylor (“I’ll have you shot”), Stephen Hendry (“Up your arse, you [c-word]”). Yet the greatest vitriol was saved for his polar opposite: snooker’s Canadian grinder, Thorburn. They played for money on Thorburn’s first day in England, which ended, Cliff recalled, with the Northern Irishman “at the top of the stairs with a ball in his hand about to throw it at me”.

Higgins won most of their matches but lost the biggest: the 1980 world championship final, when ‘the Hurricane’ blew a 9-5 lead to lose 18-16. Away from the table, during the 1983 Irish Open, Thorburn lamped Higgins and kicked him in the groin after being told he was “a Canadian [c-bomb] who is shit at snooker”. Five years later, the (ahem) famously clean-living Higgins accused Thorburn of utilising “bags of white powder”, ruining Cliff’s reputation.

For all the fallouts, a trace of respect endured. In 2009, a year before Higgins’ death, Thorburn won an embarrassingly one-sided legends match and was so upset at seeing his rival diminished that he shed a tear as they embraced afterwards.

All the signs say another financial crisis is coming. Here’s why we need to prepare for it now

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 07:00:38 GMT

War, AI disruption and markets in turmoil: the warnings are all there. But lessons from the 2008 crash could help us

Bad stuff happens in September. For some reason, it is a month that has had more than its fair share of financial crises, perhaps because problems that have been bubbling away come into sharper focus once the summer holidays are over. Britain came off the Gold Standard in September 1931. The pound was turfed out of Europe’s Exchange Rate Mechanism in September 1992. And 18 years ago this week, the collapse of Lehman Brothers plunged the global economy into deep recession. This September, there are again reasons to be nervous. There are soaring oil prices, which are feeding through into higher petrol and diesel prices, adding to cost of living pressures. There is a sell-off in government bonds around the world. There is the warning from AI bosses that it would be wise to slow the pace of development in their industry. Mixed together, they are the ingredients for another troubled September. Of course, it may all be a false alarm. It is now more than six months since the US and Israel launched their war against Iran and so far the impact of closing the strait of Hormuz has been far less severe than was expected back in the spring. It is possible the fear currently gripping bond markets will quickly pass, especially if the wars in Ukraine and Iran end soon.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The constant refrain from Donald Trump that oil tankers will soon be passing unhindered once again through the strait of Hormuz has limited the rise in crude prices. Growth has not been hit that much, and in both the US and the UK, AI has been part of that story. There are, though, signs that the war in Iran is having an effect, albeit with a longer lag than originally expected. Markets no longer believe Trump when he says a deal with Iran is about to be clinched. As a result, the rise in oil prices to more than $100 a barrel in recent weeks has heightened fears of persistent inflation and of higher interest rates from central banks. And despite crude prices not escalating, the cost of petrol and diesel remains high, thanks to a shortage of refining capacity. For months, share prices have been underpinned by the belief that there is no ceiling on the growth of technology stocks, particularly those involved in AI. That theory is now being tested and as far as Wall Street is concerned, the recent intervention by the AI bosses was spectacularly ill-timed. Trump’s rejection of the need for tighter regulation on the AI industry speaks volumes. This is only partly to do with the US-China battle to win the technology war. Financial markets now look as fragile as they have been at any time since September 2008, and with US midterm elections looming, the president needs to prevent the AI-led stock market bubble from popping. History never repeats itself exactly. There are similarities between September 2026 and September 2008, but there are differences too. The crash of 2008 was the result of banks over-reaching themselves to finance US real estate. The banks seem to be far less exposed this time, and while some of the investment in technology stocks may have been predicated on unrealistic assumptions about future profits, AI is clearly going to have a positive long-term economic impact in a way that the investment in housing pre-2008 did not. It is wrong to think all bubbles are the same. That said, there are lessons to be learned from the events of 2008. One is that if a financial crisis morphs into an economic slump – as it did 18 years ago – then orthodoxy goes out of the window. There will be no more talk of interest-rate increases from central banks or of the need for finance ministries to slash budget deficits. Indeed, the recent bond buybacks by the US treasury, which were designed to reduce the upward pressure on mortgage interest rates, car loans and credit card debt, were both an indication of how nervous the Trump administration is about the current state of financial markets and a taste of the more vigorous intervention that a full-blown financial crisis would prompt. An even bigger lesson is the need to control what happens after a crash. Last time, the left was caught unawares and allowed the right to seize the initiative. Already there are signs in Britain of the same dynamic, with the chancellor, John Healey, coming under pressure to raise taxes or cut spending in next month’s budget. This would be self-defeating, not least because it would run counter to Andy Burnham’s (to my mind, entirely correct) argument that 40 years of neoliberalism was a mistake that needs rectifying. It would also come at a time when – as this week’s TUC conference in Brighton showed – there is genuine support on the left for a comprehensive strategy to re-industrialise Britain. A range of trade unions – Unite, RMT, CWU, GMB and Equity – made it clear at the conference that they wanted a much more interventionist approach, and a collection of essays, to which I contributed, has just been published, fleshing out what Burnham would need to do to make good on his re-industrialisation pledge. If not now, then sooner or later there will be another financial crisis. People forget. They become complacent. They overlook the strains in financial markets that have been allowed to become too big and too powerful. So while recent events may blow over, it would also be sensible to plan for another September meltdown. Just in case.

Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnist

If you really hate it when music and film stars do politics, here’s the answer: give us politics that works

The Guardian Mon, 21 Sep 2026 05:00:39 GMT

The problem is not famous people speaking out, as they always have. It is the feeling that leaders have failed, obliging celebrities to fill the vacuum

Every time a public figure in entertainment speaks up about politics in a way deemed “controversial”, it is as if it’s the first time that has ever happened. The outrage is fresh; critics rediscover and announce, as if they have just captured an elusive, profound notion, that art should be separate from politics. A form of disciplining is dispensed. Please, Mr or Miss Moneybags, with your preening notions that you have anything intelligent or informed to say about immigration policy or Palestine. Stick to football. Stick to pop music. Stick to acting. Stick to children’s shows.

Even at a time when a political moment has engulfed everything, this response continues to be born again, without regard for history or ability to confront rupture. The horror of Gaza has broken the art world, roiled Hollywood, fractured literary institutions. And still, as Ed Sheeran stands alone on stage following the withdrawal of all his support acts (in solidarity with Macklemore, who was removed from the tour due to a pro-Palestinian speech), he told his audience that he wants his music to be “about unity, not division”. The speed at which his tour unravelled is not evidence of the incompatibility of music and politics, necessitating that they remain separate to avoid that “division”. It is a study in how it is becoming increasingly unnatural to separate them.

Again, this is not new. The enmeshment of entertainment and politics is organic and part of many conflicts and political outrages in recent memory. Vietnam, South Africa, Darfur – all had a cohort of celebrities involved in objecting, lobbying and raising awareness. Figures such as Macklemore or Gary Lineker or Mark Ruffalo or Ms Rachel are not breaking with convention and plunging industries into turmoil and controversy, but partaking in a long legacy of activism that includes, to name a few, Nina Simone, Donald Sutherland, Kurt Vonnegut, Marlon Brando, Mia Farrow, George Michael and George Clooney.

You can disagree with the stances they have taken. But the belief that they are somehow not qualified to take and express them, and that art and entertainment are sacrosanct, is ignorant at best, disingenuous at worst. Public figures are people who have the same passions that everybody else has, and they have politics that they wish to advance with the tools at their disposal. Some people go on protests, give money, write to their representatives; others have a public forum and a profile they can leverage.

They don’t have a responsibility to do so, but absolutely have the right to. And I suspect the reason they are met with such belittlement and outrage by their opponents is that there is an understanding that once politics spills over into entertainment, an uncontainable sort of trouble starts. This is where the separation of art and politics becomes a denial of the role the former plays in our psyches. Artists, writers, entertainers and sportspeople provide escapism, yes, if that’s what you want to get out of their work, but they also channel an expansiveness of the soul. They are fundamentally a collectivising force, one trained on a talent that stirs feeling. That is why you pick up a book or listen to a song or watch a movie or follow a team, to feel something. It is an exercise in being human, often in communion with others.

Once politics enters that relationship, it becomes ungovernable. It can move the parameters of public opinion and discourse in ways that are hard to mediate, so direct is the relationship between the artists and their audience. Which is why the main criterion that renders this activism laudable or not is how much it is blessed by political and economic establishments.

Often it is not a problem in itself; sometimes it is even rewarded. Sheeran himself headlined a concert for Ukraine. Don Cheadle and George Clooney received accolades for their Sudan activism. But when artists’ politics clashes with powerful sponsors, as it did when Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft removed Macklemore from the Sheeran lineup, it all becomes less straightforward, so complicated, so bedevilled by nuance that could not possibly be litigated adequately by dilettantes.

These collisions are an automatic feature of societies in which politics is failing. The outrage in Palestine is roiling culture because it has been so smothered in politics, because the pain and fury resulting from what the world is witnessing has not been appropriately channelled or responded to by a representative leadership – in fact, it has been policed and criminalised. The spillover into every other part of our lives is inevitable. A healthy political culture should view these spillovers not as crude transgressions into private spaces of consumption, but democracy by other means, because electoral democracy has not squared up to the task.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

As long as that remains the case, any demands that politics stay out of – you can insert any industry here – are summoning a world that does not exist, cannot exist and has never existed. In fact, they are asking for a sort of bovine state in which we are shepherded from trough to trough, chewing for momentary satiation on a cultural diet that must remain disconnected from feeling, connection and relation to other human beings. This can be a resonant message in a world in which there is so much duress. But it is an entirely unnatural state that keeps being disrupted by many people looking up from their moments of apportioned relief to be confronted with suffering of such magnitude that its acceptance can only be achieved through a sort of excising of humanity.

The problem is not the outspoken artists and entertainers; the problem is what they are speaking about. I wish that the enduring agony of Palestinians were not litigated by the sound and fury and discursive froth of high entertainment, but this is where the politics has brought us. If you want to leave politics out of it, then demand that the politics do the work. Until then, it will be in your music and literature and film, fighting the coercion and bullying that hides behind concern for purity of art, but is really in the business of making you lose your soul.

Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist
